desc:
'suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and separated the two of them, and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind.' (2Kgs 2:11).

The chariot separates them and the whirlwind does the carrying — two things, and readers usually remember one. Elisha's cry names him as the thing lost: 'My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel' (2:12).

Scripture records only two people leaving without dying, and this is the one it describes.
name: a chariot of fire with horses of fire

desc:
'Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because Joseph had been born to him in his old age; so he made him a robe of many colors.' (Gen 37:3).

The garment is how the favouritism is made visible, and then how the lie is told. It is stripped off him (37:23), dipped in goat's blood (37:31) and shown to his father as evidence (37:32). The same object carries the love and the deception.
name: a robe of many colors

desc: Twisted together and put on his head with a staff in His right hand, as part of a mock coronation the text reports without comment.
name: a crown of thorns

desc: You are as good as dead
name: as good as dead

desc:
'Tell me, what can I do for you before I am taken away from you?” “Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit,” Elisha replied.' (2Kgs 2:9).

**The condition attached is seeing, not deserving**: 'if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours. But if not, then it will not be so' (2:10). It is the inheritance formula from Deuteronomy 21:17 -- the firstborn's double share -- asked for as a son would ask, by a man who was not his son.
name: a double portion of your spirit

desc:
'For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison.' (2Cor 4:17).

A comparison with both sides weighed. The affliction is light and momentary; the glory is weighty and eternal. Rom 8:18 makes the same comparison and declines to weigh it at all — 'not worthy to be compared' — so the text states the relation twice by the same writer and reaches it two different ways.

The affliction is not said to be followed by the glory. It is said to work it.
name: an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison

desc:
'No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations.' (Gen 17:5).

**The name is changed to carry the claim, and the claim is in the past tense** -- *I have made you* -- said to a childless man of ninety-nine. Paul notices the tense and builds an argument on it: God 'calls into being what does not yet exist' (Rom 4:17).
name: a father of many nations

desc: The crowd that followed Jesus to the sea, gathered out of Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond Jordan, and about Tyre and Sidon.
name: a large crowd

desc:
'The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here.' (Matt 12:42).

The comparison is made by way of a foreigner who travelled. The argument is not that Solomon was small but that she came a long way for less, and it is one of the few places the text uses a Gentile as the standard by which Israel is judged.
name: One greater than Solomon is here

desc: The verdict on Esau's wives: they They brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.
name: a grief of mind

desc: the LORD your God, who is among you, is a jealous God (Deut 6:15).
name: a jealous God

desc:
'Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah walked with God.' (Gen 6:9).

**Ezekiel names him in a very short list**: 'even if these three men — Noah, Daniel, and Job— were in it, their righteousness could deliver only themselves' (14:14). Three names, chosen as the limit case of how much one person's righteousness can do for anybody else, and the answer given is nothing.

2 Peter 2:5 adds a description the flood narrative never gives him: 'a preacher of righteousness'.
name: a righteous man, blameless in his generation

desc: Abel is identified by occupation: 'Abel was a keeper of sheep'.
name: a keeper of sheep

desc: Simile: 'like a king poised to attack'.
name: a king poised to attack

desc: Quote: 'a land of utter darkness'
name: to a land of utter darkness

desc: nor the staff from between his feet
name: nor the staff from between his feet

desc:
'John wore a garment of camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist' (Matt 3:4); 'He was a hairy man,” they answered, “with a leather belt around his waist.' (2Kgs 1:8).

**Near enough to be recognised and not close enough to be a quotation.** Matthew has a leather belt, Kings a leather belt, and both put it about the loins. Neither text remarks on the other.

It is corroboration rather than the claim. The identification is stated outright elsewhere -- 'he is the Elijah who was to come' (Matt 11:14) -- and Mal 4:5 is what that answers. The clothing is what a reader notices first and the weakest of the three grounds.
name: a leather belt around his waist

desc:
'Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God's mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.' (Rom 12:1).

Two words Scripture otherwise keeps apart. Every other sacrifice dies; this one is asked to live. The phrase holds both halves of the paradox that Gal 2:20 states as 'I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me'.

It opens the letter's turn from argument to conduct, on 'therefore' — the second of Romans' hinges, after Rom 8:1.
name: as living sacrifices

desc:
'the LORD has sought a man after His own heart' (1Sam 13:14), and Paul quotes it back a thousand years later: 'I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety.' (Acts 13:22).

The verdict is delivered before he has done anything. 1 Samuel 13:14 comes while Saul is still king and David has not appeared in the narrative; he is not named in the verse at all. What the phrase is measuring is therefore not a record of conduct, which is the difficulty every reader of 2 Samuel 11 runs into.

Scripture keeps the verdict as well — 1 Kings 15:5 says he did right 'except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite', which names the exception and keeps the verdict.
name: a man after his own heart
a mighty hunter before the Lord
a mighty one on the earth

desc:
'Life in the villages ceased; it ended in Israel, until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel.' (Judg 5:7).

She says it of herself, in a song, in the first person. Most verdicts in the text are the narrator's; this one is the subject's, and it is sung.

She is also the only judge the book describes holding court — sat under a named tree with people coming to her for judgment (4:5) — where the others are described delivering.
name: a mother in Israel

desc:
'I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.' (Ezek 36:26).

**Every verb is first person and none of them is conditional.** Give, put, take away, give -- and nothing is asked of the hearer in the sentence, which is unusual for a passage about change.
name: I will give you a new heart

desc:
'I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.' (Rev 21:2).

**A city described as a woman dressed for a wedding**, which is two figures at once and the book does not choose between them. The chapters that follow measure it like architecture and address it like a person.

The closing images are the opening ones returned: a river, and 'a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit' (22:2) -- the tree last seen in Genesis 3 with a guard on it.
name: new Jerusalem, prepared as a bride

desc: 'purify for Himself a people for His own possession'
name: a people for His own possession

desc:
'Amos, what do you see?” asked the LORD. “A plumb line,” I replied. “Behold,” said the Lord, “I am setting a plumb line among My people Israel' (Amos 7:8).

**The figure is a measuring tool rather than a weapon**, and what it measures is whether a wall is upright. It is set *in the midst of* the people, not against them, and the judgment is what the measurement discloses.
name: a plumb line among My people

desc:
'The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him.' (Deut 18:15).

Moses is the only person in the text who describes a successor by comparison with himself, and Deuteronomy 34:10 then says it never happened: 'Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses'. The two verses are twenty-six chapters apart in one book.

Peter quotes it at Acts 3:22 and Stephen at 7:37, both applying it.
name: a prophet like me from among your brothers

desc: Kept as a saying rather than folded into `redemption`, because the two Gospels say 'for many' and 1 Timothy says 'for all', and that difference is the whole of a long argument. Recording it as one concept would settle by tidying what the verses leave open.
name: a ransom for many

desc: "Jesus got up and slipped out to a solitary place to pray".
name: a solitary place

desc: You have brought trouble upon me by making me a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the people of this land
name: a stench to the inhabitants of the land

desc:
'After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire came a still, small voice.' (1Kgs 19:12).

The passage is built entirely out of denials. A great wind, an earthquake and a fire are each named and each followed by the LORD was not in it — three standard signs of presence, ruled out in three clauses. What is left is defined only by being none of them.
name: a still small voice

desc:
'So this is what the Lord GOD says: See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken.' (Isa 28:16).

Held as a saying in its own right because the New Testament quotes it as one: 'it stands in Scripture: See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone' (1Pet 2:6). Rom 9:33 quotes it with 'As it is written' and fuses it with the stone of stumbling of Isa 8:14, so the two halves of that verse come from two places.
name: I lay a stone in Zion

desc:
'And He will be a sanctuary-but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, to the dwellers of Jerusalem a trap and a snare.' (Isa 8:14).

Quoted at Rom 9:33, where it completes a sentence begun from Isa 28:16, and again at 1Pet 2:8 where it is set against the head of the corner in the verse before. In Isaiah the sanctuary and the snare are the same 'he', which is the shape the New Testament keeps.
name: a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense

desc: I am a foreigner and an outsider among you
name: a foreigner and an outsider

desc:
'so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed-and a sword will pierce your soul as well.' (Luke 2:35).

Said to her in the temple, eight days into the child's life, by an old man who had come to see the Lord's Christ before he died. It sits in brackets in the middle of a sentence about the child.

The text never says what the sword was, and never refers to the saying again.
name: a sword will pierce your soul

desc: Never identified. The chapter says what it was for -- 'to keep me from becoming conceited' -- and not what it was.
name: a thorn in my flesh

desc: Cain is identified by occupation: 'Cain was a tiller of the soil'.
name: a tiller of the soil

aka: shall not cease from yielding fruit
desc: Jeremiah 17:8 and Psalm 1:3 are the same figure with the same conclusion -- the tree does not fail because of where it is planted, not because of what it does.
name: like a tree planted by the waters

desc:
'Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.' (Isa 7:14), quoted at Matt 1:23.

The first of Matthew's fulfilment citations and the one that sets the formula: 'All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet:' (Matt 1:22). Isaiah's setting is a sign offered to Ahaz in a war; Matthew does not mention the war, and quotes the sign.
name: the virgin will be with child

desc: the girl was who had not had relations with any man (Gen 24:16).
name: a virgin who had not had relations with any man

desc:
'whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.' (John 4:14).

**The longest recorded conversation Jesus has with anybody in the gospels is with a Samaritan woman at a well**, and she does most of the talking. Her reply to the figure is practical: 'give me this water so that I will not get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water' (4:15).

She then becomes the first person in John to bring a town to him, and the question she uses is a careful one: 'is not this the Christ?' (4:29).
name: a fount of water springing up to eternal life

desc:
'Then I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war.' (Rev 19:11).

This rider is named three times in six verses — Faithful and True, The Word of God (19:13), and KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS written on his thigh (19:16). The rider on the white horse at 6:2 is named nothing at all.

That difference is the whole of the argument about whether they are the same figure.
name: a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True

desc: Son of Amram and Jochebed; Moses' elder brother; first high priest of Israel.
name: Aaron

desc:
'saw that Aaron's staff, representing the house of Levi, had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds' (Num 17:8) -- twelve rods laid up overnight, one for each tribe, and only one alive in the morning.

**Kept as a sign rather than a relic**: 'Put Aaron's staff back in front of the Testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebellious' (17:10). Hebrews 9:4 places it inside the ark with the manna and the tables.

It answers Korah directly. The question of chapter 16 was who may come near, and chapter 17 settles it by letting a dead stick do the arguing.
name: Aaron's staff

desc: Mountain range east of the Jordan, before Nebo, where the Lord told Moses to view the promised land before his death (Num 27:12; 33:47).
name: Abarim

desc:
'Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You.' (Mark 14:36).

Three occurrences in Scripture and no more: Jesus in Gethsemane, and twice in Paul — Rom 8:15 and Gal 4:6. Four things are true of all three, and together they are why this is held as a title rather than folded into the Father's names.

It never stands alone. Every occurrence is 'Abba, Father' — the Aramaic kept and translated in the same breath. A name used as an alias is usable by itself; this one is not.

All three are vocative. Nobody in Scripture says Abba did anything. They say it to him. It is what he is called when he is being called, not when he is being described.

All three are cries. Gethsemane; 'not a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear' (Rom 8:15); 'crying out, Abba, Father!' (Gal 4:6).

The address is transferred, and Galatians says how. Mark 14:36 is the Son's word. Rom 8:15 and Gal 4:6 put it in the mouths of believers, and Gal 4:6 gives the mechanism outright: 'God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, Abba, Father!.' What is claimed is not that they have found a name for God but that the Son's own address has been given them.

Is it a term of affection? Widely read that way, and the text does not say so. What it does say is what the cry is set against: 'you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!' (Rom 8:15), and 'because you are sons' (Gal 4:6). Bondage and fear on one side, sonship on the other, with the word on the second side both times. That is the frame the text puts around it. Whether the Aramaic itself carried the warmth of a child's word for a father is a question about first-century Aramaic, not about this text.
disambiguation: the Aramaic address kept untranslated in all three of its occurrences and paired with 'Father' in each. Held as a title of its own rather than only as one of [[the_father]]'s names, because it is never used to refer to him and only ever to call him
name: Abba

The phrase appears once in Scripture and is never explained. It is inside a story Jesus tells, which is itself the only place the text describes the state of the dead in any detail, and the details are all in the mouth of a parable's characters.

Whether it describes a place, a condition or a figure of speech is argued from this one verse.

desc:
'for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus' (Rom 3:23-24).

**The hinge, and it is one sentence.** v23 closes the case Paul has been building since Rom 1:18 -- and closes it against everybody, Jew and Gentile alike, with no exception offered. v24 begins with a participle, not a new sentence: the verdict and the remedy are grammatically joined.

Three verses earlier the alternative is ruled out: 'no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law' (Rom 3:20). What replaces it is named as free and as grace, and the same argument reaches its collision six chapters later at the stone laid in Zion (Rom 9:32-33).

'Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made.' (John 1:3).

Said twice in one verse, positively and then negatively, which leaves no remainder. v10 applies it to the world in particular and adds the outcome: 'the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him.'

Genesis 1 has God create by speaking — 'And God said, Let there be light' — and John has the making done by the Word. The text never joins those two sentences; a reader who does is taking a step, and it is a short one.

desc:
'Just then the angel of the LORD called out to him from heaven' (Gen 22:11), one of many appearances under this title; the first is to Hagar at the spring (Gen 16:7).

Scripture speaks of him in two ways and does not settle which is meant. At Genesis 22:15-16 he speaks in the first person: 'By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD'; at 2 Samuel 24:16 he is distinguished from the LORD, who speaks to him. Whether he is the LORD himself, a messenger who speaks for him, or a title used of more than one figure, the text does not say.

Where he is spoken of, or is answered, as the LORD or as God: Hagar gave a name 'to the LORD who had spoken to her': 'You are the God who sees me' (Gen 16:13); at the bush 'the angel of the LORD appeared', and then 'God called out to him from within the bush' (Exod 3:2, 4); in Judges 6 the narrator says 'the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon' (6:12), then 'The LORD turned to him and said' (6:14), and Gideon cries 'Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!' (6:22); Manoah, who 'did not know that it was the angel of the LORD' (Judg 13:16) and realized it afterwards (13:21), says 'We have seen God!' (13:22). Where he is distinguished from the LORD: 'if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD' (Judg 13:16); the LORD says to the angel, 'Enough! Withdraw your hand now!' (2 Sam 24:16); the angel of the LORD asks, 'How long, O LORD of Hosts?' (Zech 1:12).
name: the angel of the Lord

Luke gives her more identifying detail than he gives most men in the chapter — a father, a tribe, a marriage of seven years, eighty-four years of widowhood, and a practice: 'She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying' (2:37).

Simeon in the same scene gets a speech the church has recited for centuries; Anna gets 'she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem' (2:38), and what she said is not recorded. desc:
'Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve ... but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' (Josh 24:15).

**The choice is offered as genuinely open and the alternatives are named** -- the gods the fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites. It is the closing speech of his life, and the commitment he makes is for a household rather than a nation.
name: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD

desc:
'Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,' (John 3:14).

The thing chosen is a brass copy of the animal that was killing them, and looking at it was the cure. Jesus makes it a figure of himself in one sentence, three verses before John 3:16.

Hezekiah 'demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it' (2Kgs 18:4). The same object is a cure, a type and an idol in three different places.
name: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness

desc:
'Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel' (Jer 18:6).

The figure is about remaking rather than making. The vessel in 18:4 is marred in the potter's hand and he makes it again — the point of the sign is the second attempt, and the chapter goes on to make the outcome conditional on what the nation does (18:7-10).

Paul uses the same figure at Romans 9:21 to argue something the conditional clauses here do not obviously support.
name: Just like clay in the potter's hand

desc:
'As it was in the days of Noah, so will it be at the coming of the Son of Man.' (Matt 24:37).

**What the comparison rests on is ordinariness, not wickedness.** The next verse lists eating, drinking, marrying and giving in marriage -- nothing condemned -- and the point made is that they 'knew not until the flood came' (24:39).
name: As it was in the days of Noah

desc:
'He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.' (Matt 3:11), spoken by John the Baptist about someone not yet named.

Four writers use the phrase and it is always a contrast with water. John sets it against his own baptism; Acts 1:5 repeats him almost word for word — 'John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit' — and Acts 2:4 is the report that it happened. Paul takes it somewhere else entirely: 'in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body' (1Cor 12:13), where the thing entered is not water and not the Spirit but the church.

The fire of Matthew 3:11 is the only element the promise names besides the Spirit, and Acts 2:3 supplies it: 'tongues like flames of fire that separated'. Whether Matthew's fire is that fire or the judgement of the next verse is a real question and the text leaves it open.

Against those, Matthew 21:19 is the fig tree with leaves only, and Luke 13:6 the one given another year.

desc:
'Truly, truly, I tell you,” Jesus declared, “before Abraham was born, I am!' (John 8:58).

The next verse is the evidence for how it was heard: 'they picked up stones to throw at Him' (8:59). The text does not say what the offence was here, but it does at John 10:33 in the same pattern: 'We are not stoning You for any good work, said the Jews, but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, declare Yourself to be God.'

Whether this reaches back to Exodus 3:14 is the question, and the text does not answer it. The two sayings are joined here because the words are the same words and readers have argued over them for centuries — not because Scripture states a connection. It does not. No verse quotes one at the other.

What can be said plainly: the Greek behind both is not held here, the Septuagint is not either, and the whole weight of the reading rests on wording in translation.
name: before Abraham was born, I am!

desc:
'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations.' (Jer 1:5).

His answer is an objection: 'Ah, Lord GOD, I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child!' (1:6). It is the opposite response to Isaiah's, to a call that is stated more absolutely.
name: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you

desc:
'before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times' (Matt 26:34), and the report of it: 'Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken ... and he went outside and wept bitterly' (26:75).

One of very few predictions in Scripture whose fulfilment is narrated in the same book, at the same length, with the same words. Luke adds the detail the others leave out: 'the Lord turned and looked at Peter' (22:61).
name: before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times

desc:
'Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him' (Isa 42:1), quoted at Matt 12:18 as 'Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him'.

The longest of Matthew's citations -- it runs to four verses (12:18-21) -- and it is quoted to explain why Jesus told those he healed not to make him known. The words about the soul being well pleased are the words of the voice at the baptism (Matt 3:17).
name: Here is My Servant

desc:
'I am the Lord's servant,” Mary answered. “May it happen to me according to your word.' (Luke 1:38).

It is an answer, and the text records the question it answers. Gabriel has just told her what will happen; she asks one practical question at 1:34 and then says this. The whole of her reply is eleven words and none of them is a condition.

The angel's greeting — 'Blessed are you among women' (1:28) — and her own reading of it — 'From now on all generations will call me blessed' (1:48) — are among the most contested sentences in Scripture, and the text records that they were said.
name: I am the Lord's servant

desc:
'The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' (John 1:29).

Said twice on consecutive days, and the second time it costs him two disciples, who leave him and follow Jesus (1:36-37). The text reports that without comment.
name: Look, the Lamb of God

desc:
'so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God,' (Col 1:10).

The one place the text puts the two words in a single phrase. Fruit and works run through the letters as separate vocabularies — Gal 5:22 calls the Spirit's output fruit and never works, and Eph 2:9-10 argues about works without once saying fruit. Reading the two as one thing is a step the reader takes, not a step Galatians or Ephesians takes.

Colossians takes it. So does Titus, from the other end: 'our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful.' (Titus 3:14). And Eph 5:11 gives the negative of the same pairing, 'the unfruitful works of darkness'.

Held as its own saying because it is the joint. Anyone tracing the Spirit's fruit toward the works believers were created for passes through here, and if they do not, they are supplying the link themselves.
name: bearing fruit in every good work

desc:
'no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again' (John 3:3), restated at 3:5 as 'born of water and the Spirit' and pressed at 3:7: 'Do not be amazed that I said, “You must be born again.”'

The exchange is built on a misunderstanding the text keeps. Nicodemus takes it literally — 'How can a man be born when he is old ... Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time?' (3:4) — and Jesus does not correct the reading so much as go past it, drawing the line at 3:6 between what is born of the flesh and what is born of the Spirit.

The saying is recorded rather than a doctrine because that is what the text supplies: three statements of it, one objection, and a figure. What being born again consists of is not stated here.

The name is a translation choice. The ASV reads 'born anew' at 3:3 and 3:7 where older versions read 'born again', and the underlying word carries both senses — a second time, and from above. Nicodemus answers as though it meant the first, which is what makes the misunderstanding work, and a reader who knows only one of the two English renderings sees only half of why.

Two more differences in the same conversation. At 3:2 the older versions have 'miracles' and the ASV 'signs' — and signs is a structural word in this gospel, which numbers them. At 3:10 the older versions have 'a master' and the ASV 'the teacher of Israel', definite, which makes the rebuke sharper than it reads here.
name: you must be born again

desc:
'Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life' (Rom 6:3-4).

This is the passage that joins the whole cluster, and it does the joining itself. A death, a burial, a raising, and a new life, in two verses, with the believer put through each in turn. Everything else in this area is a reader assembling pieces; here Scripture assembles them.

6:5 states the comparison outright — 'For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection' — and its two terms are both events rather than things.

desc:
'the bush ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed' (Exod 3:2), and Moses turning aside to see 'Why is the bush not burning up' (3:3).

The text refers back to it as a place in the text rather than a place on the ground: Mark 12:26 says 'have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him', naming a passage by its scene.

The text itself speaks of it as a place: 'the place where you are standing is holy ground' (Exod 3:5), and Deuteronomy 33:16 blesses by 'the goodwill of Him who dwelt in the burning bush'. That puts it with Mamre and Peniel — a named locale that is not a settlement — rather than with the rod and the tables.

desc:
'Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This is why the ancients were commended' (Heb 11:1-2).

Hebrews 11:1 is a definition of faith.

The chapter is a template repeated twenty times. Twenty of forty verses open "by faith" or "through faith", each attaching the same word to a different person and a different deed. The variable slot is the person; the constant is the claim about why they acted.

It ends by taking the reward away from all of them: 'These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised' (11:39). The chapter is a list of people commended for trusting something that did not arrive in their lifetimes.

Three things it does that the Old Testament does not. Genesis says Abel's offering was accepted and does not say why (Gen 4:4-5); Hebrews supplies faith as the reason. Genesis 18:12 has Sarah laugh at the promise; Hebrews names her among the faithful and does not mention it. Genesis 27 has Isaac's blessing obtained by deception; Hebrews records the blessing without it. This chapter is a reading of the older books, and a generous one.
name: the ancients were commended

desc:
'For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast' (Eph 2:8-9).

The verse that most of the faith-and-works argument is conducted on, and it is built from three negations — not of yourselves, not by works, so that no one can boast. What "that" refers to in 'that not of yourselves' has been read as the faith, the grace and the whole transaction.
name: it is by grace you have been saved through faith

desc:
'In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.' (Matt 13:14), from Isa 6:9.

Isaiah's wording is an instruction -- 'Go and tell this people, Be ever hearing, but never understanding' -- and Matthew's is a description of what happens. It is quoted to explain why Jesus taught in parables, immediately before another fulfilment citation about parables at 13:35.
name: You will be ever hearing but never understanding

desc:
'I would like to learn just one thing from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?' (Gal 3:2), and again in the same form at v5.

**The letter's question, asked twice.** It puts the Spirit, the works of the law and faith into one sentence, which is why the argument of Galatians 5 is the argument of Galatians 3 continued: the flesh-and-Spirit contrast of chapter 5 is the law-and-faith contrast of chapters 2 and 3 carried into conduct.

The same opposition drives Rom 9:32 -- 'their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works' -- where what it collides with is the stone laid in Zion.
name: by hearing with faith

desc:
'As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.' (Jas 2:24), following 'faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead' (Jas 2:17).

Set beside Eph 2:8-9 without resolving it. Paul: saved by grace through faith, 'not by works, so that no one can boast'. James: 'by his deeds and not by faith alone'. Both use faith and works, and they are not obviously saying the same thing.

The two are placed where a reader meets both, and neither is decided between. Readings that reconcile them exist and are readings; the text states the two and does not state the reconciliation.
name: a man is justified by his deeds

desc:

desc:
'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom' (Prov 9:10).

Two senses that the text sets against each other, and a reader meeting only one will misread the other. It is the beginning of wisdom in Proverbs and the thing love expels in 1 John 4:18: 'perfect love drives out fear ... The one who fears has not been perfected in love'. The text holds both and joins neither.
name: fear

desc:
A construction rather than a phrase. Two negated imperatives about fear, then a reason introduced by for, and the reason is presence.

Don’t be afraid        |  Don’t you be afraid
Don’t be dismayed      |  Don’t be dismayed
for the LORD your God  |  for I am with you
  is with you          |

Joshua 1:9 on the left, Isaiah 41:10 on the right. The phrase layer cannot join them: what they share is 'don’t' and 'for', which are function words, and nothing else.

Run as a shape, the text gives eleven. Beyond the two above: Genesis 26:24 to Isaac, Deuteronomy 20:1 before battle, Deuteronomy 31:6 from Moses to Israel, 1 Chronicles 28:20 from David to Solomon, 2 Chronicles 20:17, Isaiah 43:5, Jeremiah 1:8 at his call, Jeremiah 42:11 about the king of Babylon, and Jeremiah 46:28.

Two of them are the same charge handed down. Moses says it to Israel at Deuteronomy 31:6, Joshua is given it at Joshua 1:9, and David says it to Solomon at 1 Chronicles 28:20 in almost the same words — 'Be strong and courageous ... He will neither fail you nor forsake you'. A formula for handing over a task.

Philippians 4:6-7, 1 Peter 5:7 and John 14:27 are read by many as the same message, and this construction finds none of them. Philippians replaces the second negation with a positive instruction and moves the promise into the next verse; 1 Peter compresses the whole thing to a participle and a clause, keeping only the for; John 14:27 inverts the order and gives the promise first.

That is worth stating rather than fixing. A detector loosened until it caught all of them catches fifty-four verses, most of which are about something else entirely. The Old Testament repeats a form; the New Testament varies it.
name: Do not be afraid, for I am with you

desc:
'In all, then, there were fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the exile to Babylon, and fourteen from the exile to the Christ.' (Matt 1:17).

The text divides its own history, explicitly, at named points. This is a text stating its own structure and giving the pivots — Abraham, David, the carrying away into Babylon, Christ. Three of the four are people and the fourth is a national catastrophe.

Matt 1:1 sets the same frame in one line before the list begins: 'Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.'

Two genealogies of the same line disagree, and the text carries both. Matt 1:8 reads 'Joram the father of Uzziah'; 1Chr 3:11-12 puts Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah between them. Three names are present in Chronicles and absent from Matthew, and the identification that makes this visible — Uzziah with Azariah — rests on 2Kgs 14:21 and 2Chr 26:1 describing one coronation twice, same age and same father, under two names.

Matthew states the count as fourteen and does not say how it was arrived at. The text offers no reading that accounts for the difference. Both lines are held with their own citations, and a reader who counts finds what a reader who counts finds.

Look, I know that you are a beautiful woman

desc: Please say you are my sister, so that I will be treated well for your sake, and on account of you my life will be spared.

desc: "So when Abram entered Egypt" resumes narration; turns on "The LORD, however, afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues."
name: Sarai Taken and Pharaoh Plagued

desc: Speaker changes: "So Pharaoh summoned Abram and asked, What have you done to me?"
name: Pharaoh's Rebuke and Dismissal

I will make you into a great nation
I will bless those who bless you

name: Abram Journeys Through Canaan and Builds Altars
I will give this land to your offspring

name: God at Gen 13:14

desc: For all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever
name: God at Gen 13:15

desc: I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if one could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted
name: God at Gen 13:16

desc: Get up and walk around the land, through its length and breadth, for I will give it to you
name: God at Gen 13:17

desc: "So Abram moved his tent" -- narrative resumes after the speech and closes with "built an altar to the LORD."
name: Abram settles at Mamre and builds an altar

desc: "So Abram went up out of Egypt" opens a travel itinerary that closes at "the place of the altar... there Abram called on the name of the Lord."
name: Abram returns from Egypt to Bethel

name: The land cannot hold them both

name: Abram offers Lot the choice

desc: The words Abram spoke to Lot: Let there be no strife... After all, we are brothers. Is not the whole land before you? ... If you go to the left, I will go to the right...
name: Abraham at Gen 13:8

desc: New actor enters: "Then an escapee came and reported this to Abram the Hebrew"; closes with "He retrieved all the goods, as well as his relative Lot"
name: Abram's Rescue of Lot

desc: Scene shifts to the return: "The king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter"; "Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine" and blesses; ends "Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything"

desc: New speaker and dialogue: "The king of Sodom said to Abram, Give me the people"; answered by "But Abram replied to the king of Sodom"

Abram's answer to the king of Sodom

desc: Time marker and change of state: "As the sun was setting, Abram fell into a deep sleep, and suddenly great terror and darkness overwhelmed him" followed by the speech "Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own"; ends with the reason clause "for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."

desc: God's speech to Abram in Gen 15:13

name: the LORD's word about judgment and coming out

name: the LORD's word about Abraham's end

name: the LORD's word about the fourth generation

name: the LORD's covenant saying

name: the nations listed in Gen 15:19

name: The promise of a son and Abram's faith

desc: Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward.

desc: the list of peoples in Gen 15:20
name: the nations listed in Gen 15:20

desc: the list of peoples in Gen 15:21
name: the nations listed in Gen 15:21

name: Abraham at Gen 15:2

desc: Behold, You have given me no offspring, so a servant in my household will be my heir.
name: Abraham at Gen 15:3

desc: This one will not be your heir, but one who comes from your own body will be your heir.
name: God at Gen 15:4

desc: Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able
name: God at Gen 15:5

desc: New divine self-declaration "I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans" turns the subject from seed to land; Abram asks "how can I know that I will possess it?" and is told "Bring Me a heifer"; the section runs to the preparation of the animals.
name: The question about the land and the divided animals

desc: I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess.
name: God at Gen 15:7

desc: Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?
name: Abraham at Gen 15:8

name: God at Gen 15:9

desc: Speech ends and naming begins: "So Hagar gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her: You are the God who sees me", with the etiological "Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi"

name: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, and drives her out

name: The angel of the LORD finds Hagar in the wilderness

desc: This is My covenant with you and your descendants after you, which you are to keep: Every male among you must be circumcised.
name: The covenant of circumcision

desc: You are to circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and this will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you.
name: The token of the covenant

desc: Generation after generation, every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old, including those born in your household and those purchased from a foreigner — even those who are not your offspring.
name: The age for circumcision

desc: God commands that every male born in Abraham's house or bought with his money be circumcised; the covenant is in their flesh.
name: born in your house must needs be circumcised

desc: The penalty for an uncircumcised male: he will be cut off from his people, having broken God's covenant.
name: the uncircumcised man child shall be cut off

desc: Fresh formula "Then God said to Abraham, As for Sarai your wife" changes the subject to Sarah; Abraham answers ("O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!"), and the scene closes "When He had finished speaking with Abraham, God went up from him"
name: Sarah renamed, Isaac promised, Abraham laughs

desc: God tells Abraham not to call her Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be.
name: Sarah shall be her name

desc: God promises to bless Sarah, make her a mother of nations, and give Abraham a son by her.
name: I will bless Sarah and give you a son of her

desc: Abraham's laugh: shall a child be born at a hundred years old?
name: Abraham at Gen 17:17
O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing

desc: Bounded by "the LORD appeared to Abram" and "God went up from him" — one continuous divine encounter in three speeches.
name: The covenant speech at Mamre

desc: Opens with a dated theophany, "When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the LORD appeared to him and said, I am God Almighty"; runs through the promise of nations and land, ending "I will be their God."
name: God appears and renames Abram

desc: I am God Almighty. Walk before Me and be blameless.
name: God's call to Abram: walk before me

name: Abraham circumcises his household

desc: I will establish My covenant between Me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly.
name: God's promise of the covenant

desc: As for Me, this is My covenant with you: You will be the father of many nations.
name: God's covenant with Abram

desc: No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations.
name: The name change to Abraham

desc: I will make you exceedingly fruitful; I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you.
name: God's promise of fruitfulness

desc: I will establish My covenant as an everlasting covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you, to be your God and the God of your descendants after you.
name: The everlasting covenant

desc: And to you and your descendants I will give the land where you are residing— all the land of Canaan — as an eternal possession; and I will be their God.
name: The gift of Canaan

desc: New speech formula "God also said to Abraham, You must keep My covenant" turns from promise to obligation; closes with the sanction "he will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant."
name: The law of circumcision

name: The command to keep the covenant

desc: Can I really bear a child when I am old?

name: God at Gen 18:14

desc: Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do;
name: God at Gen 18:17

name: God at Gen 18:18

desc: The LORD's knowledge of Abraham: he will command his children and household to keep the way of the LORD, doing justice and judgment, so that the LORD may bring what he has spoken.
name: God at Gen 18:19

name: God at Gen 18:21

name: God at Gen 18:26

desc: If I find thirty there, I will not do it.
name: God at Gen 18:30

you may do as you have said

Let us make man in our image

name: Abimelech's plea: Said he not to me...

name: God at Gen 21:12

swear to me here before God

name: Abimelech at Gen 21:26

there he called upon the name of the LORD

desc: Opens with the narrative formula "Some time later God tested Abraham" and closes with the command "Offer him there as a burnt offering"; God speaks, Abraham answers "Here I am."

desc: The message told to Abraham: 'Milcah has also borne sons to your brother Nahor.'

desc: Listen to me, my lord. The land is worth four hundred shekels of silver, but what is that between you and me? Bury your dead.

desc: the land is worth four hundred shekels of silver
name: Ephron at Gen 23:15

desc: Speech ends; legal conveyance formula 'were made sure Unto Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth'.

desc: Named as a gift in order to rule something else out. Ephesians 2:8 spells out the exclusion -- 'not of yourselves' -- and Romans 6:23 sets it against wages, which is the same move: what is earned against what is given. James 1:17 puts the source above and says it does not vary. Distinct from the Old Testament's gifts, which are mostly offerings brought or bribes refused (Exod 23:8, 'a bribe blinds those who see').
name: gift

desc:
'There are different gifts, but the same Spirit.' (1Cor 12:4), and nine follow at 12:8-10: the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, faith, the gifts of healing, the working of miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, various tongues, the interpretation of tongues.

A third enumerated list attached to the Spirit, alongside the fruit and the works of the flesh, and the only one whose point is that the items differ. The refrain does the arguing: by the Spirit ... by the same Spirit ... by the same Spirit, four times in three verses, closed by 'All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines' (12:11).

That closing clause is where the passage becomes contested. It attributes the distribution to the Spirit's own will, and whether the list is a description of the first century or a standing provision is a question the verse does not answer.
name: different gifts, the same Spirit

A predication offered as the reason for an instruction, not on its own account — it answers a question about which mountain to worship on, and the answer is that the question is the wrong shape.

The word Spirit here is doing something the text should not over-read. This is a statement about what God is, in a verse whose previous line is about the Father seeking worshippers; it is not the Holy Spirit as a person, and the text does not say it is.

The letter does not leave it abstract. The verse between the two statements grounds it in an act: 'God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him' (4:9).

desc:
'Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.' (Rom 1:7).

All thirteen letters attributed to Paul open with it, nine reading God our Father and four God the Father, and every one pairs it with the Lord Jesus Christ in the same breath.

It is reasonable to ask whether a greeting means anything, and the text answers it by containing the alternative. Three letters here use the ordinary opening word — 'The apostles and the elders, your brothers ... Greetings' (Acts 15:23), 'Claudius Lysias, To His Excellency, Governor Felix: Greetings.' (Acts 23:26), and 'James, a servant of God ... greeting' (Jas 1:1). One of the three is a Roman officer's dispatch about a prisoner. Paul never uses it, in thirteen letters, substituting grace and peace every time. The departure is visible without leaving the text.

And it does something to the rest of each letter. Paul names the Father in chapter 1 and then writes God for the remainder. Eleven of the thirteen put the formula in the first three verses. Romans contains 144 verses naming God and exactly two joint formulas — 1:7 and 15:6 — the greeting and the closing doxology, so the whole argument sits inside a bracket.

Whether the later, bare references carry that specification forward is a reading, and a common one. The text states the pattern, which is checkable, and stops there.
name: Grace and peace to you from God our Father

desc:
The Holy Spirit, in Greek πνεῦμα ἅγιον; older English translations say the Holy Ghost, for the same words. Often simply "the Spirit", and the text uses both names of one moment: "Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness" (Luke 4:1). John 14 gives two more names in the same discourse: "another Advocate ... the Spirit of truth" (14:16-17) and "the Advocate, the Holy Spirit" (14:26).

So "the Spirit" is kept with this card rather than as a card of its own. The "spirit of ..." construction is not taken with it -- a spirit of fear, of slavery, of stupor -- since most of those are not this.

The Old Testament's "Spirit of God" (Gen 1:2) and "Spirit of the LORD" (Judg 6:34, 1 Sam 16:13) are kept with this card because the New Testament makes the identification itself: "The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet" (Acts 28:25); "as the Holy Spirit says", before Psalm 95 (Heb 3:7); Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1, "The Spirit of the Lord is on Me", of himself (Luke 4:18); and Peter gives Joel's "I will pour out My Spirit" as "what was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16-17). The Old Testament itself says "Your Holy Spirit" (Ps 51:11) and "His Holy Spirit" (Isa 63:10).

Also distinct from Jesus in any state: 'the Spirit of Christ' (Rom 8:9) and 'the Spirit of His Son' (Gal 4:6) are genitives the text leaves unspecified, and this graph does not resolve them into identity.

desc:
'How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation, who say to Zion, Your God reigns!' (Isa 52:7).

**Two prophets say it and one apostle quotes it.** Nah 1:15 has almost the same sentence -- 'Look to the mountains— the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace' -- and neither prophet cites the other. Rom 10:15 quotes it as scripture: 'As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.'

What the feet carry is named four times in one verse: good tidings, peace, good tidings of good, salvation. And the message itself is given at the end, addressed to a place -- 'who say to Zion, Your God reigns.'

Rom 10:15 sits two verses after 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Rom 10:13) and in the same argument that collides with the stone laid in Zion at Rom 9:33. The good tidings and the stumbling stone are laid in the same place.

Isaiah 43:10 uses the same English construction of God — 'so that you may consider and believe Me ... that I am he' — which is why the verses are gathered rather than argued over. John 18:6 reports what happened when Jesus said it: the arresting party drew back and fell to the ground.

Whether it declares being, or refuses the question, or promises presence, is argued in every direction and none of those readings is in the verse.
