desc:
'I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the beginning,' (Ps 78:2), quoted at Matt 13:35 as 'I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world'.

One of two fulfilment citations in the same chapter, both about parables and eighteen verses apart. The psalm it comes from is not prophecy in form -- it is a recital of Israel's history -- and Matthew calls it 'spoken through the prophet' anyway.
name: I will open my mouth in parables
I will surely make you prosper, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea

desc: I would despise my life
name: I despise my own life

desc: I could only beg my Judge for mercy
name: I could only beg my Judge for mercy

desc: yet would I not answer
name: I could not answer

desc: I do not believe He would listen to my voice
name: I do not believe He would listen to my voice.

desc: I have no concern for myself
name: I have no concern for myself

desc: Son of David, born in Jerusalem.
disambiguation: son of David, born in Jerusalem
name: Ibhar

desc: Canaanite city Manasseh could not drive out.
name: Ibleam

desc: Of Bethlehem; judge who had 30 sons and 30 daughters.
disambiguation: of Bethlehem
name: Ibzan

desc: frozen water, 'From whose womb does the ice emerge?'
name: ice

desc: Son of Phinehas, born as the ark was taken and Eli/Phinehas died.
name: Ichabod

desc: City where Paul and Barnabas preached after leaving Antioch in Pisidia.
name: Iconium

desc: Town of Zebulun.
name: Idalah

disambiguation: grandfather of the prophet Zechariah
name: Iddo

disambiguation: The chief at Casiphia, whose kinsmen were the temple servants; Ezra sent to him for ministers for the house of God when the caravan out of Babylon proved to have no Levites in it (Ezra 8:17).
name: Iddo

desc: One of the regions the great multitude came from: "And from Jerusalem, and from Idumea, and from beyond Jordan".
name: Idumea
Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God

desc:
'What then shall we say in response to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?' (Rom 8:31).

The turn of the chapter. Everything after it is questions -- four of them -- each answered by naming something that did not happen, or someone who is not accusing.
name: If God is for us, who can be against us

desc: God does not restrain His anger
name: God does not restrain His anger
the 'If I' clauses in Job's defence

desc: If I summoned Him and He answered me
name: If I summoned Him and He answered me

desc: If I justify myself
name: Even if I were righteous

desc:
'I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!' (Esth 4:16).

**She has just explained why it is fatal** -- anyone who approaches the king uncalled is put to death unless he holds out the sceptre, and she has not been called for thirty days (4:11). The decision is made with the risk stated in full and not minimised.

What she asks for first is a fast, by everybody, for three days.
name: if I perish, I perish

desc: if I were blameless
name: if I were blameless

desc: If I speak of strength
name: If it is a matter of strength

desc:
'and if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.' (2Chr 7:14).

Four conditions and three consequences, in one sentence. Humbling comes first and praying second, which is the reverse of how the verse is usually quoted.

It is addressed to a named people at a named moment — Solomon's temple, after the dedication — because the verse names 'my people' and a land, and who those are today is the reader's question.
name: if my people shall humble themselves

desc: If the scourge slay suddenly
name: When the scourge brings sudden death

desc:
'If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness' (1John 1:9).

**The grounds given are faithfulness and justice, not mercy**, which is not where a reader would expect the sentence to go.
name: if we confess our sins

desc: Son of Nathan of Zobah; one of David's mighty men.
disambiguation: son of Nathan of Zobah; distinct from Igal the spy of Num 13:7
name: Igal

desc: Spy sent from the tribe of Issachar.
disambiguation: son of Joseph, spy for Issachar; distinct from Igal son of Nathan of Zobah
name: Igal

desc: South-country town of Judah.
name: Iim

desc: Camp in the wilderness opposite Moab to the east (Num 21:11).
name: Iye-abarim

desc: The Tekoite; father of Ira.
name: Ikkesh

desc: 'We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain,' (Heb 6:19). One occurrence as a figure in the whole corpus, and the ground is stated in the same breath -- firm and secure -- which is what makes it worth a record at all.
name: anchor

desc:
'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power' (Acts 10:38). The verse states the identification outright — the oil is not mentioned and the Spirit stands in its place.

The figure works because the literal act is in the text first. Samuel takes a horn of oil and anoints David, 'and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward' (1Sam 16:13) — the oil and the Spirit in one sentence, the first as act and the second as consequence.

Isaiah 61:1 puts them together again and Luke 4:18 has Jesus read it aloud: 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me'.
name: anointing

desc: Job 38:15: 'their upraised arm is broken.'
name: arm

desc: the arm 'that is feeble', a figure for weakness
name: the arm that is feeble

desc:
'Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil's schemes.' (Eph 6:11).

The text builds the figure and then labels every part of it, which it does almost nowhere else. Six pieces across four verses, each named with the thing it stands for: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God.

The verbs are defensive. Stand, withstand, quench — and of the six only the sword could be used to attack. Whatever the passage is arguing, it is not arguing for advance.
name: armor

desc: A false balance is an abomination in four separate places, which makes the figure at Daniel 5:27 land the way it does: 'TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient' Isaiah 40:12 runs it the other way and weighs the mountains in them.
name: balances

desc: 'These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth.' (Dan 7:17), and again at 7:23, 'The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will appear on the earth'. The angel gives the key to Daniel when he asks for it. Four kings at 7:17 and a kingdom at 7:23 — the text itself moves between the ruler and the realm.
name: beast

desc: 'Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.' (1Cor 12:27). The figure is worked at length before it is keyed -- foot, hand, ear, eye, each protesting its place -- and the key at 12:27 is an address rather than an equation.
name: body

desc: 'Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Look, they are saying, Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off.' (Ezek 37:11). The vision is keyed in the same breath it is explained, and the key names the despair as well as the referent.
name: bones

desc: like a hut set up by a watchman (Job 27:18)
name: a hut

desc: the bottles of heaven, jars holding rain (Job 38:37)
name: water jars

desc: the phrase 'bottles of heaven' in Job 38:37, the containers of rain
name: water jars of the heavens

desc: 'I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit.' (John 15:5). The key is an address, like 'you are the salt of the earth', and the figure is worked through pruning and burning in the verses around it. Paul uses the same word for grafted Gentiles at Romans 11:17, on an olive rather than a vine.
name: branch

desc: Sometimes the figure and the thing are in the same hand: 'Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, Take and eat; this is My body.' (Matt 26:26). Elsewhere the distance is a generation -- the manna their fathers ate in the desert, answered with 'I am the bread of life' (John 6:31-35).
name: bread

desc: 'with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed' (Eph 6:14). **The figure is older than Paul** -- Isaiah 59:17 has God putting on 'righteousness as a breastplate', the same pairing, and 1 Thessalonians 5:8 pairs it instead with faith and love.
disambiguation: the figure -- the breastplate of righteousness, and of faith and love; distinct from the_breastplate_of_judgment, the twelve-stone garment Aaron wore
name: breastplate

desc:
'He breathed on them and said, Receive the Holy Spirit.' (John 20:22). The act and the naming are one sentence, which is as close to a stated key as a gesture gets.

It reaches back a long way. God breathes into the man at Genesis 2:7 and he becomes a living soul; Ezekiel is told to prophesy to the breath so the slain may live (37:9); Job 33:4 has 'the breath of the Almighty gives me life'. The text does not connect John 20:22 to any of them, and a reader will.
name: breath

desc: The figure of the bridegroom whose presence forbids fasting and whose being taken away brings it (Mark 2:19-20).
name: the bridegroom

desc: 'Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. Instead, they set it on a stand' (Matt 5:15). The absurd act carries the point; all three synoptics keep it.
name: basket

desc: Twice, and both times as the largest thing to hand. Through the eye of a needle, and swallowed whole by someone straining out a gnat.
name: camel

desc: 'the seven lampstands are the seven churches' (Rev 1:20). John is shown the vision and told what it means in the same verse. The word is also the golden lampstand of the tabernacle (Exod 25:31), which is a different thing and keeps its own verses.
disambiguation: the figure the seven churches are held as; distinct from the lampstand, the seven-branched lamp of the tabernacle
name: lampstand

desc:
'Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind.' (Ps 1:4).

**Never used of anything but what is discarded, and always in motion or on fire.** The wind drives it (Ps 1:4, Ps 35:5, Isa 17:13), the whirlwind takes it (Hos 13:3), the fire burns it (Matt 3:12). It has no weight of its own in any of them.

It is the second half of a pair wherever Psalm 1 is in view: the tree planted by the waters stands and bears, the chaff blows away.
name: chaff

desc: 'You are the light of the world. A city on a hill cannot be hidden.' (Matt 5:14). A picture set down beside an assertion, with nothing joining them but adjacency — no 'like', no 'for', no 'so'. The reader supplies the join, and the text records the two halves and the verse.
name: city

desc: Job 38:14: 'The earth takes shape like clay under a seal.'
name: clay

desc: He seizes me by the collar of my tunic
name: the collar of a coat

desc:
'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.' (Ps 118:22); 'See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone' (Isa 28:16).

Two Old Testament sayings, not one. The text carries a rejected stone that becomes the chief one, and a stone God lays as a foundation. They are quoted separately — Ps 118:22 at Matt 21:42, Mark 12:10 and Acts 4:11; Isa 28:16 at 1Pet 2:6 — and 1Pet 2:6-7 sets them side by side. Held as one image because every quotation calls it the same thing: the head of the corner.
name: corner stone

desc:
Named for the word the text actually uses. 'Creature' is in 28 verses and 'creation' in six, and 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Galatians 6:15 both say creature — so the figure is filed under that and the verb 'created' runs alongside it.

A word the text starts with and then keeps using for people. 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.' (Gen 1:1) is the first line; by 2 Corinthians 5:17 the same verb is being applied to a person: 'if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation'.

It runs through the middle too, and not only in the New Testament. 'Create in me a clean heart, O God' (Ps 51:10) asks for it in the first person. Isaiah has it twice as promise — 'Behold, I am about to do something new' (43:19) and 'I will create new heavens and a new earth' (65:17).

And it closes the text: 'Behold, I make all things new' (Rev 21:5), which is the last of the figure and the only place a voice says it of everything at once.

The text does not claim these are one idea. They are one word, used by writers a thousand years apart, and a reader who sees a thread from Genesis to Revelation is doing something the text does not do on the page.
name: creation

desc:
The instrument, used as a figure. 'the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God' (1Cor 1:18).

The text turns it into something a reader carries. 'If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.' (Luke 9:23) — said before any crucifixion has happened in the narrative, to hearers for whom it was still only a Roman execution.

Paul makes it the one thing to boast in: 'But as for me, may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.' (Gal 6:14). Kept apart from the crucifixion itself, which is an event with a place and a date, the way every figure here is kept apart from the thing it is drawn from.
name: cross

desc: Always qualified, and the qualifier is the meaning: 'the crown of righteousness' (2Tim 4:8), 'the crown of life' (Jas 1:12), 'the crown of glory that will never fade away' (1Pet 5:4). Beside the literal crowns of the kings, which are a different record.
name: crown

desc: Two figures under one word, and the verses keep them apart. The cup of the covenant: 'He took the cup, gave thanks ... This is My blood of the covenant' (Matt 26:27-28), stated outright at 1Cor 11:25 — 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood'. The cup of suffering and of wrath: 'let this cup pass from Me' (Matt 26:39), 'Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?' (Matt 20:22), and in the hand of the LORD at Ps 75:8 and Rev 14:10. The text does not join them.
name: cup

desc:
'God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.' (1John 1:5).

The text almost never uses it alone. It appears as the half of a pair — 'what fellowship does light have with darkness?' (2Cor 6:14), 'you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord' (Eph 5:8), 'Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.' (John 8:12).

John 3:19-20 gives it a motive rather than leaving it a condition: 'men loved the darkness rather than the Light because their deeds were evil. Everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come into the Light for fear that his deeds will be exposed.'
name: darkness

desc:
A word the text uses for two different things and rarely marks which. There is dying, and there is a state a living person can already be in.

'The mind of the flesh is death' (Rom 8:6). 'the wages of sin is death' (Rom 6:23). 'The one who does not love remains in death.' (1John 3:14) — said of people who are demonstrably alive.

It begins in Genesis with a warning whose timing is disputed on the page: 'in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die' (Gen 2:17), and Adam lives 930 years, and it ends with a second one: 'Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death' (Rev 20:14), which implies the first was not final.
name: death

desc: 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved.' (John 10:9), and at 10:7 more narrowly, 'I am the door of the sheep'. The same chapter runs the shepherd, the sheep, the fold and the gatekeeper, so the door here is a fold's door rather than a house's. Revelation 3:20 uses the word for a different figure entirely — 'Behold, I stand at the door, and knock' — and the text keeps them apart.
name: door

desc: Job 38:17: 'Have you seen the gates of the shadow of death?'
name: the gates of the shadow of death

desc: 'He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him.' (Matt 3:16) -- a comparison and not an identification, which matters: the verse says the descent was *like* a dove, and does not say the Spirit is one. Matthew 10:16 asks disciples to be 'harmless as doves'.
name: dove

desc: 'Then another sign appeared in heaven: a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns' (Rev 12:3), keyed six verses later as 'that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan' (Rev 12:9). Revelation keys its own vision and does it twice.
name: dragon

desc: the dust that hardens into a mass (Job 38:38)
name: dust

desc: 'they will mount up with wings like eagles' (Isa 40:31). Exodus 19:4 has 'I carried you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself', and Deuteronomy 32:11 works it at length -- 'As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young' -- which is an analogy with the predicate on both sides.
name: eagle

desc:
'placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.' (2Cor 1:22), repeated at 5:5 and again at Ephesians 1:14.

A down payment: money handed over that both proves the buyer means it and is itself part of the price. The figure claims the Spirit is not a token of something later but the first instalment of it.

One of the few figures in the New Testament drawn from commerce rather than from farming, weather or the household, and Paul is the only one who uses it.
name: pledge
name_bsb_pass: as a pledge of what is to come

desc: Job 38:13 'the ends of the earth'; Job 38:18 'the breadth of the earth'; Job 38:24 'upon the earth'.
name: the earth

desc: Job 38:24: 'the east wind scattered over the earth'.
name: the east wind

desc: Job 38:13: 'spread to the ends of the earth'.
name: the ends of the earth

desc: Anthropomorphic figure: The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous (Ps 34:15).
name: the eyes of the Lord

desc:
'Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, He went to see if there was any fruit on it. But when He reached it, He found nothing on it except leaves' (Mark 11:13), and the next morning 'they saw the fig tree withered from its roots' (11:20).

Mark wraps the temple inside it. The tree is cursed on the way in (11:12-14), the tables are overturned (11:15-19), and the withering is found on the way out (11:20-21) — one act split around another, a shape Mark uses elsewhere.

The text does not say the tree is the temple, so it is treated as a figure and not as a key.
name: fig tree

desc: 'For our God is a consuming fire' (Heb 12:29), quoting Deuteronomy 4:24. Acts 2:3 has 'tongues like flames of fire' at Pentecost, and 1 Peter 1:7 the trial of faith 'refined by fire'. Presence, purging and judgment under one word, and each verse says which.
name: fire

desc: The flood as a figure of man's passing: "a river becomes parched and dry".
name: river

desc: Paired with grass nearly every time it is used as a figure: 'The grass withers and the flowers fall' (Isa 40:7), 'he will pass away like a flower of the field' (Jas 1:10). Job sets it beside the shadow -- 'Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure.' (Job 14:2).
name: flower

desc:
'You are my refuge and my fortress' (Ps 91:2).

One of a cluster David piles up in a single verse: 'The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer' (2Sam 22:2, repeated at Ps 18:2). **Six figures for the same claim in one sentence**, which is the psalms preferring accumulation to precision.
name: fortress

desc: A fountain sealed: 'a fountain sealed'.
name: fountain sealed

desc: Song 4:15 'A fountain of gardens'.
name: garden spring

desc: 'Look at the birds of the air: They do not sow or reap' (Matt 6:26); 'Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin' (6:28). Arguments from creatures rather than comparisons to them -- the form is 'look at this, and reason' rather than 'you are like this'.
name: lilies

desc: "the birds came and devoured it" (Mark 4:4), a figure within the parable; distinct from the fowls of the creation account.
name: the fowls of the air

desc:
What a thing produces, standing for what the thing is.

One of the most heavily worked figures in the New Testament and one of the few used as a test. 'by their fruit you will recognize them' (Matt 7:20) makes it evidential — the fruit is how the tree is identified, not merely what it yields. John the Baptist demands 'fruits meet for repentance' (Matt 3:8) on the same logic.

It attaches to whatever is claimed to be the source. Of the Spirit at Galatians 5:22 and Ephesians 5:9; of abiding in Christ at John 15:5, where the vine figure supplies it; of righteousness at Philippians 1:11, Hebrews 12:11 and James 3:18; of the tree at Matthew 7:17, good or corrupt.

The text uses the word for actual produce constantly, but no particular fruit is identified as the figure.
name: fruit

desc: A garden shut up: 'you are a garden locked up'.
name: garden locked up

desc: Job 38:14: 'they stand as a garment.'
name: a garment

desc: Job 38:17: part of 'the gates of death'.
name: gate

desc: Job 38:17: 'Have the gates of death been revealed to you?'
name: the gates of death

desc: 'with the belt of truth buckled around your waist' (Eph 6:14). Isaiah 11:5 has 'Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist' -- the same garment, the concepts swapped around.
name: belt

desc: A mirror. Twice about self-knowledge that does not hold: 'we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror' (1Cor 13:12), and the hearer who is not a doer, 'looks at his face in a mirror ... and immediately forgets what he looks like'. The laver was made of them (Exod 38:8).
name: mirror

desc: "Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprouted, grew up, and produced a crop" (Mark 4:8).
name: good soil

desc: 'Likewise, every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit.' (Matt 7:17), with the application stated at 7:20: 'So then, by their fruit you will recognize them.' The figure and its use in three verses.
name: tree

desc: What the text reaches for when it means a life is short. 'As for man, his days are like grass-he blooms like a flower of the field;' (Ps 103:15). Isaiah makes it a whole argument — 'All flesh is grass ... The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever' (Isa 40:6-8) — and 1 Peter 1:24 quotes him without saying so.
name: grass

desc: 'He was assigned a grave with the wicked'
name: grave

desc: The green pastures where the shepherd makes the sheep lie down.
name: green pastures

desc: Ripeness and a deadline together. 'The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.' (Matt 9:37); 'The harvest is the end of the age' (Matt 13:39); and Jeremiah 8:20, which is the whole figure turned around -- 'The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved'
name: harvest

desc: 'The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits.' (Rev 17:9), and the angel prefaces it with 'This calls for a mind with wisdom', which is the text marking its own key as a key. Daniel 2:38 keys a head a different way -- 'You are that head of gold' -- said to Nebuchadnezzar.
name: head

desc: "the frost from heaven" (Job 38:29); "the laws of the heavens" (Job 38:33).
name: heaven

desc: 'take the helmet of salvation' (Eph 6:17), and again from Isaiah 59:17, 'the helmet of salvation on His head'. **The same two pieces are lifted from the same verse**, which is as close as the passage comes to naming its source.
name: helmet

desc: Job 38:15: 'their upraised arm is broken.'
name: their upraised arm

desc: Age as a claim on respect — 'rise in the presence of the elderly' (Lev 19:32), 'Gray hair is a crown of glory' (Prov 16:31) — and then as a description of a figure in a vision. Daniel 7:9 gives the Ancient of days hair 'like the pure wool'; Revelation 1:14 gives One like the Son of Man hair 'white like wool, as white as snow'.
name: gray head

desc: 'The ten horns you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom' (Rev 17:12), which is Daniel's key too — 'the ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom' (Dan 7:24). Revelation 5:6 puts seven horns on the Lamb, where the word means power rather than rulers.
name: horn

desc: The house of something, whose paths are known (Job 38:20).
name: house

desc: "From whose womb does the ice emerge?" (Job 38:29); "the waters become hard as stone" (Job 38:30).
name: ice

desc: 'golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints' (Rev 5:8), and again at 8:3-4 where the smoke of the incense ascends with the prayers. Psalm 141:2 asks for it directly: 'May my prayer be set before You like incense'.
name: incense

desc: The passover lamb, the lamb of the daily offering, and the Lamb of God whom John points to at John 1:29. The word is the hub; what each use means is in its own verse.
disambiguation: the word `lamb` used as a figure -- the Lamb of God at John 1:29. Distinct from the creature record, which holds the animals of the passover and the daily offering.
name: lamb

desc: 'Before the throne burned seven torches of fire. These are the seven spirits of God.' (Rev 4:5) -- keyed in the same verse. Psalm 119:105 makes it the word: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet.' The virgins' lamps of Matthew 25 are a third use.
name: lamp

desc: Keyed twice and in opposite directions. Matthew 16:12 explains the warning: 'Then they understood that He was not telling them to beware of the leaven used in bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees' 1 Corinthians 5:7-8 uses it for malice and wickedness, against 'the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth'. But Matthew 13:33 has the kingdom of heaven itself likened to leaven a woman hid in three measures of meal, which is the same word doing the opposite work.
name: leaven

desc:
Almost always set against death rather than defined on its own. 'I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life' (Deut 30:19) is the pattern, and the pairing does the work.

Scripture repeatedly describes a crossing between the two rather than a difference of degree: 'has crossed over from death to life' (John 5:24), 'We know that we have passed from death to life' (1John 3:14), 'walk in newness of life' (Rom 6:4).

'I am the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25) is the one place a person is identified with the word.
name: life

desc: 'I am the light of the world' (John 8:12, repeated 9:5), and the same words turned on the hearers at Matthew 5:14 -- 'You are the light of the world'. Psalm 119:105 makes it the word: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path'
name: light

desc: 'For just as the lightning comes from the east and flashes as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.' (Matt 24:27). **Used for suddenness and for visibility at once** -- the point is both that it is quick and that nobody has to be told it happened, which is the answer to the false christs of the verses before it.
name: lightning

desc: 'She was given clothing of fine linen, bright and pure.” For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints.' (Rev 19:8). The key is given in the same sentence as the image. Exodus 28:39 has the priest's linen coat, which is the tangible garment and a separate matter.
name: fine linen

desc: One noun, and the verses do not agree about what it carries. Revelation 5:5 has the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who has prevailed; 1 Peter 5:8 has the devil 'like a roaring lion' walking about, seeking whom he may devour. Each verse states its own ground. Physical lions are a separate matter, joined to this one: Daniel was shut in with those.
disambiguation: the word `lion` where the corpus uses it as a figure -- the Lion of the tribe of Judah at Rev 5:5, the devil prowls around like a roaring lion at 1Pet 5:8. Distinct from the creature record of the same name, which holds the animals: the ones Daniel was shut in with, the one David killed, the one in Samson's riddle. Joined to it by `drawn_from` and not merged with it.
name: lion

desc: 'whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.' (John 4:14), and 'Streams of living water will flow from within him' (John 7:38). John keys it himself in the next verse — 'He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive.' (John 7:39).
name: living water

desc: 'For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh. This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church' (Eph 5:31-32). Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and then says plainly which correspondence he has been drawing all along.
name: marriage

desc: The LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand (Deut 6:21); the hand as a figure of power.
name: mighty hand

desc: Milk: 'honey and milk are under your tongue'.
name: milk

desc: 'Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?' (Matt 7:3). The figure is the disproportion, and Matthew 7:5 states the application outright: 'First take the beam out of your own eye'.
name: beam

desc: Immovability, used to measure faith against: 'you can say to this mountain, Move from here to there,and it will move'. Isaiah 40:4 flattens them and Daniel 2:35 grows one out of a stone.
name: mountain

desc: Named only for being the smallest, and used for two different things -- what the kingdom starts as, and how little faith it takes.
name: mustard seed

desc: 'Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction' (Matt 7:13), against the narrow gate and restricted way 'that leads to life'. Two roads and two ends, with the ends named in the verses themselves.
name: gate

desc: Two settings and the same object. In the Psalms and prophets it is always laid for someone -- 'He will free my feet from the mesh' (Ps 25:15), 'But I will spread My net over him' (Ezek 12:13). In the Gospels it is work, and then a figure for the kingdom: 'like a net that was cast into the sea and caught all kinds of fish' (Matt 13:47). Luke 5:6 has the net break under the catch; John 21:11 makes a point of one that does not.
name: net

desc: The patch of "new cloth" sewn on an old garment, which makes the rent worse (Mark 2:21).
name: a patch of unshrunk cloth
image of God
desc:
Said of humankind at creation: "So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them" (Gen 1:27), given with a task: "to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air ... and over all the earth" (1:26).

Genesis says it twice more: Adam "had a son in his own likeness, after his own image" (5:3), and the reason given against shedding blood is "for in His own image God has made mankind" (9:6). James still argues from it, of men "who have been made in God's likeness" (3:9).

In the New Testament the phrase is given to Christ, "who is the image of God" (2 Cor 4:4) and "the image of the invisible God" (Col 1:15). The same Greek word, εἰκών, describes what believers are becoming: "being transformed into His image" (2 Cor 3:18), "being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator" (Col 3:10), "conformed to the image of His Son" (Rom 8:29).

'So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the presence of his brothers' (1Sam 16:13); 'You anoint my head with oil' (Ps 23:5).

In 1Sam 16:13 it commissions — the horn is brought out and the Spirit follows. In Ps 23:5 it is what a host does for a guest, in the same verse as the table and the cup.
name: oil

desc: 'Now if some branches have been broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others' (Rom 11:17). Paul runs the figure for eight verses and keys the grafting rather than the tree, because what he explains is a process, not a correspondence between two nameable things.
name: olive tree

desc: 'an orchard of pomegranates' (Song 4:13).
name: orchard

desc: 'an orchard of pomegranates' (Song 4:13).
name: orchard of pomegranates

desc: Isaiah 1:3 sets it against Israel: 'The ox knows its owner ... but Israel does not know'. Proverbs 14:4 is the dry one -- 'Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty' -- and Deuteronomy 25:4 is the verse that travels.
name: ox

desc:
'He will make your paths straight' (Prov 3:6); 'He guides me in the paths of righteousness' (Ps 23:3); 'Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths.' (Ps 25:4).

Where paths appear, someone else is directing, leading, teaching or lighting it — and the one going is not the one choosing. Ps 119:105 makes the lamp the word; Isa 30:21 puts a voice behind rather than a map ahead.

Ps 23:3 joins paths and leading. That is what lets a reader go from being told to trust (Prov 3:5-6) to being led (Ps 23), without either verse mentioning the other.
name: path

desc: 'Do not give dogs what is holy; do not throw your pearls before swine. If you do, they may trample them under their feet' (Matt 7:6). The point is left entirely to the reader; nothing in the sermon says what the pearls are.
name: pearls

desc: The figure Jesus takes up in "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick".
name: a doctor

desc: A plant as a figure of renewed growth: "put forth twigs like a sapling".
name: a sapling

desc: 'Your branches are an orchard of pomegranates' (Song 4:13).
name: branches

desc: Isaiah 2:4 beats swords into plowshares; Joel 3:10 beats plowshares back into swords, in the same words and the opposite direction. Elisha is at the plough when Elijah finds him, and Luke 9:62 makes looking back from one the disqualifying act.
name: plow

desc: A piece of pomegranate: 'Your brow behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate'.
name: pomegranate

desc: 'Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use?' (Rom 9:21), which Paul takes from Jeremiah at the potter's house: 'can’t I do with you as this potter? says the LORD. Behold, as the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand' (Jer 18:6) -- an analogy with the predicate stated on both sides. Isaiah 64:8 puts it as address: 'we are the clay, and You are the potter'.
name: potter

desc:
'God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.' (Ps 46:1).

Scripture keeps it paired with something structural — refuge and strength, refuge and fortress, 'The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms' (Deut 33:27).
name: refuge

desc: 'The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer' (Ps 18:2) -- one of a run of figures in a single verse. Paul keys a particular rock to Christ at 1Cor 10:4, and Matthew 16:18 uses the word a third way: 'upon this rock I will build my church'. The rock in Horeb is a separate record and keeps its own verses.
name: rock

desc: A shepherd's rod.
name: rod

desc: 'like a root out of dry ground'
name: root

desc: Worn for grief and for repentance — Jacob for a son he thinks is dead, Ahab after Naboth, the king of Nineveh, and in Jonah 3:6 the animals as well.
name: sackcloth

desc: 'You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, how can it be made salty again?' (Matt 5:13). The key is the address -- *you* are it -- and the figure is worked in the same verse for what happens when it fails. 'Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt' (Col 4:6) uses it a second way.
name: salt

desc: Job 38:16: 'the springs of the sea.'
name: the sea

desc:
'you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit' (Eph 1:13), and 'do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption' (Eph 4:30).

**A mark of ownership that is also a guarantee**, and Paul uses it for both at once. It belongs to the same commercial vocabulary as the earnest, which he puts in the very next clause at 2 Corinthians 1:22.
name: seal

desc: 'Now this is the meaning of the parable: The seed is the word of God.' (Luke 8:11), which is Jesus explaining his own parable. Matthew's version of the same parable keys it differently — 'the good seed represents the sons of the kingdom' (Matt 13:38) — because the two evangelists are explaining two parables and only one of them is the sower. Peter uses it a third way: born again 'not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God' (1Pet 1:23).
name: seed

desc: Revelation 12:9 names it as the devil — 'the great dragon was hurled down— that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan' — repeated at 20:2. John 3:14 makes it Christ: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up'. Genesis 3:1 has a third, the creature in the garden, 'more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made'. Three uses, two of them keyed in contrary directions, and nothing here reconciles them or claims a single meaning behind the word.
name: serpent

desc: the seven worthless heads of grain scorched by the east wind — they are seven years of famine.
name: the seven worthless heads of grain scorched by the east wind

desc: and the seven ripe heads of grain are seven years:
name: the seven ripe heads of grain

desc: The seven good cows are seven years;
name: The seven good cows

desc: the seven thin, ugly cows that came up after them are seven years;
name: the seven thin, ugly cows

desc: Five stated comparisons use it and the ground is usually given: 'Our days on earth are like a shadow, without hope.' (1Chr 29:15), 'My days are like lengthening shadows' (Ps 102:11). The stated ground is what makes this a different figure from the shadow of shelter — 'the shadow of your wings', 'the shadow of a great rock in an arid land' — which the same word carries elsewhere.
name: shadow

desc: Job 38:17: 'the gates of the shadow of death'.
name: the shadow of death

desc: David kept his father's sheep (1Sam 16:11, 17:34) and wrote 'The LORD is my shepherd' (Ps 23:1); Ezekiel has the image handed back to him — 'I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David' (Ezek 34:23); and Jesus takes it up outright at John 10:11, 'I am the good shepherd'. Four points across the canon on one word, and the man who wrote the psalm had done the job.
name: shepherd

desc: 'Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward.' (Gen 15:1), which is the first of the sort in Scripture. Ephesians 6:16 makes it 'the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one', in the same armour passage that keys the sword.
name: shield

desc: Removed on holy ground, handed over to seal a bargain (Ruth 4:7), and the measure of rank John uses -- he is not worthy to untie his sandal straps. Amos twice prices a poor man at a pair of them.
name: sandals

desc: Job 38:22: 'the treasures of the snow'.
name: snow

desc: "A farmer went out to sow his seed" (Mark 4:3) — the figure the parable is built on.
name: A farmer

desc: Support and authority in the same object. 'Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.' (Ps 23:4); Assyria is 'the staff in their hands is My wrath' (Isa 10:5); Zechariah cuts two of them and names them Beauty and Bands.
name: staff

desc: The still waters beside which the shepherd leads.
name: quiet waters

desc: 'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone' (Matt 21:42, quoting Ps 118:22), which 1 Peter 2:6-7 applies directly. The chief corner stone, the stumbling stone and the living stones are three uses of one word inside a few verses of 1 Peter 2, and each verse says which it means.
name: stone

desc:
'And He will be a sanctuary-but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' (Isa 8:14).

**The same stone, received two ways.** 1Pet 2:7-8 puts it plainly: to those who believe the stone is precious and has become the cornerstone; to the disobedient the identical stone is one of stumbling. Nothing changes about the stone. What differs is who meets it.

Rom 9:33 is where this is easiest to miss. Paul writes 'Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' -- which reads as one quotation and is two: the opening is Isa 28:16, where God lays a sure foundation, and the ending is Isa 8:14, where the stone trips people. He joins a promise to a warning in a single sentence.
name: stone of stumbling

desc: "Some fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil." (Mark 4:5).
name: rocky ground

desc: Song 4:15 'streams from Lebanon'.
name: streams

desc: Song 4:15 'and streams from Lebanon'.
name: flowing down from Lebanon

desc: "no one can enter a strong man's house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man".
name: strong man

desc: 384 verses carry the word and no particular sword is meant by most of them. Ephesians 6:17 keys its own use -- 'the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God' -- and Hebrews 4:12 comes at the same pair from the other side: 'the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword'.
name: sword

desc: The table prepared by the LORD.
name: table

desc: 'while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat' (Matt 13:25). Eight verses, all of them Matthew 13, and no weeds anywhere else — so unlike grass or the lion this word has no earlier use. Jesus keys it himself at 13:38: 'the weeds are the sons of the evil one'.
name: weeds

desc:
The temple used as a figure for where God dwells. The building in Jerusalem has its own card: [[temple]].

**God himself as a sanctuary,** to the exiles far from the temple: 'yet for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone' (Ezekiel 11:16).

**Jesus's body:** 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again' (John 2:19). His hearers take him to mean the building, and the narrator explains, 'But Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body' (John 2:21).

**The community of believers,** to the church in Corinth: 'Do you not know that you yourselves are God's temple, and that God's Spirit dwells in you?' (1 Corinthians 3:16).

**The believer's body:** 'Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God?' (1 Corinthians 6:19).

**The new Jerusalem:** 'But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple' (Revelation 21:22).

**Where readers differ.** Some passages are read in more than one way: the temple in them has been understood as the building that stood in Jerusalem when the passage was written, a temple yet to be built, a temple in heaven, the people of God, or a figure of something else. The site shows these verses and does not choose among the readings: 2 Thessalonians 2:4, of the one called 'the man of lawlessness' in verse 3, 'So he will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God'; Matthew 24:15; Haggai 2:9; Ezekiel 40-48, the temple the prophet is shown 'in visions of God' (40:2); Revelation 11:1-2; and Zechariah 6:12-15.
disambiguation: the word `temple` used as a figure. Distinct from the temple at Jerusalem, which is a place and holds the building's own verses.
name: temple

desc: The LORD's house, where the psalmist will dwell.
name: the house of the LORD

desc: A dark valley representing death's shadow.
name: the valley of the shadow of death

desc:
'If the homeowner had known in which watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have kept watch' (Matt 24:43).

Jesus uses it here, Paul at 1 Thessalonians 5:2, Peter at 2 Peter 3:10, and Revelation 16:15 puts it back in Jesus's mouth. The comparison is always to the unannounced hour and never to theft.
name: thief

desc: What the ground gives after Genesis 3:18, and after that a standing figure for whatever chokes or wounds: nations left in the land as 'thorns in your sides' (Judg 2:3), the seed choked among thorns (Matt 13:7), Paul's thorn in the flesh (2Cor 12:7). Isaiah 55:13 reverses it -- 'Instead of the thornbush, a cypress will grow'. The crown the soldiers plait is made of them.
name: thorn

desc:
'My stronghold, my refuge' (2Sam 22:3), and stated flat at Prov 18:10: 'The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe.'

'The Song of Solomon uses the same word for the opposite job. 'Your neck is like the tower of David, built with rows of stones; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors.' (Song 4:4) — a comparison, marked with 'like', and describing what a body looks like rather than what God is. The two uses share a word and nothing else.
name: tower

desc:
'A woman has pain in childbirth because her time has come; but when she brings forth her child, she forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world.' (John 16:21).

**The figure turns on the sorrow being replaced rather than removed**, which is what it is brought in to illustrate at 16:20: 'your sorrow shall be turned into joy'.
name: childbirth

desc: In the garden (Gen 2:9), in the city (Rev 22:2, 'the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations'), and in between as wisdom: 'She is a tree of life to those who embrace her' (Prov 3:18). Proverbs 11:30, 13:12 and 15:4 use it for the fruit of the righteous, desire fulfilled and a soothing tongue.
name: tree of life

desc: 'everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock' (Matt 7:24), against the foolish man who built on sand (7:26). **The one figure in the sermon that carries an explicit comparison marker** -- 'I will liken him unto' -- and it closes the whole discourse.
name: house

desc: 'No one can serve two masters ... You cannot serve both God and money' (Matt 6:24). Stated as a rule and then applied in the same verse, which is the sermon's usual shape.
name: masters

desc: 'I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard.' (John 15:1), against the vine of Israel in Psalm 80:8 and Isaiah 5. A cultivated plant Scripture reaches for whenever it wants tending and fruit.
disambiguation: the word `vine` used as a figure -- 'I am the true vine' (John 15:1), the vine brought out of Egypt (Ps 80:8). Distinct from the object record, which is the plant.
name: vine

desc:
'You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?' (Matt 3:7).

Used four times as an address and never as a description: John says it to the Pharisees and Sadducees (Matt 3:7), Luke to the multitude (Luke 3:7), and Jesus twice (Matt 12:34, Matt 23:33). The one literal viper fastens on Paul's hand at Acts 28:3.

'Matt 23:33 sets it beside the serpent: 'You snakes! You brood of vipers!'. Neither word explains the other; they are set side by side in one address.
name: viper

desc: 'The waters you saw, where the prostitute was seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues.' (Rev 17:15). An angel keying a vision outright, and one of the few places Scripture explains what a crowd of water means.
name: waters

desc: 'I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.' (John 14:6). The word runs through the wisdom books for a manner of living -- 'the LORD guards the path of the righteous' (Ps 1:6), 'The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn' (Prov 4:18) -- and John's use is a person rather than a manner, which is what makes it a saying rather than a proverb.
name: way

desc: Song 4:15 'a well of living waters'.
name: well

desc: Song 4:15 'a well of living waters'.
name: well of fresh water

desc: 'unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.' (John 12:24), said of himself two verses after 'The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified'. Paul works the same figure for the resurrection body at 1Cor 15:37, 'what you sow is not the body that will be'. In Matthew 13 the wheat is what the tares grow among.
name: kernel of wheat

desc: Revelation 7:14 is the sentence the figure hangs on: 'they have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb'. Whiteness arrived at by washing in blood, said without any sign that the writer thinks it strange.
name: white clothing

desc: They advance as through a wide breach
name: through a wide breach
the colt of a wild donkey

desc: 'The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.' (John 3:8) -- an analogy with the correspondence stated, not a bare comparison. Acts 2:2 has 'a rushing mighty wind' at Pentecost; Ephesians 4:14 has doctrine as wind that carries people about.
name: wind

desc: Where the drink stands for something. Psalm 75:8 has a cup in the hand of the LORD, 'full of foaming wine mixed with spices ... and all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs'; Revelation 14:10 makes it 'the wine of God’s anger'. Separately, Genesis 49:11 and Deuteronomy 32:14 call wine the blood of the grape.
disambiguation: the word `wine` used as a figure. Distinct from the object `wine`, the drink at Cana and in the warnings.
name: wine

desc:
A word the text personifies and then argues about. Proverbs makes her a person — 'Wisdom calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square' (1:20), 'Wisdom has built her house' (9:1).

What it is here to hold is the disagreement, and the disagreement has speakers. Not 'the text says' but these voices say:

  * Solomon, whose proverbs these are said to be (Prov 1:1, 10:1): 'She is more precious than rubies; nothing you desire compares with her' (3:15, again at 8:11); 'Wisdom is supreme; so acquire wisdom' (4:7).
  * the Preacher, who names himself at Eccl 1:1 and speaks in the first person at 1:12: 'For with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and as knowledge grows, grief increases' (1:18); 'The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?' (2:15); 'there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool' (2:16).

And the Preacher contradicts himself, not only Solomon. The same voice says 'wisdom, like money, is a shelter ... wisdom preserves the life of its owner' (7:12) and 'Wisdom is better than strength' (9:16). Reading Ecclesiastes as simply contrarian is a reading the book does not support; the tension is inside one speaker.

Whether he holds both on purpose is a reading and is not recorded here. What is recorded is that he says both, and where.
disambiguation: the personified figure of Proverbs, who cries in the streets (1:20) and builds her house (9:1); distinct from `wisdom`, the word the corpus makes statements about
name: wisdom

desc: 'Beware of false prophets, They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves' (Matt 7:15). Keyed in the same sentence -- the wolves are false prophets -- which is rare for this sermon. Paul reuses it at Acts 20:29, 'savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock'.
name: wolves

desc: Three women and three meanings, each keyed or described in its own verse. 'the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth' (Rev 17:18). Revelation 12:1 has another, 'clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet'. Revelation 21:9 has the bride, the Lamb's wife, shown as the holy city.
name: woman

desc: One word, and every use turns on who does the putting. Imposed: Rehoboam adding to it (1Kgs 12:11), a yoke of iron on the neck (Deut 28:48), the law that neither fathers nor sons could bear (Acts 15:10), the yoke of bondage (Gal 5:1). Broken: Isaiah 9:4, Leviticus 26:13, and Isaiah 58:6, where breaking it is the fast God chose. Offered: 'Take my yoke upon you ... my yoke is easy' (Matt 11:29-30), which is the only place the wearer is asked. Jeremiah wears a literal one through two chapters as a sign, so the figure and the object are the same object there.
name: yoke

disambiguation: father of the prophet Micaiah
name: Imlah

desc:
'Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.' (Isa 7:14).

Matt 1:23 quotes Isaiah and then adds the gloss: 'they will call Him Immanuel (which means, God with us).' That is unusual — most names in Scripture are left to stand — and it means the meaning is the text's own and not a reader's.

Isaiah's Hebrew is ʿImmanuʾel (Immanuel); Matthew's Greek writes Emmanouēl (Emmanuel). The Berean uses Immanuel in both. It is never used as an address or a form of speech: it is given as a name he will be called, twice, and then not used again.
disambiguation: the name given in Isa 7:14 and quoted at Matt 1:23, held as a title of its own as well as one of [[jesus]]'s names, because the corpus translates it where it translates almost nothing else -- 'which means, God with us'
name: Immanuel

desc: Father of Pashhur the priest.
disambiguation: father of Pashhur; distinct from the sons of Immer (a family of the priests, named in the roster of Ezra)
name: Immer

disambiguation: named in a genealogy at Nehemiah 11:13; the chapter gives him only as an ancestor
name: Immer

disambiguation: Named at Neh 3:29 only as the father of Zadok, one of the men who rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem.
name: Immer

disambiguation: son of Asher
name: Imnah

desc: A man who had been impotent thirty-eight years, healed by Jesus at the pool of Bethesda on the sabbath.
disambiguation: unnamed
name: The Impotent Man at Bethesda

disambiguation: Named at Neh 3:2 only as the father of Zaccur, one of the men who rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem.
name: Imri

desc: the state the brothers affirm of their father: 'Your servant our father is well'
name: in good health

desc:
'In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you' (John 14:2).

The only place Scripture gives the Father a house, and the figure is domestic rather than royal — rooms, and someone going ahead to make one ready. It opens the same discourse that gives the Comforter and 'No one comes to the Father'.
name: In My Father's house are many rooms

desc: But He is unchangeable (Job 23:13)
name: in one mind

desc:
'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.' (Gen 1:1).

Scripture's first sentence, and John's gospel opens on its first three words. Nothing precedes it and nothing in it is argued for — the beginning, the actor and the act arrive together.
name: In the beginning God created

desc:
'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1).

The first three words are Genesis 1:1's first three words. The gospel does not say it is quoting and does not need to; it is Scripture's most recognisable opening and John puts something else in the sentence.

Three clauses, and the third is not the second. With God, and God — stated in one verse without reconciliation, and repeated at v2 rather than explained.
name: In the beginning was the Word

desc:
'have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him, 'I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'?' (Mark 12:26).

The bush is used as an argument for the resurrection, which is not what a reader expects it to be for. Jesus is answering the Sadducees, and the whole weight of the reply is on a tense: God says I am, not I was, of three men long dead.

It is also how Scripture itself refers to the episode — 'in the bush' as a way of naming a passage, the way one might say the burning bush today. Stephen tells it again at Acts 7:30 and Paul never mentions it.
name: in the bush God spoke to him

desc:
'And he will go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah' (Luke 1:17), said of John the Baptist before his birth.

Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah himself — 'behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD' — and the New Testament applies it to somebody else. Matthew 11:14 makes the application conditional in an odd way: 'if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come'.

John himself denies it. Asked directly whether he is Elijah, he says 'I am not' (John 1:21).
name: in the spirit and power of Elijah

desc:
'All the families of the earth will be blessed through you' (Gen 12:3). It is spoken five times in Genesis in the LORD's name: to Abraham (12:3), of Abraham (18:18, 'through him'), to Abraham again by 'the angel of the LORD' (22:15-18, 'through your offspring'), to Isaac (26:4) and to Jacob (28:14). The wording varies between 'families' and 'nations', and between 'through you', 'through him', 'through your offspring' or, in 28:14, both you and your offspring.

The Hebrew uses two forms of the verb: one in 12:3, 18:18 and 28:14, the other in 22:18 and 26:4. Translators differ on both, rendering either 'be blessed' or 'bless themselves'.

Acts 3:25 cites it as 'Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed', and Gal 3:8 as 'All nations will be blessed through you'. Both are passive in the Greek.
name: all the families of the earth will be blessed through you

desc: that you may multiply greatly
name: multiply greatly

desc: the man increased exceedingly
name: became exceedingly prosperous

desc: "all the inhabitants of the cities" destroyed in the overthrow (Gen 19:25).
name: all the inhabitants of the cities

desc: making me a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the people of this land
name: the people of this land

desc: Named in Nehemiah 3 for one reason: they repaired and built a part of the wall of Jerusalem, the valley gate.
name: residents of Zanoah

desc: Job asks how many his iniquities are.
name: iniquities

desc: Moral wrong, as the text names it.
name: iniquity
source: bibleont.combine (declared to complete relations the batch asserts)

desc: the sin of the Amorites, not yet full
name: the iniquity of the Amorites

disambiguation: son of Esau and Oholibamah

disambiguation: son of Naphtali
name: Jezer

disambiguation: named in the roster of Ezra 10 among Israel, of the sons of Parosh
name: Izziah

desc: Town with a royal residence of Ahab; site of Naboth's vineyard and his death.
disambiguation: town of Issachar in the valley of Jezreel, distinct from Jezreel in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:56)

desc: Town of Judah, in the hill-country list.
disambiguation: hill-country town of Judah (home of David's wife Ahinoam), distinct from Jezreel in the valley of Issachar

disambiguation: son of Hosea and Gomer, named as a prophetic sign
name: Jezreel

desc: Town of Judah, in the lowland list.

disambiguation: son of Asaph, recorder under Hezekiah

disambiguation: father of Judah, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus; a man, distinct from Joanna the wife of Chuza

disambiguation: the Abiezrite of Ophrah, father of Gideon (Judg 6:11)

desc: Son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.
disambiguation: king of Israel, son of Jehoahaz, grandson of Jehu; distinct from Joash king of Judah

desc: the man to whom the Lord speaks from the whirlwind.
name: Job

desc: New conditional pair "If I sin... If I be wicked... if I be righteous", moving to the hunt: "you hunt me like a lion"
name: Hunted whether righteous or wicked

desc: Marked by "Why then did You bring me from the womb?" and the plea "Withdraw from me", ending in "to a land of darkness and gloom"
name: Why was I born? Let me alone before I go

name: Job's speech: I loathe my own life

desc: Opens with self-declaration "My soul is weary of my life... I will speak in the bitterness of my soul", then turns to address: "I will say to God: Do not condemn me"
name: Resolved to speak his complaint

desc: A chain of questions put to God: "Does it please You...", "Do You have eyes of flesh?", "Are Your days like those of a mortal?" closing with the assertion "You know that I am not guilty"
name: Does God see as man sees?

desc: Subject turns to God's fashioning of Job: "Your hands shaped me and altogether formed me", "Remember... that You molded me like clay", ending "You concealed these things in Your heart"
name: You made me, and now destroy me

desc: Zophar says no one can hinder God when He acts.
name: Zophar at Job 11:10

desc: Zophar says God knows vain men and sees wickedness.
name: Zophar at Job 11:11

desc: Zophar says vain man thinks himself wise, though he is born as a wild donkey’s colt.
name: Zophar at Job 11:12

desc: Turns to conditional exhortation, "As for you, if you direct your heart and lift up your hands to Him", with the consequence "you will lift up your face without shame"; closes on the contrast "But the eyes of the wicked will fail"
name: If You Repent, Then Blessing

desc: As for you, if you direct your heart and lift up your hands to Him;
name: Zophar's condition: prepare your heart

desc: If you put away the iniquity in your hand, and allow no injustice to dwell in your tents.
name: Zophar's condition: put away iniquity

desc: Then indeed you will lift up your face without shame; you will stand firm and unafraid:
name: Zophar's promise: lift up your face

desc: For you will forget your misery, recalling it only as waters gone by:
name: Zophar's promise: forget your misery

desc: Your life will be brighter than noonday; its darkness will be like the morning.
name: Zophar's promise: age clearer than noon

desc: You will be secure, because there is hope, and you will look around and lie down in safety.
name: Zophar's promise: secure because of hope

desc: You will lie down without fear, and many will court your favor.
name: Zophar's promise: lie down without fear

desc: Speaker formula opens the chapter: "Then Zophar the Naamathite replied"
name: Zophar Begins to Speak

desc: But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and escape will elude them; they will hope for their last breath.
name: Zophar's warning: eyes of the wicked fail

desc: The whole of Zophar's speech, from 'Should this stream of words go unanswered?' to 'when a man is born as a wild donkey’s colt.'
name: Zophar's speech to Job

desc: All of it is the one speech introduced by "Then Zophar the Naamathite replied", addressed throughout to Job in the second person ("you", "your")
name: Zophar's First Speech

desc: Opens with rhetorical challenge "Should this stream of words go unanswered?" and quotes Job back: "You have said, My doctrine is sound"; closes with "Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves"
name: Rebuke of Job's Talk and Claim to Purity

desc: Zophar's opening question.
name: Zophar at Job 11:2

desc: Zophar asks whether Job's lies and mocking should silence others.
name: Zophar at Job 11:3

desc: Zophar repeats Job's own claim about his doctrine and cleanness.
name: Zophar at Job 11:4

desc: Zophar wishes God would speak against Job.
name: Zophar at Job 11:5

desc: Zophar says God would show hidden wisdom and that Job's punishment is less than he deserves.
name: Zophar at Job 11:6

desc: Subject turns from Job's words to God's immeasurability: "Can you fathom the deep things of God?" with dimensions "high as heaven... deeper than hell... longer than the earth"

desc: Zophar questions whether Job can fully search out God.
name: Zophar at Job 11:7

desc: Zophar describes the height and depth of God's ways.
name: Zophar at Job 11:8

desc: Zophar says God's measure exceeds earth and sea.
name: Zophar at Job 11:9

desc: Job's words: The life of every living thing is in His hand, as well as the breath of all mankind.
name: Job at Job 12:10

desc: Job's words: Does not the ear test words as the tongue tastes its food??
name: Job at Job 12:11

desc: Job's words: Wisdom is found with the elderly, and understanding comes with long life.
name: Job at Job 12:12

desc: Subject shifts wholly to God in the third person, "Wisdom and strength belong to God", then a chain of "What He tears down cannot be rebuilt... He leads counselors away barefoot... He pours out contempt on nobles" to the closing image "He makes them stagger like drunkards"
name: God's power to overturn the mighty

desc: Wisdom and strength belong to God; counsel and understanding are His.
name: Job 12:13 speech

desc: What He tears down cannot be rebuilt; the man He imprisons cannot be released.

desc: If He holds back the waters, they dry up, and if He releases them, they overwhelm the land.

desc: True wisdom and power belong to Him. The deceived and the deceiver are His.
name: Job 12:16 speech

desc: He leads counselors away barefoot and makes fools of judges.
name: Job 12:17 speech

desc: He loosens the bonds placed by kings and fastens a belt around their waists.
name: Job 12:18 speech

desc: He leads priests away barefoot and overthrows the established.
name: Job 12:19 speech

desc: Speech formula opens the chapter: "Then Job answered:"
name: Job's reply begins

desc: He deprives the trusted of speech and takes away the discernment of elders.
name: Job 12:20 speech

desc: He pours out contempt on nobles and disarms the mighty.
name: Job 12:21 speech

desc: He reveals the deep things of darkness and brings deep shadows into light.
name: Job 12:22 speech

desc: He makes nations great and destroys them; He enlarges nations, then disperses them.
name: Job 12:23 speech

desc: He deprives the earth’s leaders of reason and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland.

desc: Second-person mockery of the friends, "Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die... I am not inferior to you", ending with the complaint that "The tents of robbers are safe"

desc: Job's words: Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die!.
name: Job at Job 12:2

desc: Job's words: But I also have a mind; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these??
name: Job at Job 12:3

name: Job at Job 12:4

desc: Job's words: The one at ease scorns misfortune as the fate of those whose feet are slipping.
name: Job at Job 12:5

desc: Job's words: The tents of robbers are safe, and those who provoke God are secure— those who carry their god in their hands.
name: Job at Job 12:6

desc: Turns with "But ask the animals, and they will instruct you" -- singular "you" and a new appeal to creation and to the wisdom of "the elderly"

name: Job at Job 12:8

desc: Job's words: Which of all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?
name: Job at Job 12:9

desc: Job's words: Surely He would rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality.
name: Surely He would rebuke you

desc: Job's words: Would His majesty not terrify you? Would the dread of Him not fall upon you??
name: Would His majesty not terrify you?

desc: Job's words: Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.
name: Your maxims are proverbs of ashes

desc: Job's words: "As water disappears from the sea and a river becomes parched and dry"

desc: Job's words: "so a man lies down and does not rise. Until the heavens are no more, he will not be awakened or roused from sleep"
name: Job at Job 14:12

name: If only You would hide me in Sheol

name: Job at Job 14:13

name: Job at Job 14:14

name: Job at Job 14:15

name: Job at Job 14:17

desc: Job says waters wear stones, God washes away plants, and God destroys man's hope.
name: Job at Job 14:19

desc: Job's words: "Man, who is born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble"

name: Job at Job 14:20

desc: Job says a man's sons receive honor or are brought low, but he neither knows nor perceives it.
name: Job at Job 14:21

desc: Job says the man's flesh will have pain and his soul will mourn.
name: Job at Job 14:22

desc: Job's words: "Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure"

desc: Job's words: "Do You open Your eyes to one like this? Will You bring him into judgment before You?"
name: Job at Job 14:3

desc: Job's words: "Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one!"
name: Job at Job 14:4

desc: Job's words: "Since his days are determined and the number of his months is with You, and since You have set limits that he cannot exceed"
name: Job at Job 14:5

desc: Job's words: "look away from him and let him rest, so he can enjoy his day as a hired hand"
name: Job at Job 14:6

desc: Job's words: "If its roots grow old in the ground and its stump dies in the soil"

desc: Job's words: "at the scent of water it will bud and put forth twigs like a sapling"

desc: Eliphaz asks, 'Are the consolations of God not enough for you, even words spoken gently to you?'
name: Are the consolations of God not enough for you, even words spoken gently to you?

desc: Eliphaz asks, 'Why has your heart carried you away, and why do your eyes flash'
name: Why has your heart carried you away, and why do your eyes flash,

desc: The verse: 'as you turn your spirit against God and pour such words from your mouth?'
name: so that you turn your spirit against God

desc: Turns from Job to man in general: "What is man, that he should be clean?" with "If God puts no trust in His holy ones" and "How much less man, who is vile and corrupt"

desc: The verse: 'What is man, that he should be pure, or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?'
name: What is man, that he should be pure,

desc: The verse: 'If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes'
name: If God puts no trust in His holy ones

desc: The verse: 'how much less man, who is vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water?'
name: how much less man, who is vile and corrupt

desc: The verse: 'Listen to me and I will inform you. I will describe what I have seen'
name: Listen to me and I will inform you.

desc: The verse: 'what was declared by wise men and was not concealed from their fathers'
name: Eliphaz at Job 15:18

desc: The verse: 'to whom alone the land was given when no foreigner passed among them'
name: to whom alone the land was given

desc: Speech formula opens the chapter: "Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied"
name: Eliphaz answers again

desc: Third-person doctrine begins "A wicked man writhes in pain all his days" and runs to the summarising "For the company of the godless will be barren"
name: The fate of the wicked man

desc: The verse: 'A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless'
name: Eliphaz at Job 15:20

desc: The verse: 'Sounds of terror fill his ears; in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him'
name: Sounds of terror fill his ears

desc: The verse: 'He despairs of his return from darkness; he is marked for the sword'
name: Eliphaz at Job 15:22

desc: The verse: 'He wanders about as food for vultures; he knows the day of darkness is at hand'
name: He wanders about as food for vultures

desc: The verse: 'Distress and anguish terrify him, overwhelming him like a king poised to attack'
name: Distress and anguish terrify him

desc: For he has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty.
name: Eliphaz at Job 15:25

desc: Rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield:
name: Eliphaz: he runs upon God

desc: Though his face is covered with fat and his waistline bulges with flesh.
name: Eliphaz at Job 15:27

desc: He will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble.
name: Eliphaz: he dwells in desolate cities

desc: He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure. His possessions will not overspread the land.

desc: All that follows "Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied" to the chapter's end is one continuous speech
name: Eliphaz's second speech

desc: Eliphaz asks, 'Does a wise man answer with empty counsel or fill his belly with the hot east wind?'

desc: He will not escape from the darkness; the flame will wither his shoots, and the breath of God’s mouth will carry him away.
name: Eliphaz: the flame dries up his branches

desc: Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness, for emptiness will be his reward.
name: Eliphaz: let not the deceived trust in vanity

desc: It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not flourish.
name: Eliphaz: his branch will not flourish

desc: He will be like a vine stripped of its unripe grapes, like an olive tree that sheds its blossoms.
name: Eliphaz: he shakes off his unripe grape

desc: For the company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery.
name: Eliphaz at Job 15:34

desc: They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit.
name: Eliphaz at Job 15:35

desc: Eliphaz asks, 'Should he argue with useless words or speeches that serve no purpose?'
name: Should he argue with useless words or speeches that serve no purpose?

desc: Eliphaz says, 'But you even undermine the fear of God and hinder meditation before Him'
name: But you even undermine the fear of God and hinder meditation before Him.

desc: Eliphaz says, 'For your iniquity instructs your mouth, and you choose the language of the crafty'
name: For your iniquity instructs your mouth, and you choose the language of the crafty.

desc: Eliphaz says, 'Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you'
name: Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you.

desc: New line of questioning about Job's claim to wisdom: "Were you the first man ever born?" ... "What do you know that we do not?", ending "as you turn your spirit against God"

desc: Eliphaz asks, 'Were you the first man ever born? Were you brought forth before the hills?'
name: Were you the first man ever born? Were you brought forth before the hills?

desc: Eliphaz asks, 'Do you listen in on the council of God or limit wisdom to yourself?'
name: Do you listen in on the council of God or limit wisdom to yourself?

desc: Eliphaz asks, 'What do you know that we do not? What do you understand that is not clear to us?'
name: What do you know that we do not? What do you understand that is not clear to us?
Eliphaz: does a wise man answer with empty counsel?

desc: He breaks me with wound upon wound; He rushes me like a mighty warrior.

desc: Subject shifts to Job's own mourning and innocence: "I have sewn sackcloth over my skin"... "yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure"

desc: My face is red with weeping, and deep shadows ring my eyes;
name: Job's words in Job 16:16

desc: Yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure.
