name: Job's words in Job 24:15

desc: In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves in, never to experience the light.
name: Job's words in Job 24:16

desc: For to them, deep darkness is their morning; surely they are friends with the terrors of darkness!.
name: Job's words in Job 24:17

desc: Subject shifts to singular "He is swift on the surface of the waters" and to future doom: "the worm feeds on them"; "They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone; they are brought low."
name: The wicked man's end

desc: They are but foam on the surface of the water; their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards.
name: Job's words in Job 24:18

desc: As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned.
name: Job's words in Job 24:19

desc: Opening rhetorical question frames the chapter: "Why does the Almighty not reserve times for judgment? Why may those who know Him never see His days?"
name: Why does God set no days of judgment?

desc: Why does the Almighty not reserve times for judgment? Why may those who know Him never see His days??
name: Job's words in Job 24:1

desc: The womb forgets them; the worm feeds on them; they are remembered no more. So injustice is like a broken tree.
name: Job's words in Job 24:20

desc: They prey on the barren and childless, and show no kindness to the widow.
name: Job's words in Job 24:21

desc: Yet by His power, God drags away the mighty; though rising up, they have no assurance of life.
name: Job's words in Job 24:22

desc: He gives them a sense of security, but His eyes are on their ways.
name: Job's words in Job 24:23

desc: They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like heads of grain.
name: Job's words in Job 24:24

desc: Closing formula turns to the hearers: "If this is not so, then who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?"
name: Challenge to the friends

desc: Begins with unnamed subject "Men move boundary stones" and catalogues crimes in the third person, closing on the complaint "God charges no one with wrongdoing."
name: Oppressors rob the poor and God does nothing

desc: Men move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks.
name: Job's words in Job 24:2

desc: They drive away the donkey of the fatherless and take the widow’s ox in pledge.
name: Job's words in Job 24:3

desc: They push the needy off the road and force all the poor of the land into hiding.
name: Job's words in Job 24:4

desc: Indeed, like wild donkeys in the desert, the poor go to work foraging for food; the wasteland is food for their children.
name: Job's words in Job 24:5

desc: They gather fodder in the fields and glean the vineyards of the wicked.
name: Job's words in Job 24:6

desc: Without clothing, they spend the night naked; they have no covering against the cold.
name: Job's words in Job 24:7

desc: Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rocks for want of shelter.
name: Job's words in Job 24:8

desc: The fatherless infant is snatched from the breast; the nursing child of the poor is seized for a debt.
name: Job's words in Job 24:9

desc: Repeated third-person plural verb-first clauses: "They drive away the donkey of the fatherless", "They thrust the needy off the road", "They make the naked spend the night without clothing", "They are among those who rebel against the light", "they do not know the light."
name: "They" clauses cataloguing oppression

desc: Speaker change formula: "Then Bildad the Shuhite replied"
name: Bildad Begins to Speak

desc: Opens with "Then Bildad the Shuhite replied" and runs to the chapter's end without another speaker formula
name: Bildad's Third Speech

desc: Third-person description of God, "Dominion and awe belong to God; He establishes harmony in the heights of heaven", with rhetorical questions on his armies and light
name: God's Dominion in the Heights

desc: Dominion and awe belong to God; He establishes harmony in the heights of heaven. Can His troops be numbered? On whom does His light not rise? How then can a man be just before God? How can one born of woman be pure? If even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not pure in His sight. How much less man, who is but a maggot, and the son of man, who is but a worm!?
name: Bildad at Job 25:2

desc: Bildad's words: 'Dominion and awe belong to God; He establishes harmony in the heights of heaven'
name: Bildad at Job 25:2

desc: Bildad's words: 'Can His troops be numbered? On whom does His light not rise?'
name: Bildad at Job 25:3

desc: Turn to man marked by the inference "How then can a man be just before God?" and closed by "how much less man, who is but a maggot?"
name: How Can Man Be Clean?

desc: Bildad's words: 'How then can a man be just before God? How can one born of woman be pure?'
name: Bildad at Job 25:4

desc: Bildad's words: 'If even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not pure in His sight'
name: Bildad at Job 25:5

desc: Bildad's words: 'how much less man, who is but a maggot, and the son of man, who is but a worm!'
name: Bildad at Job 25:6

desc: He has inscribed a horizon on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness.
name: Job's speech in Job 26:10

desc: The foundations of heaven quake, astounded at His rebuke.
name: Job's speech in Job 26:11

desc: By His power He stirred the sea; by His understanding He shattered Rahab.
name: Job's speech in Job 26:12

desc: "By His breath the skies were cleared; His hand pierced the fleeing serpent"
name: Job 26:13

desc: "Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways" closes the recital by pointing back at it, ending in a question: "Who then can understand the thunder of His power?"
name: Only the edges of his ways

desc: "Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways; how faint is the whisper we hear of Him! Who then can understand the thunder of His power?"
name: Job 26:14

desc: "Then Job answered:" opens a new speaker, and vv.2-4 are all second-person taunts to Bildad: "How you have helped the powerless... To whom have you uttered these words?"
name: Job mocks Bildad's help

desc: How you have helped the powerless and saved the arm that is feeble!?
name: Job's speech in Job 26:2

desc: How you have counseled the unwise and provided fully sound insight!?
name: Job's speech in Job 26:3

desc: To whom have you uttered these words? And whose spirit spoke through you??
name: Job's speech in Job 26:4

desc: The address turns from "you" to third-person description: "Sheol is naked before him", then a chain of "He stretches out the north over empty space... He wraps up the waters in His clouds... He covers the face of the full moon... He has inscribed a horizon on the face of the waters... By His power He stirred the sea"
name: God's power over deep, earth and sea

desc: The dead tremble — those beneath the waters and those who dwell in them.
name: Job's speech in Job 26:5

desc: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
name: Job's speech in Job 26:6

desc: He stretches out the north over empty space; He hangs the earth upon nothing.
name: Job's speech in Job 26:7

desc: He wraps up the waters in His clouds, yet the clouds do not burst under their own weight.
name: Job's speech in Job 26:8

desc: He covers the face of the full moon, spreading over it His cloud.
name: Job's speech in Job 26:9

desc: Headed by the formula "This is the wicked man's portion from God— the heritage the ruthless receive from the Almighty," then a catalogue of his fate down to "It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place"
name: The portion of the wicked man

desc: Job's words in Job 27:13
name: Job at Job 27:13

desc: The condition in Job's speech (Job 27:14)
name: Though his sons are many

desc: The result in Job's speech (Job 27:14)
name: they are destined for the sword; and his offspring will never have enough food.

desc: Job's words in Job 27:14
name: Job at Job 27:14

desc: Job's words in Job 27:15
name: Job at Job 27:15

desc: Job's words in Job 27:16
name: Job at Job 27:16

desc: Job's words in Job 27:17
name: Job at Job 27:17

desc: Job's words in Job 27:18
name: Job at Job 27:18

desc: Job's words in Job 27:19
name: Job at Job 27:19

desc: One unbroken speech framed by "And Job continued his discourse" with no other speaker introduced in the chapter.
name: Job's parable continued

desc: Opens with the narrative formula "And Job continued his discourse" then the oath form "As surely as God lives, who has deprived me of justice"; closes the vow with "As long as I live, my conscience will not accuse me."
name: Job's oath: I will not give up my integrity

desc: Job's words in Job 27:20
name: Job at Job 27:20

desc: Job's words in Job 27:21
name: Job at Job 27:21

desc: Job's words in Job 27:22
name: Job at Job 27:22

desc: Job's words in Job 27:23
name: Job at Job 27:23

desc: Job's speech from Job 27:2 to 12, beginning 'As surely as God lives, who has deprived me of justice — the Almighty, who has embittered my soul —' and ending 'Surely all of you have seen it for yourselves. Why then do you keep up this empty talk?'
name: Job at Job 27:2

desc: Turns from self-defence to imprecation, "May my enemy be like the wicked," followed by rhetorical questions "Will God hear his cry" and a direct rebuke to the friends, "Why then do you keep up this empty talk?"
name: The hypocrite has no hope: Job turns on his friends

desc: Job's words: "He hews out channels in the rocks, and his eyes spot every treasure"
name: Job 28:10 (speech)

desc: Job's words: "He stops up the sources of the streams to bring what is hidden to light"
name: Job 28:11 (speech)

desc: The adversative "But where can wisdom be found?" turns from ore to wisdom; the section is bounded by the price-list "It cannot be bought with gold" ... "nor can it be valued in pure gold."
name: Wisdom Cannot Be Bought

desc: Job's words: "But where can wisdom be found, and where does understanding dwell?"
name: Job 28:12 (speech)

desc: No man can know its value, nor is it found in the land of the living.
name: No man can know its value

desc: The ocean depths say, It is not in me, while the sea declares, It is not with me.
name: The depth and the sea disclaim wisdom

desc: It cannot be bought with gold, nor can its price be weighed out in silver.
name: It cannot be bought with gold

desc: It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.
name: Job at Job 28:16

desc: Neither gold nor crystal can compare to it, nor jewels of fine gold be exchanged for it.
name: Gold and crystal cannot equal it

desc: Coral and quartz are unworthy of mention; the price of wisdom is beyond rubies.
name: the price of wisdom is beyond rubies

desc: Topaz from Cush cannot compare to it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.
name: Topaz from Cush cannot compare to it

desc: Opens with "Surely there is a mine for silver" -- a unit on mining that ends with "to bring what is hidden to light", man's success at finding hidden things.
name: The Miner's Search Underground

desc: Job's words: "Surely there is a mine for silver and a place where gold is refined"
name: Job 28:1 (speech)

desc: The question is repeated as a fresh opening, "From where then does wisdom come?", and answered: "God understands its way"; closes with the quoted verdict "And He said to man, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom."
name: Only God Knows the Way to Wisdom

desc: From where then does wisdom come, and where does understanding dwell??
name: Where does wisdom come from?

desc: It is hidden from the eyes of every living thing and concealed from the birds of the air.
name: Wisdom is hid from all living

desc: Abaddon and Death say, We have heard a rumor about it.
name: Destruction and death have heard of it
‘We have heard a rumor about it.'

desc: But God understands its way, and He knows its place.
name: God understands its way

desc: For He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens;
name: He looks to the ends of the earth

desc: Job's words about God weighing the waters.
name: Job at Job 28:25

desc: Job's words about God's decree for the rain and way for lightning.
name: Job at Job 28:26

desc: Job's words about God seeing, declaring, preparing, and searching out wisdom.
name: Job at Job 28:27

desc: God's words to man about the fear of the Lord.
name: God at Job 28:28

desc: Job reports God's saying about the fear of the Lord.
name: Job at Job 28:28

desc: Job's words: "Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore"
name: Job 28:2 (speech)

desc: Job's words: "Man puts an end to the darkness; he probes the farthest recesses for ore in deepest darkness"
name: Job 28:3 (speech)

desc: Job's words: "Far from human habitation he cuts a shaft in places forgotten by the foot of man. Far from men he dangles and sways"
name: Job 28:4 (speech)

desc: Job's words: "Food may come from the earth, but from below it is transformed as by fire"
name: Job 28:5 (speech)

desc: Job's words: "Its rocks are the source of sapphires, containing flecks of gold"
name: Job 28:6 (speech)

desc: Job's words: "No bird of prey knows that path; no falcon’s eye has seen it"
name: Job 28:7 (speech)

desc: Job's words: "Proud beasts have never trodden it; no lion has ever prowled over it"
name: Job 28:8 (speech)

desc: Job's words: "The miner strikes the flint; he overturns mountains at their base"
name: Job 28:9 (speech)

desc: Personified realms answer: "The deep says, It is not in me: and the sea says, It is not with me" (14); "Abaddon and Death say, With our ears we have heard a report of it" (22).
name: The Places That Deny Having It

desc: The same refrain-question opens both halves: "from where is wisdom found? and where is the place of understanding?" (12) and "From where does wisdom come? and where is the place of understanding?" (20).
name: where does understanding dwell?

desc: The causal connective turns to grounds: "because I rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless"; "I put on righteousness", "I served as eyes to the blind".
name: Why he was blessed: justice to the poor

desc: New quoted thought: "Then I said, I shall die in my nest" — images of root, dew, glory, bow rather than deeds of justice.
name: He expected to die in his nest

desc: I will die in my nest and multiply my days as the sand.
name: Job at Job 29:18

desc: Narrator formula: "And Job continued his discourse" — frame before the speech proper.
name: Job resumes speaking

desc: Returns to the hearers with emphatic "Men listened to me with expectation, waiting silently for my counsel", closing "I ... presided as chief ... dwelt as a king".
name: His counsel awaited like rain

desc: Job says, "I chose their course and presided as chief. So I dwelt as a king among his troops, as a comforter of the mourners"
name: Job's former dignity as chief and comforter

desc: One continuous first-person recollection begun by "How I long for the months gone by" and sustained by past-tense "I was" throughout to "dwelt as a king".
name: Job's lament for his lost honor

desc: Opens with the wish "How I long for the months gone by" and a chain of "when" clauses about God: "when His lamp shone above my head", "when the Almighty was still with me".
name: Longing for the days when God was with him

desc: Subject shifts from household to public life: "When I went out to the city gate"; the young men, aged, princes, nobles all fall silent.
name: Honor at the city gate

desc: Repeated temporal frame: "When his lamp shone", "When the Almighty was still with me", "When I washed my steps in curds", "When I went out to the city gate", "When the ear heard me".
name: "When..." clauses recalling the good days

desc: You speak as a foolish woman speaks?
name: Job at Job 2:10

desc: New characters and time marker: "Now when Job's three friends —Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite — heard about all this adversity that had come upon him"; ends in the silence "no one spoke a word to him."
name: The Three Friends Come and Sit in Silence

desc: The ground for the friends' silence: "they saw how intense his suffering was".
name: they saw how intense his suffering was

desc: The narrator records that none of Job's friends spoke a word to him: "no one spoke a word to him".
name: no one spoke a word to him

desc: Opens with the repeated setting formula "On another day the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord" and closes with the LORD's permission "He is in your hands, but you must spare his life."
name: The Second Council in Heaven

desc: From roaming through the earth ... and walking back and forth in it.
name: Satan at Job 2:2

desc: Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil. He still retains his integrity, even though you incited Me against him to ruin him without cause.
name: God at Job 2:3

desc: Skin for skin! ... A man will give up all he owns in exchange for his life.
name: Satan at Job 2:4

desc: But stretch out Your hand and strike his flesh and bones, and he will surely curse You to Your face.
name: Satan at Job 2:5

desc: but you must spare his life.
name: God at Job 2:6

desc: Scene shifts from heaven to earth: "So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and infected Job with terrible boils"; narration only, no speech.
name: Job Struck with Boils

desc: New speaker introduced: "Then Job’s wife said to him", answered by "But he said unto her", and closed by the narrator's verdict "In all this, Job did not sin in what he said."
name: Job Answers His Wife

desc: Do you still retain your integrity? Curse God and die.
name: Job's wife at Job 2:9

desc: They abhor me and keep far from me...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:10

desc: Because God has unstrung my bow...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:11

desc: The rabble arises at my right...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:12

desc: They tear up my path; they profit from my destruction, with no one to restrain them.
name: Job's words in Job 30:13

desc: They advance as through a wide breach; through the ruins they keep rolling in.
name: Job's words in Job 30:14

desc: Terrors are turned loose against me; they drive away my dignity as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed like a cloud.
name: Job's words in Job 30:15

desc: "And now my soul is poured out within me" begins a shift from human tormentors to bodily affliction, "Night pierces my bones", closing "I have become like dust and ashes."
name: The body poured out

desc: And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction grip me.
name: Job's words in Job 30:16

desc: Night pierces my bones, and my gnawing pains never rest.
name: Job's words in Job 30:17

desc: With great force He grasps my garment; He seizes me by the collar of my tunic.
name: Job's words in Job 30:18

desc: He throws me into the mud, and I have become like dust and ashes.
name: Job's words in Job 30:19

desc: Opens with the reversal formula "But now they mock me, men younger than I am" and then describes their fathers, "whose fathers I considered unworthy"; the unit closes on the verdict "they were driven off the land."
name: Mocked by the sons of outcasts

desc: But now they mock me, men younger than I am...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:1

desc: The address turns to the second person: "I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer... You have ruthlessly turned on me"; ends with "I know that You will bring me down to death."
name: God does not answer

desc: I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer; when I stand up, You merely look at me.
name: Job's words in Job 30:20

desc: You have ruthlessly turned on me; You oppose me with Your strong hand.
name: Job's words in Job 30:21

desc: You snatch me up into the wind and drive me before it; You toss me about in the storm.
name: Job's words in Job 30:22

desc: Yes, I know that You will bring me down to death, to the place appointed for all the living.
name: Job's words in Job 30:23

desc: "Yet no one stretches out his hand" drops back to third person, then the rhetorical appeal "Have I not wept for those in trouble?"; closes the chapter with "My harp is tuned to mourning."
name: I wept for the poor, but evil came

desc: Yet no one stretches out his hand to a ruined man when he cries for help in his distress.
name: Job's words in Job 30:24

desc: Job's words in Job 30:25: 'Have I not wept for those in trouble? Has my soul not grieved for the needy?'
name: Job at Job 30:25

desc: Job's words in Job 30:26: 'But when I hoped for good, evil came; when I looked for light, darkness fell'
name: Job at Job 30:26

desc: Job's words in Job 30:27: 'I am churning within and cannot rest; days of affliction confront me'
name: Job at Job 30:27

desc: Job's words in Job 30:28: 'I go about blackened, but not by the sun. I stand up in the assembly and cry for help'
name: Job at Job 30:28

desc: Job's words in Job 30:29: 'I have become a brother of jackals, a companion of ostriches'
name: Job at Job 30:29

desc: What use to me was the strength of their hands...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:2

desc: Job's words in Job 30:30: 'My skin grows black and peels, and my bones burn with fever'
name: Job at Job 30:30

desc: Job's words in Job 30:31: 'My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping'
name: Job at Job 30:31

desc: Gaunt from poverty and hunger...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:3

desc: They plucked mallow among the shrubs...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:4

desc: They were banished from among men...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:5

desc: so that they lived on the slopes of the wadis...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:6

desc: They cried out among the shrubs...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:7

desc: They were children of fools...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:8

desc: "And now they mock me in song" turns from the fathers back to Job as object of scorn; ends with "my prosperity has passed like a cloud" before a new "And now" in v.16.
name: Now I am their byword

desc: And now they mock me in song...
name: Job's speech in Job 30:9

desc: Each unit begins with the temporal contrast: "But now those who are younger than I" (v.1), "And now I have become their song" (v.9), "And now my soul is poured out within me" (v.16).
name: "But now / And now" reversal opener

desc: Subject turns to household justice: "If I have rejected the cause of my manservant"; closes with "Did not He who made me in the womb also make them?"
name: If I despised my servant's cause

desc: Job's conditional self-accusation: 'If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or maidservant when they made a complaint against me'
name: Job: if I despised my servants' cause

desc: Job asks what he would do when God rises up: 'what will I do when God rises to judge? How will I answer when called to account?'
name: Job: what shall I answer when God visits

desc: Job's claim that the same God made him and his servant: 'Did not He who made me in the womb also make them?'
name: Job: God made me and my servant in the womb

desc: A chain of charges about the needy, "If I have denied the desires of the poor", to the curse "then may my arm fall from my shoulder" and reason "calamity from God terrifies me"
name: If I withheld from the poor, widow and fatherless

desc: Job's conditional: 'If I have denied the desires of the poor or allowed the widow’s eyes to fail'
name: Job: if I withheld from the poor

desc: Job's conditional: 'if I have eaten my morsel alone, not sharing it with the fatherless —'
name: Job: if I ate my morsel alone

desc: Job's claim: 'though from my youth I reared him as would a father, and from my mother’s womb I guided the widow—'
name: Job at Job 31:18

desc: Job's conditional: 'if I have seen one perish for lack of clothing, or a needy man without a cloak'
name: Job: if I have seen one perish for lack of clothing

desc: Opens the oath with "I have made a covenant with my eyes"; grounded by "For what is the allotment of God from above?" and closed by "Does He not see my ways and count my every step?"
name: Covenant with his eyes; God sees all his steps

desc: Job's conditional: 'if his heart has not blessed me for warming him with the fleece of my sheep'
name: Job: if the poor did not bless me

desc: Job's conditional: 'if I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless because I saw that I had support in the gate'
name: Job at Job 31:21

desc: Job's imprecation: 'then may my arm fall from my shoulder and be torn from its socket'
name: Job's self-curse on his arm

desc: Job's claim: 'For calamity from God terrifies me, and His splendor I cannot overpower'
name: Job: calamity from God terrifies me

desc: Turns to hidden idolatry: "If I have put my trust in gold"... "if I have beheld the sun in its radiance"; closes "for I would have denied God on high"
name: If I trusted gold or worshipped sun and moon

desc: Job's conditional: 'If I have put my trust in gold or called pure gold my security'
name: Job: if I made gold my hope

desc: Job says, 'if I have rejoiced in my great wealth because my hand had gained so much,' (Job 31:25).
name: Job at Job 31:25

desc: Job says, 'if I have beheld the sun in its radiance or the moon moving in splendor,' (Job 31:26).
name: Job: if I have beheld the sun in its radiance

desc: Job says, 'so that my heart was secretly enticed and my hand threw a kiss from my mouth,' (Job 31:27).
name: Job: And my heart has been secretly enticed

desc: Job's stated reason: this would be denying God above (Job 31:28).
name: I would have denied God on high

desc: Job's claim that this would be an iniquity deserving judgment (Job 31:28).
name: Job at Job 31:28

desc: Job says, 'this would also be an iniquity to be judged, for I would have denied God on high.' (Job 31:28).
name: Job at Job 31:28

desc: New charges of malice, hospitality and concealment: "If I have rejoiced in my enemy’s ruin"... "if I have covered my transgressions like Adam"
name: If I gloated over my enemy or hid my sin

desc: Job says, 'If I have rejoiced in my enemy's ruin, or exulted when evil befell him-' (Job 31:29).
name: Job at Job 31:29

desc: Job says, 'I have not allowed my mouth to sin by asking for his life with a curse-' (Job 31:30).
name: Job: I have not allowed my mouth to sin

desc: Job says, 'if the men of my house have not said, ‘Who is there who has not had his fill?'-' (Job 31:31).
name: Job: if the men of my house have not said

desc: Job says, 'but no stranger had to lodge on the street, for my door has been open to the traveler-' (Job 31:32).
name: Job: no stranger had to lodge on the street

desc: Job says, 'if I have covered my transgressions like Adam by hiding my guilt in my heart,' (Job 31:33).
name: Job: if I have covered my transgressions like Adam

desc: Job says, 'because I greatly feared the crowds and the contempt of the clans terrified me, so that I kept silent and would not go outside-' (Job 31:34).
name: Job: because I greatly feared the crowds

desc: The if/then form breaks for a cry: "Oh, that I had one to hear me! Here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me"
name: Job's wish that the Almighty would answer him

desc: Job says, 'Oh, that I had one to hear me! Here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me; let my accuser compose an indictment.' (Job 31:35).
name: Job: Oh, that I had one to hear me!

desc: Job says, 'Surely I would carry it on my shoulder and wear it like a crown.' (Job 31:36).
name: Job: surely I would carry it on my shoulder

desc: Job's statement in Job 31:37.
name: Job at Job 31:37

desc: Returns to the oath form, "if my land cries out against me"... "let briers grow instead of wheat", and closes with the narrator's note "Thus conclude the words of Job."
name: If my land cries against me -- and Job's words end

desc: Job's conditional statement in Job 31:38.
name: Job at Job 31:38

desc: Job's conditional statement in Job 31:39.
name: Job at Job 31:39

desc: Job's curse in Job 31:40.
name: Job at Job 31:40

desc: First full if/then self-curse: "If I have walked in falsehood... then may another eat what I have sown"
name: If I walked with vanity, let another eat my harvest

name: God at Job 38:15

desc: Series of "Have you journeyed to the vents of the sea?... Have the gates of death been revealed to you?" closing with the taunt "Surely you know, for you were already born?"
name: The Deep, Death, and the Dwelling of Light

desc: God speaking to Job: 'Have you journeyed to the vents of the sea or walked in the trenches of the deep?'
name: God at Job 38:16

desc: God speaking to Job: 'Have the gates of death been revealed to you? Have you seen the gates of the shadow of death?'
name: God at Job 38:17

desc: God speaking to Job: 'Have you surveyed the extent of the earth? Tell Me, if you know all this'
name: God at Job 38:18

desc: God speaking to Job: 'Where is the way to the home of light? Do you know where darkness resides'
name: God at Job 38:19

desc: Narrative introduction "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind" plus the summons "Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me" — the frame before the questions begin.
name: Brace Yourself Like a Man: The Challenge

desc: Opens with the narrator's formula "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said" and runs unbroken as one divine speech of interrogation to the chapter's end.
name: The LORD Answers Job Out of the Whirlwind

desc: God speaking to Job: 'so you can lead it back to its border? Do you know the paths to its home?'
name: God at Job 38:20

desc: God speaking to Job: 'Surely you know, for you were already born! And the number of your days is great!'
name: God at Job 38:21

desc: Subject shifts to stored weather: "Have you entered the storehouses of snow?" through "From whose womb does the ice emerge?" ending "when the waters become hard as stone and the surface of the deep is frozen."
name: Snow, Hail, Rain, and Ice

desc: God speaking to Job: 'Have you entered the storehouses of snow or observed the storehouses of hail'
name: God at Job 38:22

desc: God speaking to Job: 'which I hold in reserve for times of trouble, for the day of war and battle?'
name: God at Job 38:23

desc: God speaking to Job: 'In which direction is the lightning dispersed, or the east wind scattered over the earth?'
name: God at Job 38:24

desc: God's rhetorical question about dividing the watercourse and making a way for the lightning.
name: God at Job 38:25

desc: God's purpose clause about sending rain on uninhabited places.
name: God at Job 38:26

desc: God's purpose clause about satisfying the waste ground and making the bud spring forth.
name: God at Job 38:27

desc: God's rhetorical questions about the father of rain and the begetting of dew.
name: God at Job 38:28

desc: God's rhetorical questions about the origins of ice and frost.
name: God at Job 38:29
The LORD's answer out of the whirlwind

desc: God's question to Job: "Who is this who obscures My counsel by words without knowledge?"
name: Who is this who obscures My counsel

desc: God's statement about waters hiding themselves and becoming like stone and the surface of the deep frozen.
name: God at Job 38:30

desc: Turns to the heavens — "Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades" — and closes "Do you know the laws of the heavens?"
name: The Bands of the Constellations

desc: God's rhetorical question about binding Pleiades and loosing Orion.
name: God at Job 38:31

desc: God's rhetorical question: 'Can you bring forth the constellations in their seasons or lead out the Bear and her cubs?'
name: God at Job 38:32

desc: God's rhetorical question about knowing heaven's ordinances and setting its dominion.
name: God at Job 38:33

desc: Back to earth's sky: "Can you command the clouds"; ends with the dust that "hardens into a mass."
name: Clouds and Lightning at Your Command

desc: God's rhetorical question about lifting the voice to the clouds.
name: God at Job 38:34

desc: God's rhetorical question about sending lightnings.
name: God at Job 38:35

desc: God's rhetorical question about placing wisdom and giving understanding.
name: God at Job 38:36

desc: The LORD's rhetorical question: 'Who has the wisdom to count the clouds? Or who can tilt the water jars of the heavens'
name: Who has the wisdom to count the clouds?

desc: The LORD's words: 'when the dust hardens into a mass and the clods of earth stick together?'
name: when the dust hardens into a mass

desc: Subject changes entirely from weather to living creatures: "Can you hunt the prey for a lioness?" and "Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food?"
name: Who Feeds the Lion and the Raven

desc: The LORD's challenge: 'Can you hunt the prey for a lioness or satisfy the hunger of young lions'
name: Can you hunt the prey for a lioness

desc: God's command to Job: "Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me"
name: Now brace yourself like a man

desc: The LORD's words: 'when they crouch in their dens and lie in wait in the thicket?'
name: when they crouch in their dens

desc: The LORD's question: 'Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food?'
name: Who provides food for the raven

desc: First interrogation begins "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" and closes with the creation's celebration, "the morning stars sang together."
name: The Foundations of the Earth

desc: God's question: "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding"
name: God at Job 38:4

desc: God's question: "Who fixed its measurements? Surely you know! Or who stretched a measuring line across it?"
name: Who fixed its measurements?

desc: God's question: "On what were its foundations set, or who laid its cornerstone"
name: God at Job 38:6

desc: God's statement: "while the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?"
name: while the morning stars sang together

desc: New subject marked by "Who enclosed the sea behind doors"; closes with quoted decree "You may come this far, but no farther; here your proud waves must stop."
name: Bars and Doors for the Sea

desc: God's question: "Who enclosed the sea behind doors when it burst forth from the womb"
name: Who enclosed the sea behind doors

desc: God's statement: "when I made the clouds its garment and thick darkness its blanket"
name: when I made the clouds its garment

desc: Can you hold him to the furrow with a harness? Will he plow the valleys behind you??
name: God at Job 39:10

desc: Can you rely on his great strength? Will you leave your hard work to him??
name: God at Job 39:11

desc: Can you trust him to bring in your grain and gather it to your threshing floor??
name: God at Job 39:12

desc: 'The wings of the ostrich flap joyfully, but cannot match the pinions and feathers of the stork' opens; the unit is held together by 'For she leaves her eggs' and 'For God has deprived her of wisdom', ending as 'she laughs at the horse and its rider' — which hands off to the next subject.
name: The Foolish Ostrich

desc: The wings of the ostrich flap joyfully, but cannot match the pinions and feathers of the stork?
name: God at Job 39:13

desc: For she leaves her eggs on the ground and lets them warm in the sand,
name: God at Job 39:14

desc: She forgets that a foot may crush them, or a wild animal may trample them.
name: God at Job 39:15

desc: She treats her young harshly, as if not her own, with no concern that her labor was in vain;
name: God at Job 39:16

desc: For God has deprived her of wisdom; He has not endowed her with understanding.
name: God at Job 39:17

desc: Yet when she proudly spreads her wings, she laughs at the horse and its rider.
name: God at Job 39:18

desc: 'Do you give strength to the horse?' begins a sustained portrait ending with 'He catches the scent of battle from afar — the shouts of captains and the cry of war.'
name: The War Horse

desc: Do you give strength to the horse or adorn his neck with a mane??
name: God at Job 39:19

desc: Opens with the challenge 'Do you know when mountain goats give birth?' and closes when the young 'leave and do not return'; the subject shifts to the wild donkey at v.5.
name: The Wild Goats and the Hinds Giving Birth

desc: Do you know when mountain goats give birth? Have you watched the doe bear her fawn??
name: God at Job 39:1

desc: Do you make him leap like a locust, striking terror with his proud snorting?.
name: God at Job 39:20

desc: He paws in the valley and rejoices in his strength; he charges into battle.
name: God at Job 39:21

desc: He laughs at fear, frightened of nothing; he does not turn back from the sword.
name: God at Job 39:22

desc: A quiver rattles at his side, along with a flashing spear and lance.
name: God at Job 39:23

desc: Trembling with excitement, he devours the distance; he cannot stand still when the ram’s horn sounds.
name: God at Job 39:24

desc: 'At the blast of the horn, he snorts with fervor. He catches the scent of battle from afar — the shouts of captains and the cry of war'
name: God at Job 39:25

desc: 'Does the hawk take flight by your understanding' and 'Does the eagle soar at your command' start the last pair of birds; the chapter closes 'where the slain are, there he is.'
name: The Hawk and the Eagle

desc: 'Does the hawk take flight by your understanding and spread his wings toward the south?'
name: God at Job 39:26

desc: 'Does the eagle soar at your command and make his nest on high?'
name: God at Job 39:27

desc: 'He dwells on a cliff and lodges there; his stronghold is on a rocky crag'
name: God at Job 39:28

desc: 'From there he spies out food; his eyes see it from afar'
name: God at Job 39:29

desc: Can you count the months they are pregnant? Do you know the time they give birth??
name: God at Job 39:2

desc: Job 39:30: 'His young ones feast on blood; and where the slain are, there he is'
name: God at Job 39:30

desc: They crouch down and bring forth their young; they deliver their newborn.
name: God at Job 39:3

desc: Their young ones thrive and grow up in the open field; they leave and do not return.
name: The LORD describes the young ones growing up

desc: New creature and new question-form: 'Who set the wild donkey free?'; runs to 'searching for any green thing' before the wild ox is named.
name: The Free Wild Donkey

desc: Who set the wild donkey free? Who released the swift donkey from the harness??
name: The LORD asks who set the wild donkey free

desc: I made the wilderness his home and the salt flats his dwelling.
name: God at Job 39:6

desc: He scorns the tumult of the city and never hears the shouts of a driver.
name: The LORD describes the wild ass's scorn

desc: He roams the mountains for pasture, searching for any green thing.
name: The LORD describes the wild ass's pasture

desc: 'Will the wild ox consent to serve you? Will he stay by your manger at night?' begins a four-verse chain of 'Can you... Will you... Can you trust him' all about one beast.
name: The Wild Ox Will Not Serve You

desc: Will the wild ox consent to serve you? Will he stay by your manger at night??
name: God at Job 39:9

desc: For that night did not shut the doors of the womb to hide the sorrow from my eyes
name: Job at Job 3:10

desc: The curses stop and a question form opens: "Why did I not perish at birth?" followed by "For now I would be lying down in peace" and the "There the wicked cease from raging" description of Sheol.
name: Why did I not die at birth? The rest of the grave
Why did I not perish at birth
Why were there knees to receive me

desc: Job says that had he died, he would have lain still, slept, and been at rest.
name: Job at Job 3:13

desc: Job says the dead rest with kings and counselors who built desolate places.
name: Job at Job 3:14

desc: Job says the dead rest with princes who had gold and filled their houses with silver.
name: Job at Job 3:15

desc: Job wishes he had been like a hidden stillbirth or infants that never saw light.
name: Job at Job 3:16

desc: Job says in death the wicked stop troubling and the weary rest.
name: Job at Job 3:17

desc: Job says prisoners rest together in death and no longer hear the oppressor.
name: Job at Job 3:18

desc: Job says all, small and great, are in death, and the slave is freed from his master.
name: Job at Job 3:19

desc: Narrator frame in the third person: "After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth. And this is what he said" — introduces the speech that follows.
name: Job opens his mouth

desc: New question with a new subject — not his own birth but sufferers generally: "Why is light given to the miserable"; ends turning back on himself, "I sigh when food is put before me... for trouble has come."
name: Why is light given to the miserable?

desc: Job asks why light and life are given to the miserable and bitter.
name: Job at Job 3:20

desc: Job speaks of the miserable who long for death and search for it like hidden treasures.
name: Job at Job 3:21

desc: Job says the miserable rejoice when they can find the grave.
name: Job at Job 3:22

desc: Job asks why light is given to a man whose way is hidden and whom God has hedged in.
name: Job at Job 3:23

desc: Job says his sighing comes before eating and his groans pour out like water.
name: Job at Job 3:24

desc: Job's statement that the thing he greatly feared and the thing he was afraid of have come upon him.
name: Job at Job 3:25

desc: Job's statement that he had no safety, rest, or quiet, yet trouble came.
name: I am not at ease or quiet; I have no rest

desc: Begins with the jussive formula "May the day of my birth perish" and runs through a chain of "let" curses on day and night, closing with the causal "For that night did not shut the doors of the womb".
name: Curse on the day of his birth

desc: The whole speech introduced by "Job answered" and ended by the chapter break before "Then answered Eliphaz" (4:1).
name: Job's lament over his birth
May the day of my birth perish
If only that day had turned to darkness!
May darkness and gloom reclaim it
If only darkness had taken that night away!
Behold, may that night be barren
May it be cursed by those who curse the day
May its morning stars grow dark

desc: Each section opens with an unanswerable interrogative: "Why did I not die from the womb?" and "Why is light given to the one in misery"; also "Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden".
name: Why-question demanding an accounting for life given

desc: Subject changes entirely at "Look at Behemoth, which I made along with you"; the rest describes him in the third person to the chapter's end
name: Behemoth

desc: "The LORD said to Job" opens a fresh speech formula; "Will the faultfinder contend with the Almighty?"
name: The LORD's challenge to the one who contends

desc: God's words in Job 40:2: 'Will the faultfinder contend with the Almighty? Let him who argues with God give an answer'
name: God at Job 40:2

desc: Speaker changes: "Then Job answered the LORD"; Job speaks to God, "How can I reply to You?"
name: Job's hand on his mouth

desc: Job's words in Job 40:4-5: 'Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth. I have spoken once, but I have no answer — twice, but I have nothing to add'
name: Job at Job 40:4

desc: New speech formula "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said" with "Now brace yourself like a man"; closes with "Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you"
name: Brace yourself like a man: can your own right hand save you?

desc: Bounded by "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said" and running unbroken by any new speaker formula to verse 24
name: The LORD's second speech from the whirlwind

desc: God's words in Job 40:7-12: 'Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me. Would you really annul My justice? Would you condemn Me to justify yourself? Do you have an arm like God’s? Can you thunder with a voice like His? Then adorn yourself with majesty and splendor, and clothe yourself with honor and glory. Unleash the fury of your wrath; look on every proud man and bring him low. Look on every proud man and humble him; trample the wicked where they stand'
name: God at Job 40:7

desc: God's rhetorical question about standing before him.
name: God at Job 41:10

desc: God's declaration of ownership over all under heaven.
name: God at Job 41:11

desc: Announced by "I cannot keep silent about his limbs, his power and graceful form" then an anatomy in third person: face, teeth, scales, eyes, mouth, neck, flesh, heart.
name: The Parts and Armour of Leviathan

desc: God's promise to declare leviathan's parts.
name: God at Job 41:12

desc: The LORD's rhetorical question about Leviathan's garment and double bridle.
name: God at Job 41:13

desc: The LORD asks who can open Leviathan's jaws and describes his teeth as terrible.
name: God at Job 41:14

desc: The LORD describes Leviathan's scales as his pride, tightly sealed.
name: God at Job 41:15

desc: The LORD describes the closeness of Leviathan's scales.
name: God at Job 41:16

desc: The LORD describes how Leviathan's scales are inseparably joined.
name: God at Job 41:17

desc: The LORD describes Leviathan's sneezings producing light and eyes like the morning eyelids.
name: God at Job 41:18

desc: The LORD describes fire and sparks coming from Leviathan's mouth.
name: God at Job 41:19

desc: A chain of second-person taunts opening "Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook?" and closing with the imperative "If you lay a hand on him, you will remember the battle and never repeat it!"
name: Can You Catch Leviathan?

desc: God's question to Job about drawing out leviathan.
name: God at Job 41:1

desc: The LORD describes smoke from Leviathan's nostrils like a boiling pot.
name: God at Job 41:20

desc: The LORD describes Leviathan's breath kindling coals and a flame from his mouth.
name: God at Job 41:21

desc: The LORD describes strength in Leviathan's neck and the transformation of sorrow to joy.
name: God at Job 41:22

desc: The LORD describes the firm and immovable flakes of Leviathan's flesh.
name: God at Job 41:23

desc: The LORD describes Leviathan's heart as firm as a stone and hard as a lower millstone.
name: God at Job 41:24

desc: Shifts from anatomy to battle: "When Leviathan rises up, the mighty are terrified"; "The sword that reaches him has no effect"; "he laughs at the sound of the lance."
name: No Weapon Can Touch Him

desc: When Leviathan rises up, the mighty are terrified; they withdraw before his thrashing.
name: Job 41:25

desc: The sword that reaches him has no effect, nor does the spear or dart or arrow.
name: Job 41:26

desc: He regards iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood.
name: Job 41:27

desc: No arrow can make him flee; slingstones become like chaff to him.
name: Job 41:28

desc: A club is regarded as straw, and he laughs at the sound of the lance.
name: Job 41:29

desc: God's question about hooking leviathan's nose and jaw.
name: God at Job 41:2

desc: His undersides are jagged potsherds, spreading out the mud like a threshing sledge.
name: Job 41:30

desc: He makes the depths seethe like a cauldron; he makes the sea like a jar of ointment.
name: Job 41:31

desc: He leaves a glistening wake behind him; one would think the deep had white hair!.
name: Job 41:32

desc: Summary verdict: "Nothing on earth is his equal" ... "he is king over all the proud" closes the poem.
name: king over all the proud

desc: Nothing on earth is his equal— a creature devoid of fear!.
name: Job 41:33

desc: He looks down on all the haughty; he is king over all the proud.
name: Job 41:34

desc: God's question about whether leviathan will plead.
name: God at Job 41:3

desc: God's question about covenant and servanthood.
name: God at Job 41:4

desc: God's question about playing with leviathan.
name: God at Job 41:5

desc: God's question about feasting and trading leviathan.
name: God at Job 41:6

desc: God's question about piercing leviathan's hide.
name: God at Job 41:7

desc: God's command to remember the battle.
name: God at Job 41:8

desc: "Behold" opens a turn from Job's inability to God's own claim: "Then who is able to stand against Me?" and "Everything under heaven is Mine" — the first person replaces the beast as subject.
name: None Can Stand Before Me

desc: God's statement about the vain hope of capturing leviathan.
name: God at Job 41:9

desc: New subject, blessing rather than rebuke: "the LORD restored his prosperity"... "So the LORD blessed Job’s latter days more than his first", ending with the death formula "And so Job died, old and full of years"
name: Job's Fortunes Restored and His Death

desc: Speech formula opens: "Then Job replied to the LORD"; second person throughout ("I know that You can do all things") and closes with "Therefore I retract my words, and I repent in dust and ashes."
name: Job's Final Answer and Repentance

desc: Job's reply to the LORD: 'I know that You can do all things... Therefore I retract my words, and I repent in dust and ashes.'
name: Job's final answer to the LORD

desc: The LORD's rebuke and command: 'My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends... take seven bulls and seven rams...'
name: God at Job 42:7

desc: Narrative resumes and the speaker changes: "After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite"; closes when the command is carried out, "did as the LORD had told them."
name: The LORD Rebukes the Three Friends

desc: Eliphaz describes the breaking of the lion's might.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:10

desc: Eliphaz notes the perishing and scattering of the lion and its cubs.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:11

desc: "Now a word came to me secretly" begins a first-person narrative of a vision, closing with "I heard a voice, saying"
name: The night vision and the spirit

desc: Eliphaz mentions a secret thing brought to him.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:12

desc: Eliphaz's narrative of his night vision, beginning 'In disquieting visions in the night'.
name: Eliphaz's account of the night vision

desc: The quoted oracle begins after "a voice, saying": "Can a mortal be more righteous than God?" and runs to "they die without wisdom"
name: The voice: no man is pure before God

desc: Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker? If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust, who can be crushed like a moth! They are smashed to pieces from dawn to dusk; unnoticed, they perish forever. Are not their tent cords pulled up, so that they die without wisdom?.
name: a spirit at Job 4:16

desc: Narrative formula introducing a new speaker: "Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied"
name: Eliphaz begins to speak

desc: All that follows "answered and said" is one continuous speech by Eliphaz to Job
name: First speech of Eliphaz

desc: Opens with direct address to Job, "If one ventures a word with you"; holds together by the contrast "you have instructed many" ... "But now trouble has come upon you, and you are weary"
name: You instructed others, now you faint

desc: Eliphaz's opening question to Job.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:2

desc: Eliphaz reminds Job of his past instruction and strengthening.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:3

desc: Eliphaz continues about Job's supportive words.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:4

desc: Eliphaz notes that trouble has now come to Job.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:5

desc: Eliphaz questions whether Job's piety is his confidence and hope.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:6

desc: New appeal turns to general doctrine: "Consider now, I plead: Who, being innocent, has ever perished?" and ends with the lion imagery, "The old lion perishes for lack of prey"
name: The wicked reap what they sow

desc: Eliphaz asks being innocent righteous.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:7

desc: Eliphaz states that those who sow iniquity reap it.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:8

desc: Eliphaz says the wicked are destroyed by God's blast and breath.
name: Eliphaz at Job 4:9

desc: He gives rain to the earth and sends water upon the fields:
name: God gives rain

desc: He sets the lowly on high, so that mourners are lifted to safety.
name: The low exalted to safety

desc: He thwarts the schemes of the crafty, so that their hands find no success.
name: God disappoints the crafty

desc: He catches the wise in their craftiness, and sweeps away the plans of the cunning.
name: He catches the wise in their craftiness

desc: They encounter darkness by day and grope at noon as in the night.
name: They encounter darkness by day

desc: He saves the needy from the sword in their mouth and from the clutches of the powerful.
name: He saves the needy from the sword

desc: So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.
name: the poor have hope

desc: Marked off by "Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects" and the direct address "do not despise the discipline of the Almighty"; from here on all is second person promise, "He will rescue you", "You will be hidden", "You will come to the grave in full vigor."
name: Happy is the man God corrects

desc: Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty:
name: Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects

desc: For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal.
name: He wounds, but He also binds

desc: He will rescue you from six calamities; no harm will touch you in seven.
name: He will rescue you from six calamities

desc: The whole chapter continues the speech begun at "Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered" (4:1), one address to Job throughout, sealed by "hear it and know for yourself."
name: Eliphaz's second argument

desc: Opens with imperative to Job, "Call out if you please, but who will answer"; held together by "For resentment kills a fool" and "I have seen a fool taking root", closing with the maxim "Yet man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward"
name: The fool's wrath destroys him

desc: Call out if you please, but who will answer? To which of the holy ones will you turn??
name: Eliphaz asks whom Job will call

desc: In famine He will redeem you from death, and in battle from the stroke of the sword.
name: In famine He will redeem you from death

desc: You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and will not fear havoc when it comes.
name: hidden from the scourge of the tongue

desc: You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth.
name: You will laugh at destruction and famine

desc: For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the wild animals will be at peace with you.
name: a covenant with the stones of the field

desc: You will know that your tent is secure, and find nothing amiss when inspecting your home.
name: your tent is secure

desc: You will know that your offspring will be many, your descendants like the grass of the earth.
name: Eliphaz promises Job great seed and offspring

desc: You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.
name: Eliphaz promises Job a full age in the grave

desc: A closing formula in the first person plural breaks the run of promises: "Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself"
name: Closing appeal: we have searched it out

desc: Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself.
name: Eliphaz at Job 5:27

desc: For resentment kills a fool, and envy slays the simple.
name: Wrath kills the foolish man

desc: I have seen a fool taking root, but suddenly his house was cursed.
name: a fool taking root

desc: His sons are far from safety, crushed in court without a defender.
name: Children far from safety

desc: The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.
name: The hungry eat his harvest

desc: For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground;
name: Affliction comes not from dust

desc: Yet man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward.
name: Man is born to trouble

desc: Turn to first person resolve, "However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him —", then a chain of participial praise "who does great things", "He gives rain", ending in the summary "So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth"
name: Eliphaz would commit his cause to God

desc: However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him —:
name: I would appeal to God

desc: The One who does great and unsearchable things, wonders without number:
name: God does great things

desc: It still brings me comfort, and joy through unrelenting pain, that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
name: It still brings me comfort

desc: What strength do I have, that I should still hope? What is my future, that I should be patient??
name: What strength do I have, that I should still hope?

desc: Is my strength like that of stone, or my flesh made of bronze??
name: Is my strength like that of stone

desc: Job's rhetorical question: 'Is there any help within me now that success is driven from me?' (Job 6:13).
name: Job at Job 6:13

desc: Subject turns entirely to the friends: "A despairing man should have the kindness of his friend"; the brook simile is developed to "For now you are of no help; you see terror, and you are afraid"
name: Friends like a vanishing brook

desc: Job's statement about pity to the afflicted and forsaking the fear of the Almighty (Job 6:14).

desc:
A verdict the New Testament pronounces on Abraham, in Paul's letters. 'Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.' (Rom 4:3), against works explicitly: 'If Abraham was indeed justified by works, he had something to boast about, but not before God.' (Rom 4:2). Galatians 3:6 says it again in the same words.

Paired with [[justified_by_works]], the letter of James on the same man and the same deed. James gives his own frame for how the two go together: 'I will show you my faith by my deeds' (Jas 2:18), and of Abraham, 'his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did' (2:22). Both letters are there, each in its own words.

Hebrews 11 is a third voice, and it does not say quite the same thing as Paul. Paul argues that Abraham was justified by faith; Hebrews says he acted by faith — 'By faith Abraham, when called ... obeyed' (11:8), 'By faith he dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country' (11:9). The claims are close and they are not identical, and flattening one into the other would lose the difference.

What makes it belong here anyway is 11:17. Hebrews attributes to faith the same deed James names: 'By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar', and 'justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar' (Jas 2:21). One act at Moriah, which all three letters cite.
name: justified by faith

desc:

Paired with [[justified_by_faith]]. The letter names its author only as James (Jas 1:1), and which James is a reading the text does not settle.

The deed it rests on is the one Hebrews 11:17 gives as an act of faith, and James joins the two in his own words: 'You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did' (Jas 2:22). All three writers cite the same act at Moriah.

Romans 8 works by opposition throughout — flesh against Spirit at verses 1, 4, 5, 9 and 13, death against life, bondage against adoption. Five 'not X but Y' constructions in thirteen verses.

It also gives the Spirit something no other passage does: 'the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words' (8:26). An action attributed to the Spirit alone. Elsewhere the Spirit is given, sent, poured out, received or fallen upon; here it acts, and on its own initiative.

'It is written: Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.' (Matt 4:4), quoting Deut 8:3.

**Named as a quotation and not word for word.** Deuteronomy has 'man does not live on bread alone' and 'from the mouth of the LORD'; Matthew has 'shall not live on bread alone' and 'the mouth of God'. Only, alone; the LORD, God. Matthew says 'It is written' and then does not write it as it is.

desc:
'It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’ s wife' (1Cor 5:1).

He is an individual here for the same reason the woman taken in adultery is: the text describes an individual, whether or not it can name him. What it does not hold is the instruction about him. Paul tells the congregation to 'Expel the wicked man from among you' (5:13), and that is an instruction rather than an event — the letter does not report whether it was carried out.

The text offers something that reads like the sequel and never says it is one. 2 Corinthians 2:6-7: 'This punishment which was inflicted by the many is sufficient for such a one; so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive him.' A punishment inflicted, a man restored, in a later letter to the same church — and no verse connects the two. Many readers join them; the text declines, and records the possibility here where it can be weighed.

desc:
'go and tell My brothers, I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.' (John 20:17).

One sentence, both framings, kept apart. It would have been shorter to say our Father, and the verse does not. The possessive is repeated — my Father, and your Father; my God, and your God — so the sentence joins the two relations and declines to merge them.

John's Father is almost always the Son's ('To this very day My Father is at His work', 5:17); Matthew's is almost always the hearers' ('your Father in heaven'). This is the one verse that says both at once, and it is spoken to a single named person on the morning of the resurrection.

The verse is recorded; the reading is left.
name: my Father, and your Father

desc:
'My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me' (Dan 6:22).

What gets him into the den is a habit, not a confrontation. He hears the decree is signed and goes home and prays as he had done 'before' — windows open toward Jerusalem, three times a day (6:10). The text is careful to say he changed nothing.

The king spends the night fasting and comes at dawn, and it is he who asks whether the God has delivered (6:20). The rescue is narrated as an answer to somebody else's question.

The measure is the supplier rather than the need, which is the same move Rom 8:32 makes from the other direction: 'He who did not spare His own Son ... how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?'
name: my God will supply all your needs

desc:
'My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.' (2Cor 12:9), closing with 'when I am weak, then I am strong' (12:10).

**An answer to a request that was refused.** Paul asks three times for the thorn to be removed and this is what he is given instead, which is the context the verse is most often quoted without.
name: my grace is sufficient for you

desc:
'At that time Hannah prayed: My heart rejoices in the LORD' (1Sam 2:1).

Almost none of it is about the child she asked for. After the first verse it turns to reversal, and stays there: the full hire themselves for bread and the hungry cease, the barren bears seven (2:5), and 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes' (2:8).

Mary's song at Luke 1:46-55 does the same thing in the same order — opens on her own soul, turns within two verses to reversal, and ends on the mighty put down and the hungry filled. Luke does not say so.
name: My heart rejoices in the LORD

desc:
'Thomas replied, My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28).

The strongest confession in the gospels comes from the man who refused to believe it. Eight days earlier he had named his terms exactly — the print of the nails, and his hand in the side (20:25) — and the text does not record him taking them up.

The reply moves the subject off him: 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' (20:29).
name: my Lord and my God

desc:
'I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them. He will feed them and be their shepherd.' (Ezek 34:23).

Said roughly four centuries after David died, in the middle of a chapter condemning the shepherds of Israel for feeding themselves. Ezekiel 37:24 repeats it and Jeremiah 30:9 has the same thing.

It is the clearest place a man's name is used for something other than the man, and what it means by it — a descendant, a return, a figure — is exactly the argument.
name: My servant David will be their shepherd

desc:
'My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me.' (John 10:27).

Three clauses and the following comes last, after the hearing and the being known. It is the shepherd figure of Ps 23 with the direction of travel stated: in the psalm the sheep is led, here the sheep follows.
name: My sheep listen to My voice

desc:
'Then Mary said: My soul magnifies the Lord,' (Luke 1:46), opening the longest speech any woman is given in the New Testament.

**Almost none of it is about her.** After two verses it turns to what God does generally, and what it says he does is reversal: 'He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty' (1:52-53).

It is built almost entirely out of older material -- Hannah's song at 1 Samuel 2 most of all -- and Luke does not say so.
name: My soul magnifies the Lord

desc:
'But He said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.' (2Cor 12:9).

The answer to a request refused three times (2Cor 12:8). It is the only place where Paul reports asking for something and being told no with a reason attached, and the reason is not that the thing asked for was wrong.
name: My power is perfected in weakness

aka: neither are your ways my ways
desc:
'For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts' (Isa 55:8-9).

**Two verses that say the same thing twice, and the second is not a repetition.** v8 denies that they are the same; v9 says how they differ, and gives a measure -- the distance between the heavens and the earth.

It belongs with the path verses because it supplies their reason. Prov 3:5 says lean not on your own understanding and does not say why; this says why. Ps 25:4 asks to be shewn his ways, which is a request that only makes sense if they are not already known.
name: my thoughts are not your thoughts

desc:
'And on her forehead a mysterious name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.' (Rev 17:5).

The capitals are the text telling you it is an inscription and not a description. The chapter then gives one key — 'And the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth' (17:18) — and no more.

Which city is the whole of a very old argument. What the text records is that a name was written, that it was written on a forehead, and that the name is called a mystery.
name: MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT

desc: The temple servants, 'David and the officials had appointed them to assist the Levites.' (Ezra 8:20). Iddo's kinsmen at Casiphia were of them, and two hundred and twenty came up with Ezra, all of them expressed by name; Nehemiah later found them dwelling in Ophel.

desc:
'Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!' (2Cor 5:17), and again at Galatians 6:15 where it is set against circumcision as the thing that actually counts.

It states a completed change and gives no process. Nothing here says how, or when, or whether it can be undone — only that old things are passed away.

The neighbouring figures each supply a different half. [[born_again]] gives it a birth, [[buried_with_him_by_baptism]] gives it a death and a raising, and [[old_man_and_new_man]] gives it a change of clothes. Scripture never puts two of them in the same sentence, and that is worth knowing before deciding they are one doctrine.
name: a new creation

desc:
'I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.' (Rev 21:2).

The text names it separately from Jerusalem the city and describes it as arriving rather than standing, and whether the two are one place is a reading the text does not settle. A reader who holds them as one can see both.
name: the new Jerusalem

desc:
'I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.' (John 14:6).

An exclusive claim. Three verses later the same conversation gives the other half: 'Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father' (14:9), answering Philip's request to be shown him.

The two verses are usually read together and are doing different things — 14:6 is about access and 14:9 about sight.
name: No one comes to the Father
No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back

desc: The shape shared by the cloth saying and the wine saying: no man joins a new thing to an old one, else the old is spoiled. Two instances stand side by side in Mark 2:21-22.
name: No one puts the new on the old

desc:
'I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism' (Acts 10:34), said by Peter in the house of Cornelius, and stated flatly by Paul at Romans 2:11: 'For God does not show favoritism'.

Two writers, two arguments, one conclusion, and neither cites the other. Peter reaches it by watching the Spirit fall on Gentiles; Paul reaches it by reasoning about law and judgment. Acts 10:36 names Jesus — 'preaching peace by Jesus Christ' — but the saying itself is about God.
name: God does not show favoritism

disambiguation: One of the four who received the silver, the gold and the vessels by weight in the house of God in Jerusalem, 'Everything was verified by number and weight' (Ezra 8:33-34).
name: Noadiah

disambiguation: son of Lamech; distinct from Noah (daughter of Zelophehad)
name: Noah

desc:
'then even if these three men-Noah, Daniel, and Job-were in it, their righteousness could deliver only themselves' (Ezek 14:14), and the same three again at 14:20.

Chosen as a limit case, and the answer given is nothing. The question the chapter is arguing is how far one person's righteousness reaches on somebody else's behalf, and the three names are picked because they are the strongest examples available — a man who survived the flood, a man who survived the lions, and a man who survived everything. Even they, the verse says, would deliver 'neither son nor daughter' (14:20).

The three are not otherwise associated anywhere in Scripture. Ezekiel puts them together and nothing else does.
name: Noah, Daniel, and Job

desc: Daughter of Zelophehad.
disambiguation: daughter of Zelophehad; distinct from Noah of the flood
name: Noah

desc: After the flood, Noah lived 350 years.
name: after the flood, Noah lived 350 years

desc:
'Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood' (Gen 6:14).

Scripture itself makes it a figure, and says which of. 1 Peter 3:20-21 moves from eight souls saved by water to 'this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also' — and then immediately qualifies what it means, 'not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God'.

A reader should know the English is doing something the original does not. This and the ark of the covenant are different words.
disambiguation: the vessel Noah built; distinct from the ark of the covenant, which the corpus calls by the same English word
name: the ark

desc: "Go into the ark, you and all your family" (Gen 7:1); "Noah went into the ship with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives with him" (Gen 7:7).

**A man asking permission to die, having got what he was promised.** The promise was that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ (2:26), and what he has seen is an infant carried in by two poor parents with a pair of birds to offer.

Anna is in the same scene and gets three verses and no quoted words -- 'Coming forward at that moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem' (2:38).

The question is asked as a cry and answered in the next breath, and the answer is a person rather than a method. What follows immediately is the summary that hands the argument to chapter 8.

Sworn by the man being hunted to the man hunting him, and asked for by the hunter -- Saul has just conceded 'Now I know for sure that you will be king' (24:20).

Put off, put on — something the reader does, repeatedly if need be.

Which sits oddly beside Romans 6:6, where the old self is not put off but executed: 'our old self was crucified with Him'. The same words, two figures — a garment in Ephesians and a body in Romans.

Colossians 3:10 reaches back to Genesis in passing: the new self is 'renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator'.

Mark has a different ending: the scribe agrees, says it is 'more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices', and Jesus tells him he is not far from the kingdom of God (Mark 12:32-34).
name: All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments

'So then, this is how you should pray: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name.' (Matt 6:9).

The one prayer given as a form, given twice, and the two versions differ: Luke 11:2 is shorter and its clauses are ordered differently.

Our, not my. Every other address to the Father in the gospels is singular on one side or the other — the Son's Father or the hearers' Father — and this is the plural the hearers are told to use.
name: Our Father in heaven

desc:
'If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost?' (Matt 18:12).

Told twice to opposite audiences. In Matthew it answers the disciples asking who is greatest; in Luke 15:4 it answers the Pharisees murmuring that he receives sinners. Same figure, two arguments.
name: the parable of the lost sheep

desc: Named by Jesus himself: 'Consider, then, the parable of the sower:' (Matt 13:18). He gives the key in the same breath at Luke 8:11 -- 'Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God' -- and Matthew 13:19-23 reads the four soils as four hearings of it.
name: the parable of the sower

desc: Named at Matt 13:36, when the disciples ask for it: 'Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.' The key follows in three verses: 'The One who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is the world, and the good seed represents the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, and the enemy who sows them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels' (Matt 13:37-39).
name: the parable of the weeds in the field

desc:
'Because of this, the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.' (Matt 18:23) -- **the comparison marker is explicit**, which is rarer in the teaching than the parables suggest.

It answers a counted question. Peter asks whether to forgive seven times and is told 'Not seven times, but seventy-seven times' (18:21-22), and the parable follows on 'therefore'. The application is stated outright at 18:35: 'That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.'
name: the parable of the unmerciful servant

desc: "He holds back his soul from the pit" (v.18), "Redeem him from going down to the pit" (v.24), "from passing into the pit" (v.28), "to bring back his soul from the pit" (v.30).
