desc: "Behold, you have instructed many" (v.3) and "Behold, he does not trust his servants" (v.18) each introduce evidence for the argument
name: "Behold" opening an appeal to shared knowledge

desc: Repeated "Behold" at vv. 2, 6, 7, 12 marks each new step of the argument.
name: "Behold" Opening a Turn

desc: Twice a section closes on the limit of human knowledge: "he does great things and we do not know" (v.5) and "The Almighty, we have not found him" (v.23).
name: He is past finding out

desc: Isaac: "make you fruitful, and multiply you... that you may possess the land"; the LORD: "your seed will be like the dust of the earth... to you I will give it, and to your seed".
name: Blessing formula: be fruitful, multiply, inherit the land

desc: "And the border of the Canaanite was from Sidon, as you come toward Gerar" (v.19) matches "And their dwelling was from Mesha, as you come toward Sephar" (v.30) -- same shape, geographic limits given just before the colophon.
name: Territory note closing a branch

desc: 'And Abraham rose and bowed down to the people of the land' (v7) and 'And Abraham bowed down before the people of the land' (v12) each open a fresh round of negotiation.
name: Abraham bows, then speaks a new proposal

desc: Repeated act at each confirmation: "And the man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD" (v.26); "he worshiped the LORD, bowing himself to the ground" (v.52); also recounted in v.48
name: He bowed down and worshiped the LORD

desc: Twice a named brother breaks the plot with a proposal: "And Reuben heard it... Let us not kill him" and "And Judah said... let us sell him."
name: A brother interposes: "Let us not"

desc: Both scene-openings use the same temporal formula: "And it happened, when he drew near to enter Egypt" and "And it happened, when Abram came into Egypt".
name: And it happened, when...

desc: Each unit opens with a second-person challenge — "Have you commanded the morning", "Have you entered the springs of the sea", "Have you entered the storehouses of snow", "Can you bind", "Can you lift up your voice", "Will you hunt the prey".
name: Rhetorical 'Have/Can you...?' Challenge

desc: Each unit opens with a second-person interrogative addressed to Job — 'Do you know', 'Who sent out', 'Will the wild ox... serve you', 'Did you give', 'Do you give', 'Does the hawk soar by your understanding' — then drops the question and describes the creature in the third person.
name: Do You Know / Can You Do This? — Challenge Opening a Creature Portrait

desc: 'died, and she was buried below Bethel'; 'Rachel died, and was buried on the road to Ephrath'; 'died, and was gathered to his people... his sons... buried him'.
name: Death and burial notice with a named place

desc: Both oracles use the same pair: "the dew of the heavens, and the fatness of the earth" (v.28) and "the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of the heavens" (v.39).
name: "The dew of heaven and the richness of the earth"

desc: Both frame the chapter with the same acts: 'the physicians embalmed Israel' and 'they embalmed him, and he was placed in a coffin in Egypt.'
name: Death, embalming, and burial notice

desc: The lie is planned in v20, "we will say, An evil beast has devoured him", and spoken by Jacob in v33, "an evil beast has devoured him."
name: "An evil beast has devoured him"

desc: Twice the people come and speak ('Give us bread, and why should we die before you?' / 'buy us and our land for bread'), and Joseph takes a new possession in return.
name: Petition to Joseph answered by an exchange

desc: Repeated third-person future declarations of doom: "the light of the wicked will go out", "his lamp above him will go out", "They will thrust him from light into darkness"
name: The lamp of the wicked put out

desc: v.3 "And Abram fell on his face"; v.17 "And Abraham fell on his face and laughed" — the same gesture, once in awe, once in disbelief.
name: Abraham falls on his face before God's word

desc: "These are to find favor in the eyes of my lord" (v.8) and "let me find favor in the eyes of my lord" (v.15); cf. "if now I have found favor in your eyes" (v.10)
name: Seeking Grace in My Lord's Sight

desc: 'Come, let us make bricks' and 'Come, let us build ourselves a city' are answered by 'Come, let us go down, and there confuse their language'.
name: 'Go to, let us...' resolve

desc: Brothers: "Far be it from your servants to do such a thing"; Joseph: "Far be it from me to do this".
name: "God forbid" refusal

desc: Twice the divine inspection precedes the sentence: "And the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth" (v.5) and "And God looked upon the earth and saw that it was corrupt" (v.12), each leading to the announcement "I will destroy".
name: God saw the earth and it was corrupt

desc: Repeated in the interpretation: "God has told Pharaoh what He is about to do" (v25) and "What God is about to do He has shown to Pharaoh" (v28); echoed by Pharaoh, "Since God has made known to you all this".
name: God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do

desc: Repeated in v29 "you will bring down my gray hair in calamity to Sheol" and v31 "will bring down the gray hair of your servant our father in sorrow to Sheol".
name: bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow

desc: The escalating refrain of the brothers' feeling: "they hated him" (v4), "they hated him even more" (v5), "they hated him even more for his dreams" (v8), "his brothers were jealous of him" (v11).
name: they hated him even more

desc: "And he blessed Joseph, and said" (v15) and "And he blessed them that day, saying" (v20) each introduce a blessing.
name: "And he blessed..." blessing formula

desc: repeated third-person clauses with God as subject: "He has walled up my way", "He has stripped my glory from me", "He has torn me down on every side", "He has kindled His anger", "He has put my brothers far from me"
name: "He has..." Chain of Divine Assault

desc: 'Listen to us, sir' (v6), 'No, my lord. Listen to me' (v11), 'Listen to me, my lord' (v15) — a courtesy formula marking each speech.
name: 'My lord, hear me' opening of each reply

desc: "Hear now my argument, and listen to the pleadings of my lips" (v6) and "Listen carefully to my speech, and my declaration in your ears" (v17) each open a new appeal
name: Summons to listen before a plea

desc: "hear my speeches, and give ear to all my words" (v.1) and "hear me: be silent" (vv.31,33) frame the speech with the same call.
name: Summons to Hear Me

desc: "said to him, Abraham: and he said, Here I am" (v.1) and "Abraham, Abraham: and he said, Here I am" (v.11); Isaac's call to his father echoes it in v.7.
name: Called by name, answering "Here am I"

desc: "of the son of the slave woman I will make him into a nation" (v13) and "for I will make him into a great nation" (v18).
name: Promise to make Ishmael a nation

desc: "If it is a matter of strength", "If I am righteous", "If I say, I will forget my complaint", "If I wash myself with snow; then You will plunge me"
name: "If I ... yet/then" hypothetical of futile self-defence

desc: Each new speech to Joseph is marked by the same formula: "And Jacob said unto Joseph" (v3), "And Israel said unto Joseph" (v11, v21).
name: "And Israel/Jacob said to Joseph" speech-opener

desc: Repeated begetting formula: "And Adam had relations with his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain" / "And Cain had relations with his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Enoch" / "And Adam again had relations with his wife, and she gave birth to a son".
name: He knew his wife; she conceived and gave birth
let us get our father drunk with wine

desc: "And Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan" is answered by "Lift up now your eyes, and see... northward, and southward" -- same gesture, one man's choosing, one God's giving.
name: Lifting up the eyes and beholding land

desc: Ten repetitions of a fixed three-verse shape: age at fathering, remaining years with 'and had other sons and daughters', then 'So X lived a total of ... years, and then he died.' Enoch and Noah are the marked exceptions.
name: X lived N years and fathered Y... and all his days were N: and he died

desc: Each new movement opens with the divine name and a verb of making: "the LORD God formed the man", "the LORD God planted a garden", "the LORD God took the man", "from the ground the LORD God formed every beast", "the LORD God caused a deep sleep".
name: "And the Lord God" + act of forming or planting

desc: Each divine turn is opened by "And the LORD said to Cain" / "And the LORD said to him".
name: And the LORD said to Cain

desc: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man" / "But the LORD was with Joseph, and extended kindness to him"; both end with all things committed to Joseph's hand and the master looking to nothing.

desc: Repeated conveyance formula at v17-18 and v20 frames the burial notice.
name: 'Made sure to Abraham for a possession'

desc: "Lest harm befall him" (v4) and "if harm befalls him on the way" (v38) frame the chapter

desc: Repeated shape: birth, then "And [Rachel/Leah] said, [explanation]... and she called his name [X]" -- Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph.

desc: "Abraham called the name of his son... Isaac" answered by Sarah's "God has made laughter for me"; and "Therefore he called that place Beersheba; because there the two of them swore."

desc: "And she conceived, and bore a son; and he called his name Er" repeats through the sons, and recurs at the twins: "his name was called Perez", "his name was called Zerah".

desc:
Ten in Exodus 7 to 12: the river turned to blood, frogs, lice, flies, a severe plague on the livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and the death of the firstborn.

The text's own word for them is signs rather than punishments — 'I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt' (Exod 7:3) — and it says what they are for: 'that you may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians' (10:2). They are given as something to be recounted afterwards.

The word plague appears too, and later: 'I will send all My plagues against you' (9:14), and 'I will bring yet one more plague' (11:1).

Two psalms retell them and neither keeps the order or the count. Psalm 78:44-51 gives seven and Psalm 105:28-36 gives eight, in different sequences.
name: the plagues of Egypt

desc:
'be transformed by the renewing of your mind' (Rom 12:2).

A thread that runs the length of the text and is never once cross-referenced. Renew a right spirit (Ps 51:10); a new heart and a new spirit (Ezek 36:26); renew their strength (Isa 40:31); the renewing of your mind (Rom 12:2); to be renewed in the spirit of your minds (Eph 4:23); renewed in knowledge (Col 3:10); the renewing of the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5); the inward man renewed day by day (2Cor 4:16).

Eight passages, five writers, both testaments, and what is renewed is different every time — spirit, heart, strength, mind, knowledge, the inward man. The passages join because they share a word, and say no more than that.

desc:
'Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.' (1Cor 15:20).

The empty tomb is told as narrative—who ran where, who saw whom—but the letters use the resurrection as the ground of their argument.

1 Corinthians 15 stakes everything on it and says so twice, in the negative: 'And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith' (15:14), and 'And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins' (15:17). The chapter argues by supposing the opposite.

Romans splits the work between the two events: 'delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification' (4:25). Two clauses, two purposes.

The vocabulary is worth watching. Fifty-four verses say risen or rose again, forty-two say raised him or raised up, forty say resurrection—and the passive is the commoner form: he is more often raised than rises.

'Now there was a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen' (Luke 16:19), and Lazarus at his gate; both die, and the conversation that follows is held across a gulf between Abraham and the rich man.

The text does not call it a parable — Luke 15:3 says 'He told them this parable' of the lost sheep, and no such marker introduces this one. It is filed as a parable here on its form, which is a reading; that it names one of its characters is unique among them.

No teller is recorded. Luke 16 opens 'Jesus also said to His disciples' (16:1), and neither Luke 15 nor Luke 16 names Jesus anywhere, so there is no verse to carry the edge. The same refusal the checker made of the Sermon on the Mount at Matt 5:1 — which Matthew 7:28 later rescued, and Luke offers no equivalent.

Hebrews credits her with faith at the point Genesis records her laughing (Gen 18:12); both verses are about the same moment.

1 Peter 3:6 makes her an example on entirely different grounds: 'just as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord'.

desc:
'So she laughed to herself, saying, After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?' (Gen 18:12).

She denies it and the text records the denial and the contradiction in one verse: 'But Sarah was afraid, so she denied it and said, I did not laugh. No, replied the LORD, but you did laugh' (18:15).

The laughing comes back as the child's name and as her own reading of it: 'God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me' (21:6). Abraham had laughed first, at 17:17, and nobody reproves him for it.

desc:
'When Jesus saw the crowds, He went up on the mountain and sat down. His disciples came to Him, and He began to teach them, saying' (Matt 5:1-2), closing at 7:28 with 'the crowds were astonished at His teaching'.

Its imagery works by assertion and depiction rather than comparison. 'You are the salt of the earth' carries no marker; the two houses are a scene set down beside its point. Two templates run through it: the beatitude, 'Blessed are X, for Y', eight times in 5:3-10 with the ground stated each time; and the antithesis, 'You have heard that it was said ... But I tell you', six times in 5:21-44, each quoting a commandment without naming it.

desc:
'Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground' (Exod 3:5).

Said twice in the text and quoted a third time. Joshua gets almost the same sentence from The Commander of the LORD’s army at Jericho: 'Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.' (Josh 5:15). Stephen quotes the Exodus version back at the council (Acts 7:33).

The two scenes are built alike — a man alone, a figure that is not a man, an instruction about footwear before anything else is said — and the text draws no connection between them. Joshua is Moses's successor and this is the nearest the book comes to saying so without saying it.

A phrase search for 'holy ground' finds Exodus and Acts and misses Joshua, which says only 'is holy'. Noted here because the near miss is exactly the kind a reader makes and an index does not.

Does it tie to the tabernacle? Not in the text. The text has a great deal of holiness-of-place language — the holy place, the most holy, the sanctuary, most of it in Ezekiel, Leviticus, Numbers and Exodus — and Psalm 15:1 even sets tabernacle and holy hill in parallel. But nothing joins any of it to the ground at the bush. The phrase 'holy ground' is these two verses and no more.

The gesture does not carry the meaning either. Removing a shoe recurs four more times for reasons that have nothing to do with holiness: a legal repudiation before the elders (Deut 25:9), a sign of coming captivity (Isa 20:2-4), and David going barefoot up the Mount of Olives in mourning (2Sam 15:30).

So the connection a reader feels between this ground and the sanctuary is a reader's, and a good one, and not the text's.
name: the place where you are standing is holy

desc:
The house built for the LORD in Jerusalem. The temple as a figure has its own card: [[image_temple]].

**Solomon built the first:** 'The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high' (1 Kings 6:2). At its dedication 'the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD' (1 Kings 8:11), and Solomon prays: 'The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built' (1 Kings 8:27).

**Destroyed and rebuilt:** the Babylonians 'burned down the house of the LORD' (2 Kings 25:9), and the returned exiles built it again: 'this temple was completed on the third day of the month of Adar' (Ezra 6:15).

**In the Gospels** Jesus teaches in its courts and 'drove all from the temple courts' (John 2:15); at his death 'the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom' (Matthew 27:51).

**Where readers differ.** Some passages are read in more than one way: the temple in them has been understood as the building that stood in Jerusalem when the passage was written, a temple yet to be built, a temple in heaven, the people of God, or a figure of something else. The site shows these verses and does not choose among the readings: 2 Thessalonians 2:4, of the one called 'the man of lawlessness' in verse 3, 'So he will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God'; Matthew 24:15; Haggai 2:9; Ezekiel 40-48, the temple the prophet is shown 'in visions of God' (40:2); Revelation 11:1-2; and Zechariah 6:12-15.

desc:
**A hundred and one verses say 'the blood of', and ninety-two of them are outside the gospels.** It is a word the law and the letters share and the narrative barely touches.

Leviticus states the principle -- 'the life of the flesh is in the blood ... it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul' (17:11) -- and Hebrews restates it as a rule: 'without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness' (9:22).

Hebrews then turns it on the whole sacrificial system: 'He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood' (9:12). **Not more blood, and not different blood, but the last of it** -- which is the argument the epistle exists to make.

Revelation keeps it and makes it a means of victory: 'They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb' (12:11).
