desc: Twelve stones in four rows, one per tribe, each engraved as a signet with a name. Worn over the heart as the shoulder stones are worn on the shoulders -- the same twelve names carried twice, borne and remembered.
disambiguation: Aaron's garment of twelve stones; distinct from the image_breastplate used figuratively for righteousness and faith in Ephesians 6:14 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8
name: a breastpiece of judgment

desc: Heated 'seven times hotter than usual', which kills the men who carry them to it. Daniel 3:27 is careful about the result: the fire had no power on their bodies, Not a hair of their heads was singed, their robes were unaffected, and there was no smell of fire on them.
name: the blazing fiery furnace

desc: A calf tender and good, fetched by Abraham and dressed for the meal.
name: calf

desc: Beaten from one piece of pure gold, seven lamps, almond-shaped bowls. Zechariah 4 sees it again with two olive trees beside it and asks what it means; the answer given there is 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit'.
disambiguation: the seven-branched lamp of the tabernacle; distinct from the lampstand as an image, the figure the letters to the seven churches are addressed to
name: the lampstand

desc: Abram heard that his relative had been captured.
name: the capture of Lot

desc: A fire pan for incense, and Scripture almost always brings it up when someone is using it who should not be. Nadab and Abihu with strange fire, Korah's two hundred and fifty, Uzziah in the temple. Revelation 8:5 fills one with fire from the altar and casts it at the earth.
name: the censer

desc:
'Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind.' (Ps 1:4).

The answer to the verse before it. Psalm 1 sets a tree planted by rivers of water against chaff with nothing under it, and the whole psalm is those two pictures.
name: chaff driven off by the wind

desc: The Chaldeans formed three bands, raided the camels, and took them away
name: the Chaldean raid

desc: Pharaoh's chief baker, hanged as Joseph interpreted (Gen 40:22).
name: the chief baker

desc: Pharaoh's chief butler, whom Joseph interprets for and who forgets Joseph (Gen 40:23).
name: the chief butler

desc: The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.
name: The chief butler forgot Joseph

desc: "they bore them children" (Gen 6:4)
name: children born to the daughters of men

desc:
'I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate to be with you forever' (John 14:16).

Four verses, all in one discourse, and John 14:26 states the identification outright: 'the Advocate, the Holy Spirit'. No reader has to supply it, which is unusual for this material.

Another Advocate is doing quiet work in 14:16 — it implies a first, and the speaker is the one about to leave. John 16:7 makes the departure the condition: 'Unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you'. The text records the word and not the inference.
disambiguation: the title, held apart from the Holy Spirit, who carries it as an alias; this record is for what the corpus does with the words
name: the Advocate

desc: the company of the godless will be barren
name: the company of the godless will be barren

desc: "One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields" (Mark 2:23).
name: the grainfields
the counsel of the wicked
source: declared to complete relations the batch asserts

desc: A guarded courtyard in the palace of the king of Judah where Jeremiah was confined during the siege of Jerusalem.
name: the courtyard of the guard

desc: As one of their own prophets has said, Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.
name: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons

desc: The dark cloud through which Job questions God's seeing.
name: thick darkness

desc: The darkness that existed before the first day, distinct from the concept of darkness.
name: the darkness

desc: "the daughters of men" (Gen 6:2)
name: the daughters of men

desc: The day Job was born, which he curses. The verse says 'cursed the day of his birth' (Job 3:1) and 'May the day of my birth perish' (Job 3:3).
name: the day of Job's birth

desc: When Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the region, saw her, he took her and lay with her by force.
name: the defiling of Dinah

desc: Sealed with the king's own signet and the signet of his lords, so that 'nothing concerning Daniel could be changed' -- the seal binds the king as much as the stone binds Daniel. Darius spends the night fasting and comes at dawn to ask whether it worked.
name: the den of lions

desc: The adversary; disputed with Michael, and walks about as a roaring lion. Job and Zechariah call him הַשָּׂטָן, 'the adversary', with the article (Job 1:6, Zech 3:1), which the Berean renders 'Satan'; Revelation joins the names: 'that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan' (Rev 12:9).
name: Satan

desc:
'You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder.' (Jas 2:19).

The text sets a limit on its own most-repeated verb. What is affirmed is granted — 'Good for you' — and then shown to be shared by parties nobody would call saved. It stands three verses before 'a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone' (Jas 2:24).
name: Even the demons believe that-and shudder

desc: Four verses and never on an actual head. Job wears judgement as one; Isaiah 62:3 has Zion be one, held in the hand of God rather than worn; Ezekiel 21:26 removes it. The word only ever appears where something else is being called one.
name: the turban

desc:
'One of His disciples, the one whom Jesus loved, was reclining at His side' (John 13:23), and again at 19:26, 20:2, 21:7 and 21:20. **John names him five times and never names him.**

He outruns Peter to the empty tomb and goes in second (20:4-8); he is the one who recognises Jesus on the shore (21:7); and the book closes by making him its author: 'This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true' (21:24).

**He is traditionally identified with John son of Zebedee**, and the identification is not made anywhere in the text -- John's gospel never names either of Zebedee's sons individually, which is part of why the reading is drawn. It is recorded as a reading and not as data; `john_son_of_zebedee` is a separate id resting on the verses that name him.
name: the disciple whom Jesus loved

desc: 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture.' (John 10:9).
name: the gate

desc: Told twice with the detail reversed: in Luke the net breaks, in John 'but even with so many, the net was not torn'.
name: the catch of fishes

desc: 'The elder, To the chosen lady and her children' (2 John 1:1); 'The elder, To the beloved Gaius' (3 John 1:1).
disambiguation: self-designation of the author of 2 and 3 John; the letters do not give a proper name, so no authorship is asserted beyond this self-designation
name: the elder

desc: The house of Job's eldest son, where the feast was held and which the great wind struck (Job 1:13, 1:19).
name: the oldest brother’s house

desc: The high priest's shoulder garment, with the twelve tribes cut into two onyx stones on the shoulder straps so that Aaron 'is to bear their names on his two shoulders as a memorial before the LORD'. Also worn plain and linen by the boy Samuel and by David dancing before the ark.
name: the ephod

desc: Made from the golden earrings of the Midianite spoil and set up in Ophrah. Held apart from the priestly ephod because it is a different object and the verse that reports it also passes sentence on it: 'all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household.'
name: the ephod Gideon made

desc: the excellency of dignity
name: excelling in honor

desc: the excellency of power
name: excelling in power

desc:
'it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God' (Matt 19:24).

**The disciples' reaction shows how the figure was heard**: they were 'greatly astonished and asked, Who then can be saved?' (19:25), which is not the reaction to a merely difficult thing.

The answer given moves it off the man entirely: 'With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible' (19:26). *The one verse a reader usually remembers is the one before that.*
name: the eye of a needle

sorted.why: Gen 33:10, 'like seeing the face of God' — face, in a simile

desc: Bildad's repeated description of the destruction awaiting the wicked man.
name: the fate of the wicked

aka: the Father which is in heaven
desc:
'you have one Father, who is in heaven' (Matt 23:9).

Held apart from God on purpose, and the reason is mechanical rather than doctrinal. The text distinguishes Jesus from the Father in some verses and from God in others, and folded into one those two sets become indistinguishable. Separated, the pattern is visible and a reader can check it: of the fifteen statements setting Jesus apart, six name the Father, seven name God, and two name both — and three of the seven address or name the Father in the same breath (John 17:3, Eph 1:17, John 20:17).

Every relation here points at whichever one its verse actually names. Nothing is normalised, because the normalising is the thing under examination.
disambiguation: God under the name the corpus uses when it speaks of him in relation to the Son; joined to [[god]] by the twelve verses reading 'God the Father'. Distinct from the Son and from the Holy Spirit, and distinct from every human father in the graph.
name: the Father

desc:
'No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day.' (John 6:44).

The mirror of John 14:6, and between them they close a circle: no one reaches the Father except by the Son, and no one reaches the Son unless the Father draws him. The text states both and does not comment on the shape they make together.

The next verse softens the mechanism into hearing: 'Everyone who has heard the Father and learned from Him comes to Me' (6:45). Whether draw and hear and learn are one act is the whole of a long argument, and this carries the two verses and no verdict.
name: except the Father draw him

desc:
'The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands.' (John 3:35), and again at 5:20 with a different verb of showing.

John 5:19-26 is the densest statement in Scripture of what the Father does and what the Son does, and every clause runs one way: 'The Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it' (5:19); 'the Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son' (5:22); 'as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself' (5:26).

The passage is cited by every side of the argument about what the two are to one another, because it makes the Son's authority total and its source external in the same breath. The text records the clauses and joins none of them into a conclusion.
name: The Father loves the Son

desc:
'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge' (Prov 1:7).

Thirty verses, and twenty-nine of them are in the Old Testament. Fourteen in Proverbs, six in Isaiah, four in 2 Chronicles, three in the Psalms. The single New Testament use is Acts 9:31, where the churches walk in it. A vocabulary that belongs almost entirely to one half of Scripture, in the way trust does and faith does not.

And the text defines it nine times, differently each time.

    Ps 19:9      is clean, enduring for ever
    Ps 111:10    the beginning of wisdom
    Prov 1:7     the beginning of knowledge
    Prov 8:13    is to hate evil
    Prov 14:26   is strong confidence
    Prov 14:27   a fountain of life
    Prov 15:33   the instruction of wisdom
    Isa 33:6     is his treasure
    Job 28:28    that is wisdom

Nine predicates for one subject, and no verse reconciles them. Two of the nine put it at the beginning of something — which is where it earns its place as a candidate for the text's declared entry point rather than a computed one.

Held apart from fear. Nothing in that list is said of being afraid. It is clean, it is a treasure, it is strong confidence, and it is a fountain of life; the text's other fear is what perfect love casts out (1John 4:18). The words are shared and the uses are not, which is why this is a concept of its own and not a qualified instance of the other.
disambiguation: a settled phrase of the wisdom literature, held apart from [[fear]] because the corpus never treats it as an instance of being afraid: it is called clean, a treasure, a fountain of life and strong confidence, none of which fear is called anywhere
name: the fear of the LORD

desc:
'The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death.' (Prov 14:27), immediately after 'He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge.' (Prov 14:26).

Two definitions in consecutive verses, and both are about safety rather than knowledge -- confidence, refuge, a fountain, escape from snares. The verses either side of them in the same chapter are the ones usually quoted about wisdom.
name: The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life

desc:
'The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever; the judgments of the LORD are true, being altogether righteous.' (Ps 19:9).

The sixth of six statements in Ps 19:7-9, each naming a thing of the LORD and what it is: the law perfect, the testimony sure, the statutes right, the commandment pure, the fear clean, the judgments true. It is listed among things given rather than among things felt, which is the clearest single reason to hold it apart from fear.
name: The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever

desc:
'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom' (Prov 9:10), and the identical sentence at Psalm 111:10, with Proverbs 1:7 reading 'knowledge' for 'wisdom'.

**Three books, one formula, and no verse marks the repetition.** It is the clearest case in the wisdom literature of a saying circulating rather than being composed once.
name: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom

desc:
'To fear the LORD is to hate evil; I hate arrogant pride, evil conduct, and perverse speech.' (Prov 8:13).

The only one of the nine definitions that names what is hated, and it names four things: pride, arrogancy, the evil way, perverse speech. The verse then shifts speaker -- 'do I hate' -- so the hating is attributed rather than left general.
name: To fear the LORD is to hate evil

desc:
'And He said to man, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.' (Job 28:28).

The end of a chapter asking where wisdom is found, which has just said that it is not in the deep, not in the sea, and cannot be bought with gold. The answer given is not a place.

Said as an identity rather than a beginning -- Proverbs and the Psalm make it where wisdom starts, Job makes it what wisdom is.
name: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom

desc: while Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house
name: the feast at the oldest brother’s house

desc: The field where Isaac went to meditate in the early evening (Gen 24:63).
name: the field

desc:
'death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the way that Adam transgressed. He is a pattern of the One to come.' (Rom 5:14).

Scripture names its own typology. Everywhere else a reader has to notice that one figure stands for another; here Paul says it in the sentence, and the man he says it of is the first one in the book.

The comparison is then built by contrast rather than resemblance: 'For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous' (5:19). The two are alike in shape and opposite in content, which is the whole argument of the passage.
name: a pattern of the One to come

desc: The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants
name: the fire of God

desc: 'Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last,' (Rev 1:17), and again at 22:13 with 'I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End'.
name: the first and the last

desc:
'The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.' (1Cor 15:45), and 'The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven' (15:47).

Adam's name is given to somebody else. Not like Adam, not a second Adam — the last Adam, as though the name were an office rather than a person. It is the same move Scripture makes with David at Ezekiel 34:23, and this one is in the New Testament and about Christ.

'For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive' (15:22) states the parallel as a pair of memberships. What all covers in each half is read differently by different traditions and the text does not settle it.
name: the first man Adam, the last Adam

desc: the flame will wither his shoots
name: the flame will wither his shoots

desc:
'behold, I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew only on the fleece and all the ground is dry, then I will know that You are going to save Israel by my hand' (Judg 6:37).

He asks twice, and the second time he reverses it — dry fleece, wet ground — and apologises for asking: 'Do not be angry with me' (6:39). The text records the asking, the apology and the granting, and passes no comment on any of them.
name: a fleece of wool on the threshing floor

desc: The forty-day flood sent upon the earth; 'For forty days the flood kept coming on the earth' (Gen 7:17).
name: the flood

desc: all the food of the seven years, gathered and laid up in the cities.
name: the food

desc: Unnamed; "He instructed the one in the lead" (Gen 32:17).
name: the one in the lead

desc: Nebuchadnezzar's words, and the text leaves them his: he says what the fourth figure looks like to him and the narrative does not confirm or correct it. At 3:28 he calls the same figure an angel.
name: the fourth looks like a son of the gods!

desc: The four men who bore the paralytic: "Then a paralytic was brought to Him, carried by four men"; they uncover and break up the roof and let down the bed.
name: the four

desc:
A white horse whose rider has a bow and a crown and goes 'to overcome and conquer' (Rev 6:2); a red horse whose rider takes peace from the earth (6:4); a black horse whose rider has 'a pair of scales' (6:5); and a pale horse (6:8).

Only the fourth rider is named: 'Its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed close behind' (6:8). The other three are described by what they carry and what they do, and the text never says who they are.

The first is the contested one. A crown, a bow, and conquering — and readers have taken him for Christ, for conquest, and for a counterfeit, on the strength of a white horse appearing again at 19:11 with a rider who is named. The text holds both verses and declines to join them.
name: the white, red, black and pale horses

desc:
'And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God.' (Jas 2:23).

Three books call him it and none of them is Genesis. Isaiah 41:8, 2 Chronicles 20:7 and James 2:23 — and James says he was called, without saying by whom or where. It is a title Scripture attributes to itself and cannot locate.
disambiguation: the title, held apart from Abraham himself; this record is for what the corpus does with the words
name: a friend of God

desc: 'glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ' (Titus 2:13)
name: glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ

desc: to the glory of God
name: the glory of God

desc:
'And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you.' (1Pet 5:10).

**Four concepts in one sentence and an order imposed on them**: grace, glory, suffering, strength -- with the suffering placed before the strengthening and given a duration, *a while*.
name: the God of all grace

desc: God names himself so: 'I am the God of Bethel'.
name: the God of Bethel

desc: An omer of manna laid before the LORD to be preserved. Hebrews 9:4 puts it inside the ark with Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant -- one verse naming four objects at once.
name: the golden pot of manna

desc:
'Each one had a harp, and they were holding golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.' (Rev 5:8).

Another stated key, and an unusually gentle one in a book of beasts and seals: the incense is prayer, said plainly, in a relative clause. It is repeated at 8:3-4 with the smoke ascending 'with the prayers of the saints ... before God'.

The figure rests on the altar of incense in the tabernacle, and Revelation is where the text finally says what that was for.
name: golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints

desc: Claimed at John 10:11; The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
name: the good shepherd

desc:
'For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do.' (Rom 7:19), stated first at v15 and again as a discovery at v21: 'So this is the principle I have discovered: When I want to do good, evil is right there with me'

The division is inside one person and the pronoun never changes. It is not that he does not know what is right, nor that he does not want it -- 'I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out' (v18).
name: I do not do the good I want to do

desc: "proclaimed the gospel of God" (Mark 1:14). The ASV, BSB and YLT read only 'the gospel of God' here.
name: the gospel of God

desc: The place of the dead, where the weary rest and the wicked cease troubling.
name: the grave

desc:
'And the great dragon was hurled down-that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.' (Rev 12:9), and the same four names again at 20:2.

Four names in one clause, twice. It is the most explicit identification of a figure anywhere in Scripture — dragon, serpent, Devil, Satan, stated as one, with no room left for a reader to do the joining.

Old is doing quiet work: it points back at Genesis 3 without citing it, and Genesis never calls the serpent any of the other three names.
name: the great dragon, that old serpent

desc: Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.
name: a great feast

desc: 'our great God and Savior Jesus Christ' (Titus 2:13)
name: our great God and Savior Jesus Christ

desc: a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house
name: the great wind from the wilderness
the greatest man of all the people of the East

desc: the ground, cursed for Adam's sake and the ground to which man returns (Gen 3:17, 3:19); distinct from the concept 'ground'.
name: the ground

desc:
'Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.' (Luke 19:8).

**He is not asked for any of it.** Nothing has been required, and the fourfold restitution he offers is the law's penalty for stealing a sheep -- he applies the harshest available measure to himself.

The tree is the detail everyone keeps: 'he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him' (19:4), because he was short and the crowd was in the way.
name: half of my possessions I give to the poor

desc: the plural heavens of Genesis 2:1 and 2:4, made by the Lord God; distinct from the singular expanse/heaven.
name: the heavens

desc: The lofty ones whom God judges (Job 21:22).
name: those on high

desc: The office named in "at the time of Abiathar the high priest".
name: the high priest

desc: Set against the good shepherd by what he owns: 'whose own the sheep are not'. The failure is contractual before it is moral.
name: The man runs away

desc: The title cried out in the synagogue at Capernaum: "I know who You are — the Holy One of God". Kept apart from the existing title `the_holy_one` pending a decision.
name: the Holy One of God

desc: The house in Capernaum where Jesus was: "the people heard that He was home".
name: home

desc: Both houses get the same storm. The parable turns on the foundation and not on the weather, and the two builders are told apart by doing rather than hearing.
name: the house built upon a rock

desc: The verse says 'who is the image of God'.
name: the image of God

desc: "After the arrest of John" -- Mark dates the beginning of Jesus's Galilean preaching from it and names no captor here.
name: John put in prison

desc: the inhabitants of the waters, in Job's speech
name: those who dwell in them

desc:
'Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day.' (2Cor 4:16).

Two things happening at once in one person and in opposite directions, which is the same shape as 'I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me' (Gal 2:20) and 'as living sacrifices' (Rom 12:1). The renewal is dated -- day by day -- and the perishing is not.
name: our inner self is being renewed day by day

desc:
'since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.' (Neh 8:10).

One of the few places the text explains one of these words by another. It is said to a crowd that has just heard the law read and started weeping, which is the reason for the instruction not to be sorry.
name: the joy of the LORD is your strength

desc: Every fiftieth year: debts released, land returned, servants freed. No narrative anywhere records it being kept. It is held the way the day of atonement is held — as a commanded observance — and that a command has no observance narrative behind it is a fact about the text, not a gap in the text.
name: the Jubilee
the Judge of all the earth

desc: the righteous will wear (Job 27:17)
name: the righteous

desc:
'the righteous will live by faith' (Hab 2:4).

Eight words in a minor prophet, quoted three times in the New Testament, and the engine of the Reformation. Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11 and Hebrews 10:38 all cite it, and each puts the emphasis in a different place — the just, or shall live, or by faith.

In Habakkuk it answers a complaint about violence going unpunished. The prophet has asked how long, been told the Chaldeans are coming, and objected that the cure is worse than the disease. This is part of the reply, and the text records where it sits before recording where it went.
name: the righteous will live by faith

desc: the keeper of the prison in Joseph's time
name: the prison warden

desc:
'who holds the key of David. What He opens no one can shut' (Rev 3:7).

Lifted from Isaiah 22:22 almost word for word, where it is said of Eliakim, a steward given authority over a household: 'I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut'. Revelation drops the house of and keeps everything else.

Scripture holds both verses and does not say what the reuse means.
name: the key of David

desc:
'I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven' (Matt 16:19).

The binding half is said again two chapters later to everybody: 'whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven' (Matt 18:18), plural, with no keys attached. Scripture holds both verses and does not say what the difference between them is.
name: the keys of the kingdom of heaven

desc: The settled phrase Jesus preaches: "the kingdom of God is at hand".
name: the kingdom of God

desc:
'The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers.' (Ruth 2:20), and the transaction itself: 'Ruth the Moabitess ... I have acquired Ruth the Moabitess, Mahlon's widow, as my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance' (4:10).

It is a legal provision before it is anything else — Leviticus 25:25 sets it out, a relative buying back what a poor man had to sell. Ruth is Scripture's one worked example of it, with the shoe changing hands and a nearer kinsman declining first.

Readers take it as a figure and the text does not say so. Job 19:25 uses the same word — 'I know that my Redeemer lives' — and the text holds the legal sense and the redemption concept as separate meanings joined by the verses, not merged.
name: the kinsman that has right to redeem

desc: the unnamed land where the seed shall be strangers
name: a land that is not their own

desc: Quote: 'to a land of darkness and gloom' (10:21); 'A land of darkness' (10:22)
name: a land of darkness and gloom

desc: A brass basin for washing, set between the tabernacle and the altar. Exodus 38:8 says what it was made from: 'the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting'.
name: the basin

desc:
'So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.' (Rom 7:12), and 'the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin.' (Rom 7:14).

**The verdict that stops the chapter being read as an attack on the law.** Four adjectives in one sentence, none qualified. Whatever has gone wrong in Romans 7, the text does not locate it in the law -- v14 puts it in the other party.
name: the law is holy

desc:
'The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is trustworthy, making wise the simple.' (Ps 19:7).

Six statements in three verses, each naming a thing of the LORD and what it does. This is the first, and its verb is the one Ps 23:3 uses of the shepherd.
name: The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul

desc:
'For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit of life set you free from the law of sin and death.' (Rom 8:2).

Two laws in one sentence, both named as laws and set against each other. The chapter opens on this contrast and works it out through flesh and Spirit for the next eleven verses.
name: the law of the Spirit of life

desc:
'In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it' (John 1:4-5).

**Genesis 1's first two things, in Genesis 1's order, with an outcome added.** There the light is made and divided from the darkness; here it shines in the darkness and is not comprehended. Neither the making nor the dividing is mentioned; what is carried over is the pair.

The chain of identifications runs life, then light, then -- at v9 -- 'the true Light'.
name: that life was the light of men

desc: The light that God caused to be at the command 'Let there be light', distinct from the concept of light in general.
name: the light

desc: Quote: 'where even the light is like darkness'
name: even the light is like darkness

desc: Claimed at John 8:12.
name: the light of the world

desc:
'you have tied this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down' (Josh 2:18).

The sign is the rope she used to save them, kept in place to save her. The text makes nothing further of the colour.

Hebrews 11 and James 2 both name her, as both name Abraham: Hebrews for her faith, 'By faith the prostitute Rahab ... did not perish' (Heb 11:31), James for her actions, 'was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions' (Jas 2:25). Matthew 1:5 names a Rahab in the genealogy; the text does not say it is she.
name: this scarlet cord in the window

desc:
'Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll' (Rev 5:5) — and what John then turns and sees is not a lion: 'Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne' (5:6).

The announcement and the sight do not match, and the text does not remark on it. He is told a lion has conquered and shown a killed lamb, in consecutive verses, and the book proceeds as though these were the same thing.

It is the clearest instance in Scripture of a figure being corrected by the next figure rather than explained, and any reading of Revelation has to account for it.
name: behold the Lion ... a Lamb who appeared to have been slain

desc: Ezekiel is handed a roll and told to eat it, and it is 'as sweet as honey in my mouth'. John is handed a little book by an angel and told the same thing: sweet as honey in the mouth, and 'when I had eaten it, my stomach turned bitter'. Held as one record because the second repeats the first almost exactly and then adds what happens next.
name: the little book that was eaten

desc:
'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD' (Job 1:21).

He attributes both halves to the same source and blesses him for the pair, which is what the next verse singles out: 'In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing' (1:22).

The book then spends thirty-five chapters on him charging God with a good deal, and the text does not treat that as a contradiction of this verse.
name: the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away

desc:
'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.' (Ps 23:1).

**Written, by its own superscription, by a shepherd** -- and the psalm puts him on the other side of the figure. He is the sheep in it.

The best-known verse in it changes person: the psalm speaks *about* the shepherd until the valley, and then speaks *to* him -- 'for You are with me' (23:4). That turn is the construction this project has found again and again in the verses people memorise.
name: the LORD is my shepherd

desc:
'Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out: The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,' (Exod 34:6), continuing 'Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished' (34:7).

The most travelled formula in Scripture. It is taken up at Nehemiah 9:17, Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8, Psalm 145:8, Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2 — one verse across four genres.

Jonah is the sharpest of the six. He quotes it as a complaint: he fled because he knew God was merciful and gracious and would relent, which is the formula used against the outcome it usually comforts. The second half travels less than the first, and which portion a later writer takes is worth watching.
name: The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious

desc:
'Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.' (Exod 33:11).

Twenty-nine verses later the same chapter says he could not: 'You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live' (33:20). Scripture puts both in one chapter and does not reconcile them.

Deuteronomy 34:10 makes it the thing that was never repeated: 'Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face'.
name: the LORD would speak to Moses face to face

desc: The middle of three in Luke 15, between the lost sheep and the lost son, and the only one where the thing lost cannot look for itself.
name: the lost piece of silver

desc: Unnamed man, spoken of by Lamech as 'a man to my wounding'.
name: the man Lamech said he slew

desc: Unnamed; "there a man wrestled with him until daybreak" (Gen 32:24).
name: a man

desc: all the streaked or spotted male goats and every speckled or spotted female goat — every one that had any white on it — and every dark-colored lamb
name: the marked animals removed

desc: The men whom Hirah asked: 'the men of that place' (Gen 38:21).
name: the men of that place

desc: Hebrews 9:5 names it with one Greek word, ἱλαστήριον. Exodus 25:22 is what the object is for: 'There I will meet with you, and I will tell you from above the mercy seat'.
name: the mercy seat

desc: the midwife who said unto Rachel, Do not be afraid, for you are having another son (Gen 35:17)
name: the midwife

desc: Those who long for death and rejoice when they find the grave.
name: them that are in misery and bitter in soul

desc: The high priest's linen headdress, carrying the golden plate on a blue lace across the forefront.
disambiguation: the linen headdress itself; the golden plate fixed to its front is a separate record, and Exodus 29:6 keeps them apart -- the holy crown is put *on the turban
name: the turban

desc: Behind the second veil, entered once a year by one man. Hebrews argues from the restriction rather than from the room: that the way in 'had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing' (Heb 9:8).
name: the most holy place

desc:
'And Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living' (Gen 3:20).

The naming comes immediately after the sentence of death. Genesis 3:19 ends with dust returning to dust and the very next verse calls her the mother of all living. The text does not comment on the order, and it is hard to read as accidental.
name: the mother of all the living

desc: Those who mourn, whom Job says he comforted: "as a comforter of the mourners."
name: the mourners

desc: The crowd that came to Jesus by the sea: "All the people came to Him, and He taught them".
name: the people

desc: The thing said to be given to the hearers to know in Mark 4:11.
name: the mystery of the kingdom of God

desc:
'The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe.' (Prov 18:10).

A hundred and eight verses, and it behaves as a thing rather than a label: it is called upon (Gen 4:26, Joel 2:32), run into (Prov 18:10), remembered against chariots and horses (Ps 20:7), and blasphemed or hallowed. What is done to it is done to him.

The promise attached to calling on it is quoted twice in the New Testament -- Acts 2:21 and Rom 10:13 both cite Joel 2:32 -- and both times the word 'saved' replaces Joel's 'delivered'.
name: the name of the Lord

desc:
'The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe.' (Prov 18:10).

A name given as a place, entered by running. The verse following puts a rich man's wealth in the same position -- 'his fortified city; it is like a high wall in his imagination' (Prov 18:11) -- so the figure is used twice on facing pages, once as fact and once as self-deception.
name: The name of the Lord is a strong tower

desc: The nation God will make of Ishmael: I will also make a nation of the slave woman’s son; I will make him into a great nation.
name: the nation of the slave woman's son

desc: The night on which Job was conceived, mentioned in Job 3:3: 'the night it was said, A boy is conceived.'
name: the night of Job's conception

desc: The vision described in Job 4:13-16, in which a spirit appears to Eliphaz.
name: the night vision

desc: the oak under which Deborah Rebekah's nurse was buried; also called Allon-bachuth.
name: the oak beneath Bethel

desc: the oak tree under which Jacob hid the strange gods and earrings; located by Shechem.
name: the oak near Shechem

desc: The ancient path which wicked men have trodden.
name: the ancient path

aka: the merchant man seeking goodly pearls
name: the pearl of great price

desc: by these He judges the nations
name: the nations

desc: the nation in the land not theirs, whom the seed shall serve, cited as 'them' and 'that nation'
name: the people of the land

desc:
'The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.' (Isa 9:2), quoted at Matt 4:16.

Matthew has them sitting where Isaiah has them walking, and applies it to Galilee at the start of the ministry. The verse two before it in Isaiah is the one about a child born and a son given.
name: the people living in darkness have seen a great light

desc: the pieces of the divided animals Abram prepared in Gen 15:10
name: the halves of the carcasses

desc: A place where gold is fined: "a place where gold is refined".
name: a place where gold

desc: The place where understanding resides, asked after in "where does understanding dwell?"
name: the place of understanding

desc: "all the plain" which God overthrew (Gen 19:25).
name: plain

aka: the plate of the holy crown
desc: Engraved 'the way a gem cutter engraves a seal' with two words, and fixed to the front of the turban.
name: the plate of pure gold

desc: the poor of the earth (Job 24:4), who are driven out and oppressed
name: the poor

desc: Son of David, king in Jerusalem; speaks throughout Ecclesiastes.
disambiguation: unnamed; the book calls him only the Preacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem, and does not identify him with Solomon
name: the Teacher

desc: The crowd at the house in Capernaum: "they gathered in such large numbers that there was no more room, not even outside the door"; called "the press" at Mark 2:4.
name: the press

desc: The title the scribes use in their charge: "By the prince of the demons He drives out demons." (Mark 3:22).
name: the prince of the demons
You must not eat from any tree in the garden
You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die

desc: As it is written in the prophets (Mark 1:2).
name: Isaiah the prophet

desc: in Job's speech: 'by His understanding He shattered Rahab' (Job 26:12)
name: Rahab

desc: the helpers of Rahab cower beneath Him
name: the helpers of Rahab cower beneath Him

desc:
'The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia. The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece' (Dan 8:20-21).

The only place in Scripture where a figure is decoded into named nations. Elsewhere Daniel keeps the key general — four beasts, four kings — and here it gives three proper names in two verses. The text records that the naming happens, and nothing about what follows from it.
name: the ram is Media and Persia, the goat is Greece

desc: 'Then Abraham looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns. So he went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.' (Gen 22:13). **'in place of his son' is the verse's own phrase**, and it is the whole of what the chapter says about the substitution.
name: the ram caught in a thicket

desc: The rams Jacob saw in the dream.
name: the males that are mating with the flock

desc: The food the LORD provides for the raven: 'Who provides food for the raven?'
name: the raven his food

desc: Burnt whole outside the camp, ashes kept for a water of separation. Everyone who handles it is made unclean by the rite that makes others clean -- the priest, the burner, and the man who gathers the ashes.
name: the red heifer

desc: 'I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.' (John 11:25), said to Martha at her brother's grave.
name: the resurrection

desc: 'a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen, who lived each day in joyous splendor' (Luke 16:19). He speaks eight verses and is never named, opposite a beggar who is — the reverse of Scripture's habit, where the poor go unnamed and the rich are recorded.
name: the rich man

desc: Those upon whom the eyes of the Lord are, who cry, who have many afflictions, and whom the wicked hate (Ps 34:15,17,19,21).
name: the righteous

desc:
'Aaron's staff, representing the house of Levi, had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds' (Num 17:8).

**The sign is a dead stick doing four things at once** -- budding, blooming and fruiting, stages that in a living tree are months apart. It settles a dispute about who may serve, and it is then kept 'as a sign for the rebellious' (17:10).
name: the rod of Aaron budded

desc: Dictated to Baruch, read to the king three or four leaves at a time, cut with a penknife and thrown on the hearth until all of it burned. Jeremiah dictates it again -- 'And many similar words were added to them'. The book that survives is longer because it was destroyed.
name: the roll Jehoiakim burned

desc: The roof of the house at Capernaum: "they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening".
name: the roof

desc: 'I, Jesus, have sent My angel to give you this testimony for the churches. I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star.' (Rev 22:16). Both directions at once -- the root David came from and the offspring that came from David -- which the verse states without resolving.
name: the root and the offspring of David

desc: the Sabeans swooped down and took them away
name: the Sabean raid

desc:
'The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.' (Ps 51:17), after 'You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it' (51:16).

**The word is kept and its content replaced**, which is a different move from Hosea 6:6 -- Hosea sets mercy against sacrifice, and this calls the broken spirit the sacrifice.
name: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit

desc:
'He came to Jesus at night and said, Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God.' (John 3:2).

John mentions the night three times, and the third is at the burial: 'Nicodemus, who had previously come to Jesus at night, also brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds' (19:39).

The detail is carried forward deliberately across sixteen chapters, and the last time it appears the man is doing something in daylight that no one else risked. The text does not comment on the change and does not let a reader miss it.
name: He came to Jesus at night

desc: we who have the same spirit of faith
name: the same spirit of faith

desc: One of two goats, chosen by lot. The other is killed; this one is kept alive, has the iniquities of Israel confessed over its head, and is led away into the wilderness. **It is the only offering in Leviticus that is not offered.**
name: the scapegoat

desc: The rod of a ruler, and in Esther the difference between living and dying: no one may approach the king unsummoned 'Only if the king extends the gold scepter may that person live'.
name: The scepter
The scepter will not depart from Judah

desc: The event of Abimelech's servants violently taking away the well (Gen 21:25).
name: the seizing of the well

desc:
'just as Eve was deceived by the serpent's cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ.' (2Cor 11:3).

Paul uses her as a warning about how persuasion works, not about who is to blame — the danger in the verse is a mind being moved off something simple. 1 Timothy 2:14 puts it differently: 'And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression'

Those two verses are read together and against each other, and Scripture holds both without reconciling them. Genesis 3:13 has her own account: 'The serpent deceived me ... I ate'.
name: the serpent deceived Eve

desc: the men with him
name: the men with Abraham's servant

desc: Seven men of honest report chosen by the disciples at Jerusalem and appointed by the apostles to oversee the daily distribution of food.
name: the seven

desc: The first seven cows in Pharaoh's dream, which came up from the river and were eaten by the lean cows.
name: seven cows, well-fed and sleek

desc: The seven good heads of grain in one stalk, devoured by the thin ears.
name: seven ears, full and good

desc: The seven lean cows that came after and ate up the fat cows, remaining ugly.
name: seven other cows, sickly, ugly, and thin

aka: the mystery of the seven stars
desc:
'This is the mystery of the seven stars you saw in My right hand and of the seven golden lampstands: The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.' (Rev 1:20).

**Revelation opens by decoding two of its own figures and then decodes almost nothing else for twenty-one chapters.** A reader who takes 1:20 as a promise that the book explains itself is being misled by its first page.

The word used for the giving of the key is *mystery*, which in this corpus means a thing disclosed rather than a thing withheld.
name: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches

desc: The seven thin ears that sprung up after the good and devoured them.
name: seven heads of grain, withered, thin, and scorched by the east wind

desc:
'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me' (Matt 25:40).

The longest judgment scene in the gospels, and every criterion in it is an act: meat, drink, lodging, clothing, visiting. Nothing is asked about belief on either side, and neither group knows what it did — both ask when.

This is the strongest works-side passage in the gospels. It carries no verdict: readers who hold that faith alone justifies read the acts as the evidence rather than the ground, and the passage does not say which.
name: the sheep and the goats

desc: The unnamed shepherds Jacob met at the well in the field near Haran.
name: the shepherds at the well

aka: the table of the Bread of the Presence
desc: Twelve cakes set out weekly and eaten only by the priests (Lev 24:5-9). Its whole narrative weight is that the rule was broken once and the breach was later cited with approval.
name: the Bread of the Presence

desc: The vessel Jesus taught from: "He got into a boat and sat in it" (Mark 4:1).
name: a boat

disambiguation:
The woman of the Song, and the only speaker in the book the text ever names: 'Come back, come back, O Shulammite! Come back, come back, that we may gaze upon you' (Song 6:13). She speaks in the first person from 1:5 -- 'I am dark, yet lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem' -- and hers are the seven comparisons of Song 5:11-15, describing the man: his head as most fine gold, his eyes as the eyes of doves, his legs as pillars of marble.

The graph does not identify her with anyone. Naming her the bride, the church, or a historical queen are all readings, and the book supplies none of them.
name: the Shulammite

desc: The only sign offered to a generation asking for one, and it is another prophet's three days. Luke 11:30 gives the comparison without the whale.
name: the sign of the prophet Jonah

desc: A seal carried on the person, standing for the authority of whoever owns it -- which is why Judah handing his over as a pledge is enough to convict him three months later, and why Jeremiah and Haggai can use one man's removal and another's appointment as the same figure run backwards.
name: seal

desc:
'This is the record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham:' (Matt 1:1) — the first line of the New Testament, and it names two ancestors and stops.

It is the crowd's word before it is a doctrine: 'Hosanna to the Son of David' (Matt 21:9), shouted at the entry into Jerusalem, and before that by two blind men who wanted mercy (9:27). It is what people call him when they want something, which is not how titles usually enter Scripture.

Matthew 22:42-45 has Jesus turn the title into a question — if David calls him Lord, how is he his son — and the text records that the question is asked and not what it settles.
disambiguation: the title, held apart from David himself; this record is for what the corpus does with the words
name: the Son of David

desc:
The complement, and the counts invert. Son of man is 74 of 76 narrative; his Son is 18 of 21 epistolary. The gospels and the letters have different vocabulary for the same figure, and a reader moving between them is reading two idioms rather than one.

What the letters do with it is argue. Romans 1:4 makes the resurrection the declaration — 'declared to be the Son of God with power ... by the resurrection from the dead'. Galatians 4:4 makes it a sending, into time and under law. Hebrews 1:5 makes it a quotation of Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14, applied to no angel.

Romans 8:32 is the one that reaches back: 'He who did not spare His own Son' is the language of Genesis 22:12, 'you have not withheld your only son', said to Abraham. Paul does not mention Abraham in the verse, and the text records the wording rather than the claim.
disambiguation: the title, held apart from Jesus himself, who carries it as an alias; this record is for what the corpus does with the words
name: the Son of God

desc:
**Seventy-six verses, and seventy-four are in the gospels.** It is the title the narrative uses and the letters do not: two occurrences outside Matthew, Mark, Luke, John and Acts in the whole New Testament.

It is also the one Jesus uses of himself, and almost nobody uses of him. Stephen at Acts 7:56 is the exception, and he is dying.

Its source is stated at Mark 14:62, which quotes it back at the high priest: 'you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven' -- Daniel 7:13, 'One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven'. **The answer that gets him condemned is a quotation.**
disambiguation: the title, held apart from Jesus himself, who carries it as an alias; this record is for what the corpus does with the words
name: the Son of Man

desc: Thrown at David twice, and then stuck in the ground at Saul's bolster while he sleeps, where David takes it instead of using it. Saul is leaning on it when he dies (2Sam 1:6).
name: the spear of Saul

desc:
'Now the earth was formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.' (Gen 1:2).

The Spirit is present in Scripture's second sentence, before anything is made and before anything is said.
name: the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters

desc:
'the Spirit of truth. The world cannot receive Him, because it neither sees Him nor knows Him.' (John 14:17).

The second title in the same discourse, and twice it is laid directly alongside the first — 'another Advocate ... the Spirit of truth' (14:16-17), 'When the Advocate comes ... the Spirit of truth' (15:26). One speaker, one evening, two names.

John 16:13 is the verse that draws a line Scripture rarely draws between the persons: 'He will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears'.
disambiguation: the title, held apart from the Holy Spirit, who carries it as an alias; this record is for what the corpus does with the words
name: the Spirit of truth

aka: The stone which the builders rejected
desc:
'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes' (Ps 118:22-23).

The most-quoted of the stone sayings. Jesus cites it against the chief priests (Matt 21:42, Mark 12:10), Peter before the council (Acts 4:11), and 1Pet 2:7 sets it beside Isa 28:16. Matt 21:42 quotes verse 23 with it, so the marvel is part of what is repeated.
name: The stone the builders rejected
the narrow gate and the narrow way

desc: Foreign wives taken by men of the return and put away. The text names them only as a class and never individually.
disambiguation: unnamed; recorded as a class because Ezra 10 speaks of 'strange wives' throughout and never distinguishes one from another. A wife per man would invent a distinction the chapter withholds.
name: the strange wives

desc: one people will be stronger than the other.
name: the stronger people

desc:
'I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us.' (Rom 8:18).

**A comparison the verse declines to make**, which is the point of it: the two are said to be incommensurable rather than weighed.
name: our present sufferings

desc:
'I will make with you an everlasting covenant-My loving devotion promised to David.' (Isa 55:3).

**The mercies are David's and the covenant is with somebody else** -- Isaiah offers what was promised to one man to whoever will incline their ear. Paul reads it as fulfilled in the resurrection: 'never to see decay. As He has said: I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David.' (Acts 13:34).
name: My loving devotion promised to David

aka: the sword of Goliath the Philistine
desc: Taken off the body David had just killed with a stone, and kept at Nob wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. When David arrives unarmed and asks what weapons are there, the priest offers this one, and David answers 'There is none like it; give it to me.' Doeg reports the transaction and it is part of what gets the priests of Nob killed.
name: the sword of Goliath

desc: The synagogue Jesus enters again in Mark 3:1: "Once again Jesus entered the synagogue". The verse does not name the town.
name: the synagogue

desc:
'In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David.' (Amos 9:11).

James quotes it at the Jerusalem council to settle an argument about Gentiles (Acts 15:16), which is a striking use: a promise about rebuilding a Jewish ruin, produced as the reason for not burdening non-Jews. The text records the quotation and the argument it was used in, and stops there.
name: tent of David

desc: "He was there in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals" -- the forty days Jesus spent in the wilderness.
name: the temptation in the wilderness

desc: the thing as it is, i.e., the truth, in Job's question
name: sound insight

desc: If you do this one thing for me
name: this one thing

desc: The thing Job says he greatly feared, which then came upon him.
name: the thing I feared

desc:
'So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.' (2Cor 4:18).

**The same phrase Hebrews uses to define faith.** Heb 11:1 calls faith 'the certainty of what we do not see'; here the things not seen are given a property -- they are the lasting ones -- and the seen are the temporary ones. Two writers, one phrase, and neither cites the other.

What it is attached to matters as much. It closes an argument about affliction (v17) and comes one chapter before 'For we walk by faith, not by sight' (2Cor 5:7), which is the same contrast turned into a way of going about.
name: what is unseen is eternal

desc: what is seen is temporary
name: what is seen is temporary

desc:
'So they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said to me, Throw it to the potter' (Zech 11:12-13), quoted at Matt 27:9-10.

Matthew attributes it to Jeremiah. 'Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled' — and the silver, the price, and the potter are all in Zechariah, not in Jeremiah. Jeremiah has a potter (18:1-6) and a field bought for silver (32:6-9), which is as close as Scripture comes.

Held as it stands, with both books cited, because the discrepancy is in the text and the text's job is to show it rather than to pick a side. The same principle Scripture's own scribes worked by: copy what is there.
name: the thirty pieces of silver

desc:
The places Scripture names the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in one breath.

'baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matt 28:19). 'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit' (2Cor 13:14).

And 1 John 5:7: 'For there are three that testify' This is the most explicit statement of the three in Scripture and it is the one whose text is disputed. The clause is known as the Johannine Comma and is absent from the early Greek manuscripts. The following verse reads 'the Spirit, the water, and the blood'.

It is recorded here because leaving out a verse readers will look for is its own kind of claim, and it carries its textual status because a proof text without one would discredit every other citation.
name: the three named together

desc: The unnamed wives of Shem, Ham, and Japheth; 'and the three wives of his sons' (Gen 7:13).
name: the three wives of his sons

desc:
'He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore.' (Isa 9:7).

A phrase Scripture keeps using long after the throne is gone. 2 Samuel 7:16 promises it; Isaiah and Jeremiah use it while the monarchy is failing or finished; Gabriel uses it of an unborn child 'in the time of Herod king of Judea' (Luke 1:5) — 'The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David' (Luke 1:32).

What the phrase refers to after the last king in Jerusalem is taken to Babylon (2 Kgs 25:7) is the question, and the text does not answer it.
name: the throne of David

desc: A tenth. Older than the law -- Abram pays it to Melchizedek in Genesis 14 and Jacob vows it at Bethel -- and Hebrews 7 argues from that priority, that Levi 'paid the tenth through Abraham' while still in his ancestor's loins.
name: the tithe

desc: the socket of Jacob's hip was struck near that tendon (Gen 32:32)
name: the touching of Jacob's thigh

desc: He hides it again before buying the field, and the parable does not remark on that.
name: the treasure hid in a field

desc: Asked for, produced by someone else, and turned into a question about whose face is on it. The coin does the argument rather than the answer does.
name: the tribute penny

desc:
'The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.' (John 1:9).

The adjective does work: a true light implies others. It is the same claim John 8:12 puts in the first person, 'I am the light of the world', and here it is made about him rather than by him.
name: the true Light

desc: Claimed at John 15:1, with the Father as the keeper of the vineyard.
name: the true vine

desc:
'The three companies blew their horns and shattered their jars. Holding the torches in their left hands' (Judg 7:20).

**Three hundred men, and no weapon in the account of the attack.** Each carries a trumpet in one hand and a lamp in the other, which leaves nothing to fight with, and the chapter has already explained why the army was reduced from thirty-two thousand: 'lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, My own hand has saved me' (7:2).
name: the trumpets, and the pitchers, and the lamps

desc: Bilhah and Zilpah, called 'the two handmaids' in Gen 33:1.
name: the two maidservants

desc: two of his young men who went with Abraham and Isaac
name: the two young men
the unjust
source: declared to complete relations the batch asserts

desc: Put inside the breastplate of judgment; Scripture never says what they were or how they worked, and every later mention is about asking. Joshua is to be answered through them (Num 27:21); Saul is not answered by them (1Sam 28:6); the returned exiles suspend a question until a priest holding them appears (Ezra 2:63).
name: the Urim and Thummim

desc:
'We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away.' (2Cor 3:13).

**Paul takes an object out of the Exodus narrative and makes it a figure for reading.** The veil moves from Moses's face to the hearers' minds within two verses -- 'to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted' (3:14) -- and then becomes something removable: 'But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away' (3:16).

*Three different things wear it in four verses*, and the passage never says it has changed the subject.
name: the veil over his face

desc:
'A voice of one calling: Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness' (Isa 40:3).

**All four gospels apply it to John, and John applies it to himself.** Asked who he is, he answers with the verse and nothing else: 'I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness' (John 1:23). It is the rare case where the identification is made by the person identified.
name: A voice of one calling in the wilderness

desc:
'For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.' (Rom 6:23).

**Wages against gift, and the pairing is the argument.** One is earned and the other is not, and the verse sets the two economies in the same sentence rather than arguing from one to the other.
name: the wages of sin is death

desc: Two halves that do not match on purpose: wages against gift, earned against given.
name: the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life

desc:
'He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.' (Titus 3:5).

**Another not-X-but-Y, and the X being denied is righteousness.**
name: the washing of new birth

desc:
'The waters you saw, where the prostitute was seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues' (Rev 17:15).

Three keys are given in one chapter and they are the densest run of self-interpretation in the book: the seven heads are seven mountains (17:9), the waters are peoples (17:15), and the woman is that great city (17:18).

What the great city is, the chapter does not say. It gives a name written on a forehead — 'MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT' (17:5) — and stops.
name: the waters which you saw are peoples

desc: 'I am the way and the truth and the life' (John 14:6).
name: the way

desc: the road to Ephrath, where Rachel died and was buried, which is Bethlehem (Gen 35:18-19)
name: the way to Ephrath

desc: Those with weak hands and feeble knees, strengthened by Job.

desc: all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.
name: the wells which Abraham's servants dug

desc:
'Put on the full armor of God' (Eph 6:11), and six pieces follow, each named with what it stands for.

A declared list, and unusually the passage supplies its own key. Elsewhere a figure is left to the reader; here every item is glossed in the same clause that introduces it — the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, 'which is the word of God' (6:17).

It is stitched from Isaiah. The breastplate and helmet come from Isaiah 59:17 as a pair, and the belt from Isaiah 11:5 with the concepts exchanged. The text does not say so, and a reader who reads the two together will see it.
name: the full armor of God

desc:
'We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time.' (Rom 8:22).

Four verses whose subject is not people. The creature waits (v19), was subjected to futility, not by its own will (v20), and is to be delivered into 'the glorious freedom of the children of God' (v21) -- its release tied to theirs. This is the first of three groanings in the chapter: creation (v22), believers (v23), and the Spirit (v26).
name: the whole creation has been groaning

desc: Job 38:13 'shake the wicked out of it'; Job 38:15 'Light is withheld from the wicked'.

name: A wicked man

desc: The people Job describes who spend their days in wealth, go down to the grave, and are likened to stubble and chaff.
name: the wicked people

desc: The text prices them exactly — 'two small copper coins, which amounted to a small fraction of a denarius' — and then says she cast in more than all the rest, which only works because the sum is stated.
name: the widow's two mites

desc: "whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother".
name: the will of God
the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving

desc:
'He sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt, and all the wise men thereof ... but there was none that could interpret them unto Pharaoh' (Gen 41:8).

The same scene happens twice, a thousand years and an empire apart, and neither text mentions the other. A foreign king is troubled by a dream; the professionals of the court are summoned and fail; a Hebrew captive is produced, disclaims the ability himself, credits God, interprets, and is promoted to rule over the province.

Daniel 2:27-28 is almost a restatement of Genesis 41:16: 'No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires. But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries'.

This is a shape rather than a citation. No verse joins the two episodes.
name: the magicians could not show the king

desc: 'and His name is The Word of God' (Rev 19:13); 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). A name given to a person, which is a different thing from what God speaks; the question of how they are related is not settled in the text.
disambiguation: a name for Christ. Distinct from `word_of_god`, which is what God speaks -- the thing that comes to the prophets and is called a sword at Eph 6:17.
name: The Word of God

desc:
'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.' (John 1:14).

**The verse that closes the loop on v1 and v3.** The Word that was in the beginning and by whom all things were made is now made -- the same verb the making of v3 uses, turned on the maker.

v17 names him for the first time in the chapter: 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.' Fourteen verses of Word, light and life, and then a name.
name: The Word became flesh

desc: What the brothers told their father: 'we relayed your words to him'
name: the words of my lord

desc: A real yoke on a real neck, worn through two chapters as a sign to the kings. Hananiah breaks it off him and says God will break Babylon's the same way; Jeremiah is sent back to say the wooden yoke has been replaced with one of iron. Held apart from the figure for the reason Gideon's ephod is held apart from Aaron's: this one is an object somebody made.
name: the yoke Jeremiah wore

desc: The young children who despised Job and spoke against him.
name: little boys

name: the young man Lamech said he slew

name: they that were with him

desc:
'Therefore, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,' (Luke 1:3), and 'In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote' (Acts 1:1).

Two verses in all of Scripture, and they are the opening lines of two of its books. Most excellent is the same form of address Paul uses to a Roman governor — 'most excellent Festus' (Acts 26:25), 'most excellent Felix' (Acts 23:26) — which is as much as the text gives about who he was.

The asymmetry is the interesting part and it runs the opposite way from the letters. Luke names his reader and never names himself. He writes 'it seemed good also to me' and 'The first book I wrote' and stops there. Paul opens thirteen letters with his own name and this writer opens two books with somebody else's.

The text names a person, twice addressed, by someone unnamed; naming Luke would be importing a tradition the text never states.
disambiguation: the addressee of Luke and Acts; the only person the corpus names as the recipient of a gospel
name: Theophilus

desc:
'My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb' (Judg 16:17).

The strength is attached to a vow rather than to the hair, and the vow was made for him before he was born (13:5). What the hair does is keep the vow visible.

The verse a reader usually misses is the next one about waking: 'he did not know that the LORD had departed from him' (16:20). The text puts the loss somewhere other than the haircut.
name: My hair has never been cut

desc:
'So God made the expanse and separated the waters beneath it from the waters above. And it was so.' (Gen 1:7).

The word therefore appears throughout Genesis.
name: therefore

desc:
'These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth.' (Dan 7:17).

**Daniel asks for the interpretation inside his own vision** -- 'I approached one of those who were standing there, and I asked him the true meaning of all this' (7:16) -- which is unusual: the seer is a character who does not understand what he is seeing.

The key is given and kept general. Four beasts, four kings, and no kingdom named.
name: These four great beasts are four kings

desc:
'They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.' (Ps 22:18), quoted at Matt 27:35.

The last of Matthew's fulfilment citations and the smallest detail any of them cover -- not a birth, a place, or a ministry, but what soldiers did with clothing. Psalm 22 opens with the words spoken from the cross at Matt 27:46.
name: They divide my garments among them

name: They profess to know God

desc:
'those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint.' (Isa 40:31).

**The three clauses descend rather than climb** -- mount up, run, walk -- and the promise attached to each gets smaller and more ordinary. It ends at not fainting while walking.
name: they shall renew their strength

'Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent.' (John 17:3).

The one place the text defines the phrase, and it defines it as knowing rather than lasting. It is also a verse cited on both sides of arguments about the Son's relation to the Father, because of what it puts beside the only true God.
name: this is eternal life

desc:
'You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.' (Ps 23:5).

The verse where the psalm changes figure. Four verses of shepherd and sheep, and then a table, a guest, and a host attending to him — in front of the enemies rather than away from them.

The anointing here is hospitality, not commission. That distinction is the whole of why this verse sits next to 1Sam 16:13 in the text and is not the same thing: both have the word and the oil, and only one has the Spirit that follows.
name: You anoint my head with oil

desc:
'Then Nathan said to David, You are that man!' (2Sam 12:7).

The rebuke arrives after the verdict, and the verdict is David's own. Nathan tells a story about a rich man taking a poor man's one ewe lamb (12:3); David is 'greatly kindled' and pronounces sentence; and then four words turn the sentence round on him.

It is the clearest demonstration in Scripture of what a parable is for. The hearer is made to judge the case before he knows he is in it, and by then he cannot un-judge it.
name: You are that man

desc:
'You are that head of gold.' (Dan 2:38).

Daniel names the head and stops; the silver, brass and iron are given successors without names, and the text does not supply the names readers have proposed for them since.

The stone is the part the passage spends most on: 'cut out without hands' (2:34), and it breaks the image rather than joining it. What it is said to be is a kingdom (2:44), and what it is not said to be is anybody.
name: You are that head of gold

desc: "know that you are still alive"
name: you are still alive

desc:
'But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.' (Matt 2:6), citing Mic 5:2.

It is put in the mouths of the chief priests and scribes, answering Herod's question about where the Christ was to be born (Matt 2:4-5). The text has the establishment locate him correctly and take no action on it.

Micah says 'who are small among the clans of Judah'; Matthew has 'are by no means least among the rulers of Judah'. The sense is inverted and the text does not remark on it.
name: you Bethlehem

desc:
'And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.' (Deut 6:5).

Quoted three times in the gospels and the list is different every time.

    Deut 6:5     heart, soul, might
    Matt 22:37   heart, soul, mind
    Mark 12:30   heart, soul, mind, strength
    Luke 10:27   heart, soul, strength, mind

Deuteronomy gives three and the last is might. Matthew gives three and the last is mind. Mark gives four. Luke gives the same four in a different order. No two agree, and none of the gospels remarks on the difference or on departing from the verse being quoted.
name: you shall love the LORD your God

desc:
'love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.' (Lev 19:18).

The second of the two, and unlike the first it is quoted the same way every time -- Matt 22:39, Mark 12:31 and Luke 10:27 all give it word for word.

**Both commandments come out of the law.** Jesus answers a question about which commandment is greatest by quoting Deuteronomy and Leviticus rather than by adding anything, and Matt 22:40 says what that is for: 'All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.'
name: love your neighbor as yourself

desc: A line of Mosaic livestock law, quoted twice by Paul to argue that those who preach should be paid -- and at 1Cor 9:9 he puts the objection himself: 'Is it about oxen that God is concerned?' Held as one record because both letters quote it as scripture rather than alluding to it.
name: Do not muzzle an ox

desc:
'For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich.' (2Cor 8:9).

The same exchange as 2Cor 5:21 with wealth in place of righteousness, and here Paul names what he is describing: he calls it grace, in the clause before the exchange itself.
name: though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor

desc:
'If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal.' (1Cor 13:1).

**Three verses that subtract.** Tongues, prophecy, all mysteries, all knowledge, faith enough to move mountains, everything given to the poor, the body burned -- each granted in full and then cancelled by the same clause.

It sits immediately after the list of the gifts of the Spirit and before the ranking at 13:13, and it is doing the same work as both: *this one is not like the others.*
name: but have not love, I am nothing

Matthew drops the rejoicing and the shouting and keeps the king, the meekness and the animal. It is the citation attached to the entry into Jerusalem, and the only one in the sweep whose fulfilment the crowd is watching happen.
name: your King comes to you

desc:
'Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed.' (Gen 32:28).

A name given for having won a fight the text does not explain. The opponent is called a man in 32:24, and Jacob calls the place Peniel 'I have seen God face to face' (32:30). Hosea 12:4 calls the same opponent an angel.

Three descriptions of one wrestler, none of them reconciled. And the name given becomes the name of a nation, which is the largest consequence any naming in the text has.
name: Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel

desc: The LORD's rod and staff comfort the psalmist.
name: your rod and your staff they comfort me

name: your wickedness great

desc:
'Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.' (Ps 119:105).

A lamp reaches as far as the next step and a light shows the way ahead. Two figures in one verse, at two distances, and the same thing is both.

It belongs with the other path verses because it answers the same question differently. Prov 3:6 has him direct the path, Ps 23:3 has him lead along it, Ps 25:4 asks to be taught it — here nothing is said about being led at all. What is given is enough light to walk by.
name: Your word is a lamp to my feet
