desc:
'And in the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.' (Gen 2:9).

Named four times, all in two chapters, and never again. The text that returns to the tree of life at its last page does not mention this one after Genesis 3.

The two are introduced in the same sentence and stand in the same place — 'in the middle of the garden' is said of the tree of life at 2:9 and of the forbidden tree by Eve at 3:3. Which tree is in the midst is a question the text creates and does not answer.

Genesis 3:22 is where they meet: having eaten of the one, the man must be kept from the other.
name: the tree of the knowledge of good and evil

desc:
Eleven verses, and they fall in three places with nothing in between: Genesis, Proverbs, Revelation.

It stands in the middle of the garden (Gen 2:9), and the garden is shut with cherubim "to guard the way to the tree of life" (3:24). It reappears at the very end -- "On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit" (Rev 22:2) -- and the way is opened again: "To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God" (Rev 2:7); "Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life" (22:14). A share in it can also be taken away (22:19).

Whether the two are one tree is not stated. Revelation 2:7 places it "in the Paradise of God", and paradise (παράδεισος) is the Septuagint's word for the garden of Genesis 2 -- which is as close as the text comes.

In between, Proverbs uses it four times as a comparison and never twice for the same thing: wisdom (3:18), the fruit of the righteous (11:30), a desire fulfilled (13:12), and a soothing tongue (15:4). A figure this fixed at both ends is remarkably loose in the middle.
name: the tree of life

'As it is written: For Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.' (Rom 8:36), quoting Ps 44:22.

Placed in the middle of the list of things that cannot separate, and the only item Paul supports from scripture. The psalm is a complaint and he cites it without softening it, then answers it in the next verse rather than denying it.
name: we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered

desc:
'And now we proclaim to you the good news: What God promised our fathers He has fulfilled for us, their children, by raising up Jesus' (Acts 13:32-33).

The glad tidings are given as a promise kept rather than as news. What is announced is not that something has begun but that something long-standing has been completed, and the hearers are named as the children of the people it was made to.

The chapter around it walks the history — Egypt, the wilderness, the judges, Samuel, Saul, David — and then quotes Ps 2:7, Isa 55:3, Ps 16:10 and Hab 1:5 to read it forward.
name: we proclaim to you the good news

desc:
'In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace' (Eph 1:7).

**A commercial figure with the price named in the same clause.** Job 19:25 uses the older sense the word carries in the law -- a kinsman who buys back what was lost: 'But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth'.
name: we have redemption through his blood

desc:
'For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct Him?” But we have the mind of Christ.' (1Cor 2:16).

**A rhetorical question from Isaiah 40:13 answered in a way the original does not invite.** The question expects nobody; the reply claims something.
name: we have the mind of Christ

desc:
'For we walk by faith, not by sight' (2Cor 5:7).

Here it is not a definition or a property but a manner of going — what is done rather than what is believed.
name: we walk by faith, not by sight

desc: The answer the father is to say unto his son (Deut 6:21).
name: “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.

desc:
'My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.' (2Cor 12:9).

Rare as a noun — seven verses — and load-bearing where it appears. The text does not treat it as a state to be escaped: strength is perfected in it (2Cor 12:9), the Spirit helps it (Rom 8:26), the weak things are chosen (1Cor 1:27), and the high priest is touched with the feeling of it (Heb 4:15).

It is the one place Paul reports being refused. He asked three times for the thorn to be removed (2Cor 12:8) and was told no, with a reason.
name: weakness

desc: 'We will find all manner of precious goods; we will fill our houses with plunder.' (Prov 1:13).
name: wealth

desc:
'He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?' (Mic 6:8).

**A declared list of three**, and it arrives as the answer to a question about sacrifices -- the verses before it offer burnt offerings, thousands of rams, and a firstborn child.
name: what does the LORD require of you

desc:
'Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.' (Acts 10:15), said three times to a sheet let down from heaven full of animals.

Peter draws the conclusion himself and it is not about food: 'God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean' (10:28). The vision is about beasts and the application is about people, and the text makes the move explicitly rather than leaving it to a reader.
name: Do not call anything impure that God has made clean

desc:
'What is truth?' Pilate asked. And having said this, he went out again' (John 18:38).

He does not wait for an answer. The verse puts the question and the leaving in one sentence, and the text does not say whether it was asked seriously.

The other thing recorded of him is a gesture: 'he took water and washed his hands before the crowd. "I am innocent of this man's blood," he said.' (Matt 27:24) — a ritual of dissociation performed by the man with the authority to stop it.
name: what is truth?

desc: The son's question quoted in Deut 6:20.
name: “What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the LORD our God has commanded you?”

desc:
'Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake: For when I am weak, then I am strong' (2Cor 12:10).

Stated as a conclusion drawn from v9 rather than as a paradox offered for its own sake -- 'therefore'. The list before it is of circumstances, not virtues.
name: when I am weak, then I am strong

desc: Quote: 'never to return'
name: never to return

desc:
'The fire and the wood are here,' said Isaac, 'but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?' (Gen 22:7) — the only thing Isaac says in the whole episode, and it is a question about what is missing.

The answer given is 'God Himself will provide the lamb' (22:8), and what is actually provided six verses later is a ram (22:13). The text does not comment on the difference between the answer and the provision, and readers have made a great deal of it.
name: where is the lamb for the burnt offering

desc:
'Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding.' (Job 38:4), spoken 'out of the whirlwind' (38:1).

**The answer to thirty-five chapters of argument is four chapters of questions, and none of them is about the argument.** Job's complaint is never addressed; what he is given instead is an inventory of things he did not make and cannot do.

His reply concedes the form rather than the content: 'Surely I spoke of things I did not understand' (42:3).
name: Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth

desc: the white stripes Jacob peeled in the rods
name: white inner wood

desc:
'Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.' (Ruth 1:16).

**Said by a Moabite to her mother-in-law**, which is worth holding on to, because it is read at weddings and it is not addressed to a husband. What is being promised is a change of people and of God, by someone with no obligation left to anybody.
name: wherever you go, I will go

desc:
'Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?' (Rom 8:35).

Seven candidates in v35, then ten more in v38-39 -- death, life, angels, principalities, powers, things present, things to come, height, depth, and 'any other creature', which closes the list by refusing to be one. The answer is never given as a name; it is given as an exhaustion of names.
name: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ

desc:
'And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.' (Rom 8:30).

Four links, each taking up the last word of the one before, and every verb in the past tense including the final one. v29 supplies what the predestining is toward: 'to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers.'
name: those He predestined, He also called

desc:
'And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved' (Joel 2:32), quoted at Acts 2:21 by Peter at Pentecost and again at Rom 10:13.

**Both New Testament quotations change the last word.** Joel says delivered; Acts and Romans say saved. Recorded rather than reconciled -- it is the same promise arriving with a different ending twice, by two writers, from one source.
name: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD

desc:
'For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it' (Mark 8:35).

Four times in the gospels, and a fifth in different words. Matt 16:25, Mark 8:35 and Luke 9:24 give it almost identically; Luke 17:33 repeats it in a wholly different setting, with no cross mentioned; John 12:25 recasts it as loving and hating one's life. Few sayings in the gospels are attested this often.

In Matthew, Mark and Luke 9 it follows immediately on taking up a cross (Mark 8:34). In John it follows immediately on a seed dying to bear fruit (John 12:24). The saying itself never explains the paradox — it states it, four times, and leaves the two placements to say what it is for.
name: whoever wants to save his life will lose it

desc: 212 verses, and most of them mean the drink. Jesus made it from water at Cana, 'the beginning of miracles' (John 2:9-11); Proverbs warns against it -- 'Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler' (Prov 20:1) -- and Paul tells Timothy to use a little for his stomach's sake (1Tim 5:23). Ephesians 5:18 sets it against the Spirit rather than against water: 'Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit'.
disambiguation: the drink. Distinct from the image `wine`, which carries the verses where it is a figure -- the wine of wrath -- and from the cup, which is what the gospels put in Jesus' hand at the last supper.
name: wine

desc: Eliphaz asks, 'why do your eyes flash.'
name: flash

desc: James 1:5 is the verse that tells a reader what to do rather than what to think: 'Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault.' James 3:17 then describes what arrives — first pure, then peaceable, gentle, accommodating. Set against that, 1 Corinthians 3:19 says the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight, and 1:24 calls Christ the wisdom of God, so the word is doing two jobs and Scripture marks which is which.
disambiguation: the word the corpus makes statements about; distinct from `image_wisdom`, the personified figure who cries in the streets (Prov 1:20) and builds her house (Prov 9:1)
name: wisdom

desc:
'With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps. With the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men.' (Judg 15:16).

It is a couplet, and he is making a joke — the Hebrew puns on the word for donkey and the word for heap, which the translation cannot carry. The very next thing that happens is that he is thirsty and complains to God about it (15:18).
name: With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps

desc:
'So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.' (Rom 7:25).

**The last sentence of the chapter, and the one Rom 8:2 picks up.** It ends the argument where it began -- divided, serving both -- after the thanksgiving rather than before it, which is why the chapter does not resolve on the note it was heading for.

Rom 8:1 opens with 'therefore' and this is what it points back at. Rom 8:2 then repeats 'the law of sin' from this verse word for word and puts a different law against it.
name: with my mind I serve the law of God

desc:
'He will testify about Me ... And you also must testify' (John 15:26-27).

John 15:26-27 has the Spirit testify and the disciples bear witness. Where it appears it is rarely solitary. The Spirit bears witness with our spirit (Rom 8:16); the Spirit bears witness because the Spirit is truth (1John 5:6); the disciples are to be witnesses after receiving power (Acts 1:8). Heb 11:1 uses the noun for something else again — faith as 'the certainty of what we do not see'.
name: witness

desc: What God says, and in 261 verses a thing that comes to somebody: 'the word of the LORD came to' Abram, Samuel, Nathan, Elijah, Jonah. 47 more say 'the word of God'. The text treats it as an actor — it comes, it is heard, it is kept, it endures (Isa 40:8), it is made of none effect by tradition (Mark 7:13).
disambiguation: what God speaks. Distinct from The Word of God as a name for Christ (Rev 19:13, John 1:1), which is a title and is kept separate.
name: the word of God

desc:
'not by works, so that no one can boast.' (Eph 2:9). 'For we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works' (Eph 2:10).

One word, and the text does not change it. Works of the law (Gal 2:16, Rom 9:32), works of the flesh (Gal 5:19), good works (Eph 2:10) — the qualifier moves and the noun does not. Eph 2:9 and 2:10 use it bare, consecutively, once to exclude and once to command.
name: works

desc: not by the righteous deeds we had done
name: righteous deeds

desc:
'The acts of the flesh are obvious:' (Gal 5:19), and seventeen follow across three verses.

The counterpart, and the text builds it as one: two lists in one paragraph, seventeen against nine, and Galatians 5:17 sits between them saying what the relation is — 'the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other'. The text itself states the opposition, which is rare.

The two lists are not built alike, though, and the asymmetry is in the text. The works close with 'and such like' (5:21) — explicitly open-ended. The fruit closes with 'Against such things there is no law'. One list says there are more; the other says the law has nothing to say about these.
name: The acts of the flesh

desc:
'know that a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ' (Gal 2:16).

A phrase used in five verses — Rom 9:32, Gal 2:16, Gal 3:2, Gal 3:5, Gal 3:10 — and twice more as 'works of the law' (Rom 3:20, Rom 3:28), always set against faith and never on its own.
disambiguation: the law-keeping Paul sets against faith, not the conduct of Gal 5:19-21. Galatians uses 'works' for both and means different things by them: works of the law are things done in obedience that cannot justify, works of the flesh are things done that the Spirit is contrary to. Distinct from [[works_of_the_flesh]]
name: works of the law

Gen 1:1 is not this name. The creation account opens with Elohim and the LORD God appears first at Gen 2:4.

desc:
'You snakes! You brood of vipers! How will you escape the sentence of hell?' (Matt 23:33).

**The verse that puts the two words together.** John calls the Pharisees and Sadducees a generation of vipers at Matt 3:7 and the word serpent is nowhere near it; Jesus uses the same address at Matt 12:34 and again here, and here alone he sets serpents beside it.

So a reader going from the vipers of Matt 3:7 to the serpent of Genesis 3 travels through Matthew rather than through Eden. Nothing in Matt 3:7 reaches back to the garden; Matt 23:33 is what joins the vocabularies, and it joins them without explaining either.
name: You snakes! You brood of vipers!

desc:
'As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this-to preserve the lives of many people.' (Gen 50:20).

**Both halves are asserted and neither is withdrawn.** The brothers meant evil; it is not reinterpreted as something else. What is added is a second intention running through the same events, and the verse holds the two without explaining how they fit.

He says a version of it twice, the first time much earlier and more gently: 'Now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you' (45:5).
name: what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good

desc:
'In the same way, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.' (Matt 5:16), and the phrase repeats through Matthew in that exact shape.

Matthew's Father is the hearers' Father, and John's is the Son's, and the difference is not incidental: it is the possessive, and it is consistent across both books. Matthew says your Father and your heavenly Father to a crowd; John has Jesus say my Father more than thirty times.

What is claimed of him here is domestic and attentive rather than sovereign — he sees in secret (6:4), knows what is needed before he is asked (6:8), feeds birds (6:26), notices a sparrow fall (10:29), and is unwilling that one little one should perish (18:14).
name: your Father in heaven
